## Two Types of Constants

{% raw %}

### *Thursday, March 25, 2021*

Here’s my hypothesis: some constants are built into the math, like Euler’s Constant $e$, while others are specific to our universe and simply have Aligned with the Miracles, such as $\pi$ and the Feigenbaum Constants, (and the gravitational constant and the planck speed – and the list continues\!) By the way, this isn’t a new idea for me – I’ve been thinking about this constant thing for years.   
On the side of my refrigerator, for example, is the equation: ${G}_{l}=Ul+{G}_{\oplus }$, which essentially theorizes what the equation of a universe’s gravitational constant is based upon its cross sectional “distance” to our universe in some fifth dimension. Perhaps this fifth dimension is a dimension of space, a dimension of time, or something new entirely, but it would take the form of the $l$. $U$ is the multiverse – gravitational constant, which is basically the slope, (assuming this whole system is linear, of course). ${G}_{\oplus }$ is our universe’s gravitational constant, and ${G}_{l}$ is the gravitational constant at cross sectional “distance” $l$ from us\!  
As for the constants, the *Universe Dependent Constants* like $\pi$ and $c$ vary based on which universe we’re talking about, and they shift continuously as we traverse the dimension separating the universes. But, I think, as looking at the neatness of its continued fraction, $e$ is probably just built into the system, and is instead *Universe Independent*. Don’t even put it in the same category as something like $\pi$ or $G$, just because it is a feature of the land rather than a boat on the river so to speak.  
How’s about I list where I think some of these constants are?

| UNIVERSE | MATH |
| :---- | :---- |
| $\pi$, Pi | $e$, Euler’s Number |
| $\delta$, Feigenbaum Constant | $\varphi$, Golden Ratio |
| $G$, The Newtonian Gravitational Constant | $\sqrt{2}$, The Square Root of Two |
| $c$, The Planck Speed | $1$, Wau |

As for the ones I don’t know where to sort as of now: *The Euler–Mascheroni constant*, *Apéry's constant*, and others like that.   
What about $i$, the square root of negative one? Is it dependent on our universe, or is it built into the framework of mathematics on a more fundamental level? Well, it can be written as $\sqrt{-1}$, which suggests that it is independent, (to an extent – I mean, I could easily see this assumption getting thrown out once we learn more about the nature of the complex plane and the number line’s infinity/finite relation to complex numbers…), but also it can be written like this: $\frac{ln\left({-1}\right)}{\pi }$, which you may notice involves a universe constant, $\pi$, and a math one, $e$. Conversely to the last counterargument: maybe, however, the very nature of taking a natural logarithm transcends this math realm, and “cancels out” the $\pi$’s $\pi$ness. Maybe this has something to do with the trouble of taking a logarithm of something physical like a meter or a year? If we can find the inner meaning behind this, will we be that much closer to unlocking my $j$constant’s nature???  
Also note, a possible edit is that these fundamental constants can only be dimensionless, and therefore something like $G$ or $c$ is in fact just a function of one or several more fundamental constants like *The Fine Structure Constant*.

## The Arrow of Time

I figured I would use this space to jot down some of my ideas on time. At a glance, my take on the theory of everything is that we’re going to figure out these two things: 1\) the master equation, and 2\) the fundamental constants. If you feed these fundamental constants into that master equation, well, that is what we call the universe. The multiverse, on the other hand, is all possible permutations of this concept, which is spread out over a multidimensional space, all using a form of this same overarching equation, just with different fundamental constants based upon different coordinates in the multiverse. I originally wrote about this idea [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1s2zvExEYp1PSNCAMoMfDiTp9GalY_OgIzR2NO6b9mBA/edit?usp=sharing). I also added a bit more to it [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.73lryre2vdts), in which I included the concept of a time-object which is fueling these constants of our universe, sort of like tidal-forces on Earth.  
Another idea I had, was what if we threw out the distinction between space and time altogether, and just imagined that these were in fact two forms of the same kind of quantity, which I will refer to here as *Ambul*. What we have come to call time, is just another Ambul, but instead measuring our flow through this higher dimensional Ambul space. So, rather than thinking of it like three dimensions of space and one dimension of time, let’s call it four dimensions of Ambul. The reason something like a meter and a second are distinct, is not because of some inherent difference in quantity, but rather because we do not yet know enough about the multiverse to describe a second in terms of a meter.  
Obviously, our location in Ambul space from one second to the next is different, and so we have defined a second as that Ambul displacement perpendicular to our direction of travel. This also implies that the universe one Ambul behind us is still totally just as valid as the one we are currently occupying, it’s just that we are now away from it. In other words, every moment exists at once just as every permutation does. It is all laid out in this crazy grid somewhere, and what we have falsely come to think of as progress is simply the displacement in this Ambul space – but specifically in this single orientation of “time”.  
So the question is, why are we moving in this specified direction through Amul space?  
Actually, as a really young child – maybe first grade or so, I had this crazy thought experiment – what if the Earth kept on changing into different Earths at every instant, as if there were a trillion Earths all in a line and we just kept teleporting consciousness from one to the next. Frankly, that’s not too different than this hypothesis I’m proposing now.   
What is the nature of our orientation to this time object? Cartesian? Circular? Fractal? A combination of the three? Something else entirely?  
Also, we know without a doubt here that we are three dimensional beings, one for each “dimension of space” – and time is one of these abstract, out of reach dimensions like the ones governing the fundamental constants. We only just happen to be in on time because we can chart its effects on entropy.  
And, maybe this can explain quantum fluctuations once I adapt it more. I mean, maybe they act as a kind of error sifting as our “arrow of time orientations” shifts ever so slightly here and there. Or, maybe they represent where everything doesn’t quite line up, since time passes at different rates at different places after all. In this case, picture the universe flowing through with certain bits going at different speeds, and thus we’re all sprawled out like a waving flag instead of going like some perfect rectangle.  
Another question to ask is why entropy and time line up so well. We’ve become so accustomed to entropy increasing as members of the universe, that when you watch a backwards playing video of a vase un-smashing, that it just looks completely off to you. I mean, maybe this is the criteria of time in a way. That might suggest that entropy is like a concrete axis in Ambul Space that time is somewhat aligning with, just staying from ever so slightly all the time, before just falling back into place and maybe going the other way – like a new driver trying to stay in the middle of their lane.  
The craziest part of all of this, which I can sort of picture but not quite write with the same depth, is what if the reason we experience time is just because we are the instances of the ray of entropy/time. Literally the line *is* us. Merely by being a thing, it makes us a thing. In a way, the object and the class are one. The ray is the class, and we are the object, (coding terms). Just like how by telling a story, you in a way make that story *real* by bringing it into the world, in a way the story of that ray *is* us because by simply existing in full form, it is synonymous with our existence. So, simply by laying that ray out, without even doing anything to it, just by introducing the concept of it the multiverse has equally generated us, the universe, or in other words that ray. (Four dimensional ray I mean – we exist in three dimensions, and so as a normal ray is to a zero dimension point, that four dimensional ray has become to our three dimensions. That just means an added dimension of time to our three dimensions we can interact with). The ray is there and it exists silently, and merely by looking at it and understanding it, in turn so too does the universe exist. I mean, I’m reading back through this and frankly it doesn’t match 100% with my inner vision of this ray, but well, close enough for now. Like… I guess, if you wrote a perfect book and put it on the table, the book itself is static, but just by having those specific words on those specific pages, there exists this constant story associated with that book. It doesn’t have to do with somebody picking it up and reading it – that’s just the process of *them* getting an idea of that story – but the story itself is just something else, abstract, that exists – sort of. And in that analogy, we would be the story. The book is the physical ray spanning across Ambul Space, and this crazy series of events, which we can never explain why we just happen to be falling through, is the story. Again, sometimes I just hate analogies and this might be a pretty goddamn good example of that, but at least I’ve *begun* to put this idea down on paper.  
Oh, and there also should be *another* dimension still, which represents the spatial permutations of entropy – aka every possible alignment of the stuff of the universe – the stereotypical *multiverse*. In one of these universe points, you have a different name, or ate something different for breakfast yesterday. That kind of thing.  
So in total, this gives us the dimensions of:

## **Miracleist “Value” of Planet Earth**

What is the value of our planet and the life upon its surface? And how would one measure such a value? Dollars? Kilograms? Area?  
The other day I came up with a simple means of approximating such a value. All approximations of Earth’s value that I’ve seen have the problem of not including a time factor. So what I would do is:  
Multiply the area of the Earth by the amount of time the Earth has existed. This comes out to an absolutely massive number: 2 quintillion square kilometer years. Perhaps this kind of time factored type of value should be the realm of a new unit, meant to measure the value of Earth, rather than just using plain dollars.

## **When in the Year was Eta?**

We can plot the exact time in the year of certain holidays, like Fourth of July, Thanksgiving, or Greek Independence Day. But where on the calendar is the day the Dark Era ended?   
Obviously I have no means of calculating a definite answer right now, but maybe I can start to brainstorm some methods and maybe give them a shot at a later date.   
First things first, the simplest approach – straight radiocarbon dating. Thing is, this is kind of a stupid idea, and I’ll tell you exactly why: it happened just too long ago. Radiocarbon dating is a process of randomness as much as algorithm, and so while we can theoretically triangulate a time, the more closely we approach, the more data we need for the next iteration. Because of this, as of right now we haven’t even narrowed it down within a twenty-two thousand year window. So, as you can probably guess, narrowing the approximation down within a day is basically unachievable. Not to mention, even if we could do this, we would also have to perfectly integrate the day lengths and year lengths all the way back to that date, which is frankly even harder. Even a fraction of a percent of a day change would throw off the whole calculation over that length of time. In short, let’s not even go here.   
But here’s another idea I thought of: if the days, months, and years have different lengths 66 million years ago, then we should really be defining a constant statistic that we will pass from one time to another. I think this statistic needs to be the position in the seasons. If we’re 28% through spring in the northern hemisphere when the asteroid hits, for instance, then we know straight from there that the anniversary of that fateful day will be whatever 28% of the way through spring is in *our* system. In other words, we should pass the seasonal time code in order to most efficiently get the same general “*time of year*”.   
So, if the season is our parameter, then from there we can look at the axial tilt. Regardless of whatever that tilt may be, if we can somehow plot its relative location with respect to the sun and the moon, then we will have a means for getting our seasonal time code. This is where the brainstorming comes in – we’ve got to figure out a way how to do this. Maybe we could plot the ash settlement across the globe, digging into the ground and finding ever so slight differences in the concentration? Then we could plot a world map, (maybe of only land, but whatever), and if we could hit this accurately enough, we could simulate solar system gravity and get a time code??? Maybe something as simple as Walker Circulation could pinpoint the day code.   
Maybe we could use the jet stream? I mean, we already have an idea of how it might have worked with that continent configuration, so I guess that’s an option, too?  
I’m just thinking that the more specific, seemingly useless data we get on this event, the better. One day we might just be able to put it all to use, and get a yearly time code of when the asteroid hit the earth.

## **Relation Between Danger and Risk**

### *Saturday, May 29, 2021*

More Dark Era stuff. I know – I’m kind of obsessing over this, but hey, whatever.  
Short answer to this heading: *Danger is the derivative of Risk with respect to time*. (Sort of). Long answer?  
Here’s the equation: $R(t)\ =1-{e}^{-m\ t}$, where $R$ is the death risk, $m$ is the danger, and $t$ is the amount of time passed since whenever we started counting.  
To start explaining this, let’s settle a few things, first. I’m sure you could define plenty of things as *danger*, but I want to specifically define the *physics* or whatever definition of danger as specific to an event. Sort of like how density is specific to your *substance*, and gravity is specific to your *planet*, I want to make it so that danger is specific to your *event*. In order to do this, all you have to do is make danger the derivative of death risk with respect to time. As for *why*, I mean, I kind of just eureka-ed it, but maybe I can try and explain it. One explanation is like the whole [rain thing](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.w52wzx7pb0om), where, in the Dark Era, for instance, infinite supply of crisis and time means you should divide them to get your true property. Another way of explaining it is, if you think about how deadly a certain activity is, like hang gliding or riding a motorcycle, like, in micromorts, you’ll notice that you have to specify how many “laps” or “skydives” or whatever you’re putting into it. In other words, death risk is not specific to the event, but instead how long and how often it’s being done. The thing that stands out to me, here, is just time. It’s almost like these death risk values are like definite integrals of danger – but not even almost – literally. So, if we divide the net death risk by the amount of time doing it, you’ll get the average rate of death risk, which is in fact specific to an event, at least on average. And that’s all there is to it.  
You can look back [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.fup8lys5fwa0) at my unit I defined to describe this quantity of danger, so if you’re ready, let’s keep going.  
The other thing to consider, now, is how these aren’t perfectly linear. Normally, if a derivative is constant, then we get this nice, infinite line, that stretches away to infinity. But… death risk can only ever go as far as $1$. You can’t have an 101% chance of death, or a 400% chance of death. It would just be 100%. If you want to picture this, it’s just an upside down and backwards exponential function that roofs away at 1, (and goes through 0). Your distance to 100% chance of death is dropping by the second, and eventually you even get to a point where you’re so close to it, that it’s *more* likely than not, like overall spending months in the Dark Era. But the key thing to keep in mind is that it’s all relative to your start point. Whenever you start counting, which in the case of danger starts whenever you’re actually *in* the danger, and death risk counts up from there on out. I mean, you could really put this start point wherever the heck you want. If you’re not dead, you can put it right now in fact\! Here’s the chance of death equation based on time: $R(t)\ =\ 1\ -\ (C{)}^{\frac{t}{{T}_{C}}}$. $C$ is the chance of surviving at whatever time interval ${T}_{C}$ we want to be our basis. If $C$ is a half, we call ${T}_{C}$ half-life, for instance. But this $C$ and ${T}_{C}$ is like a generalization of half life, for thirds, five sixths, or whatever the heck you want to be your basis. In other words, ${T}_{C}$ is like a $t$ value you get to pick, and $C$ is the $1-R$ value that corresponds to it, (aka the survival likelihood). We pick a definite point on the graph, and the rest of the thing warps to fit it.   
All I did with my new equation is, I made it so we find $R$ in terms of constant danger instead of $C$ and ${T}_{C}$. To solve this, we take the derivative, $R'(t)=-\frac{{C}^{\frac{t}{{T}_{C}}}ln({T}_{C})}{{T}_{C}}$, then set $t$ to 0, $R'(0)\ =\ -\frac{ln(C)}{{T}_{C}}$. Set this to $m$, and solve for either $C$ or ${T}_{C}$. My educated guess here was that since the whole function is totally dependant on $m$, the danger, there’s definitely going to be some canceling, so than only $m$ is left instead of ${T}_{C}$ AND $C$. Let’s pick ${T}_{C}$. ${T}_{C}=-\frac{ln(C)}{m}$. Substitute this back into the original equation, which gets us $R(t)=\ 1-{C}^{-\frac{t}{\frac{ln(C)}{m}}}=1-{e}^{-m\ t}$. And there we have it\!  
My next idea was, “*Hey, I wonder what’ll happen if $m$ ISN’T constant\!*” I can’t say for sure what the answer to that is, but I certainly do have another guess. If you look at that $m\ t$ bit in the exponent of the $e$, if you think about it, we’re just multiplying a quantity of death risk per time, by time, which cancels the time and gets us only death risk. So, why not integrate this? Again, I don’t know for sure if this is legit, but here’s my hunch: $R(t)=1-{e}^{-\int\limits_{S}^{S+t}m(t)\ dt}$.   
The derivative of that would be [$R'(t)\ =\ m(t)\ {e}^{-\int\limits_{S}^{S+t}m(t)\ dt}$](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=m%28t%29+e%5E%28-+integral_0%5Et+m%28a%29+da%29), and the second derivative would be [$R''(t)\ =\ \left({m'(t)\ -\ {\left({m(t)}\right)}^{2}}\right){\times e}^{-\int\limits_{S}^{S+t}m(t)\ dt}$](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=%28m%27%28t%29+-+m%28t%29%5E2%29+e%5E%28-+integral_0%5Et+m%28a%29+da%29). Oh, and another way to write this is as $R''(t)\ =\ \left({m'(t)\ -\ {\left({m(t)}\right)}^{2}}\right)\times \left({1-R\left({t}\right)}\right)$. This is important, because for a human life in 21st century America, the graph of death risk all throughout life is crucially CONCAVE UP. Here’s a rough graph of it:   
This means, automatically, that $\left({m'(t)\ -\ {\left({m(t)}\right)}^{2}}\right)\times \left({1-R\left({t}\right)}\right)>0$. We know that $\left({1-R\left({t}\right)}\right)$ will always be positive, so we can turn that inequality into: $\left({m'(t)\ -\ {\left({m(t)}\right)}^{2}}\right)>0$. This can easily turn into $m'(t)>{\left({m(t)}\right)}^{2}$, or $\frac{dm}{dt}>{m}^{2}$, aka $\frac{dm}{{m}^{2}}>dt$. Integrate both sides, which gets us $-\frac{1}{m}>t+C$ or $t+\frac{1}{m}<C$. Solve for $m$, now. $\frac{1}{m}<C-t$ and then $m>\frac{1}{C-t}$. Now we need to just pick the right $C$. Just as a test run… how about we try $C=0$. Therefore, $m>-\frac{1}{t}$. But… that has an asymptote in the way, so I think $C=-1$ might be better\! $m>-\frac{1}{t+1}$.  
Alrighty, after all that, and the graph didn’t come out looking how I’d hoped. (Must have been an error somewhere along the line), so how about I trace it backwards, and try to actually get $m$ from the whole $R(t)$. That way, we can put in some Google Sheets values for life expectancy, (the stuff that generated the above graph), and get a legit polynomial fit. So, first up, $1-R(t)={e}^{-\int\limits_{S}^{S+t}m(t)\ dt}$, then $-ln\left({1-R(t)}\right)=\int\limits_{S}^{S+t}m(t)\ dt$, and finally $-\frac{d}{dt}ln\left({1-R(t)}\right)=m(t)$. Oh, and we can also write that as $m(t)\ =\ \frac{R'(t)}{1-R(t)}$. Putting that through Google Sheets for human life data gave me this graph:   
And, low and behold, a polynomial fit equation for this has the following coefficients:

| $1.9183502535372021$ | $1$ |
| :---- | :---- |
| $-1.0754124168513033$ | $x$ |
| $2.2387647360678292\times 1{0}^{-1}$ | ${x}^{2}$ |
| $-2.3926605687518528\times 1{0}^{-2}$ | ${x}^{3}$ |
| $1.5146596290036007\times 1{0}^{-3}$ | ${x}^{4}$ |
| $-6.0846863790635366\times 1{0}^{-5}$ | ${x}^{5}$ |

Now, the amazing thing is, we can cut this off at any starting point $S$, and only run the integral ($R(t)=1-{e}^{-\int\limits_{S}^{S+t}m(t)\ dt}$) from there\! Risk is just a kind of definite interval of danger, so if you want to get your life expectancy, you just find the point where your risk crossed 50%, and you start the integral counting not at birth, but just your current age. All the danger from here onward is the only danger that can count against you, since you’ve already lived through and thus invalidated all danger that came prior. I, for example, am 17, and so just by being that old, my life expectancy has automatically jumped from 76 years, (taking from birth), to 82 years (taking from 17)\! My dad, who will be 50 soon, has a life expectancy closer to 83, instead, as of right now at least. Keep in mind that all of these values are only pulling from complete average, or *normal*, stats, so if you follow what the average person would, then these numbers will apply to you. If we got any added variables for specific people, then obviously these graphs would warp and shift for them, but so long as we don’t have those variables, we can pretty comfortably say that they will follow the average.  
Here’s another useful equation: The life expectancy can be found by ${T}_{Life}=\frac{ln(2)\ morts}{m}$ where $m$ is in morts per whatever unit you want, (assuming $m$ is constant). If $m$ is strictly *not* constant, then the equation becomes ${T}_{Life}={M}^{-1}(ln(2)\ morts)$, where $M(t)$ here is the INTEGRAL of the danger with respect to time, (so not the normal use of $M$ for me). But, I feel like this particular equation is only useful for a constant $m$ anyways, since a graph would be way easier for a varying $m$. If we want to write the life expectancy in terms of millipares, we just have to write it as ${T}_{Life}=\frac{1{0}^{6}\ ln(2)}{14\ M}\ days$, where $M$ is the danger value specifically in millipares. If you want a simple approximation formula, (which I bet I’m going to be using a lot now), we can write the life expectancy as ${T}_{Life}=\frac{135.6\ years}{M}$, where $M$ is the danger in millipares, with all of the quantitative units stripped off of it, or in other words the danger value *per* millipare.

## **Eta Perfection and Rarity of Attribute**

### *Saturday, September 18, 2021*

If we were to find an attribute of Hooma or Eta that was very rare, what would that mean? For instance, if we were to identify that Hooma’s carbon concentration or something was very uncommon in the Solar System, what would that mean? I would argue that such a discovery is a sign that the attribute in question represents a higher weight in the Miracle’s events as opposed to the majority of other attributes/factors.   
The less important an attribute is to the optimality of the Miracle, the more “common” we would expect that attribute to be, (that is, the less “rare”). That is, *IF an attribute is considerably unimportant to the optimality of the Miracle, THEN we would expect to see that attribute be more common as opposed to rare*. Another way of phrasing this might be: *The closer an attribute is to Rebetary to the optimality of the Miracle, the more common we would expect it to be*. And maybe we can use an argument for true Rebetary things, (which are probably statistically impossible, however there will be a lot of circumstances where we tend strikingly close to it, so consider it a guideline more than anything): ***IF an attribute is Rebetary to the optimality of the Miracle, THEN that attribute would follow a normal expectancy***. That is, if it truly is Rebetary to things, then it will have a totally fair, unbiased roll of the dice of probability, whereas all that crazy Prerequisite involved stuff will be rigged toward certain musts.   
The contrapositive of this is: ***IF a Miracle attribute does not follow a normal expectancy, THEN that attribute is not Rebetary to the optimality of the Miracle***.   
The other cool thing to consider about these statements, is that just because an attribute is Rebetary, doesn’t mean it has to be completely common. There still have to be examples of rare Reberary events, they just have to balance out with the common ones. Also, those rare Rebetary events are going to be, well, rare in number, at least compared to the total count of Rebetary events.   
So, the bit of information that sparked this idea in the first place is I heard in [this video](https://youtu.be/dD1jwEs_6xs) that Hooma is known to be a C-type asteroid, (Carbonaceous Chondrite). But the thing is, those asteroids are in fact much more uncommon in large size like Hooma than for small size, meaning in order for Hooma to be large, (which is kind of a must), it would have to be one of the few large Carbonaceous Chondrites instead of one of the many different types of asteroids. My assumption about this is that this is a sign that this attribute of being a C-type asteroid is actually NOT Rebetary to the optimal status of the Miracle, and is in fact closer to Linked. But let’s actually use my if-then statement on this before I jump to conclusions.   
Let’s define the function $A(x)$ as the number of asteroids in our Solar System larger than diameter $x$, and $C(x)$ as the number of C-type asteroids in our Solar System with a diameter larger than $x$. My goal here is to identify what percentage of $10\ km$ asteroids are C-type, however since we aren’t looking at perfectly continuous distributions here for asteroids, my trick is going to be to calculate this using continuous intuition and seeing if it works. Here goes\! So, to start off, now we have our functions. The simple $\frac{C(x)}{A(x)}$ tells us what percentage of asteroids over $x$ will be C-type, but frankly that does no good to our answer, so let’s go deeper. If we define a diameter range here, say $a$ as the low bound and $b$ as the high bound, then there are $A(a)-A(b)$ asteroid in our Solar System between $a$ and $b$ in diameter, and the corresponding result for C-type. Therefore, we can write $\frac{C(a)\ -\ C(b)}{A(a)\ -\ A(b)}$ as the percentage of asteroid between diameters $a$ and $b$ in our Solar System that are C-type. If we set one of these bounds to an actual value, like say $a=10\ km$, we get $\frac{C(10\ km)\ -\ C(b)}{A(10\ km)\ -\ A(b)}$, and if we take a limit now, we turn this into $\lim\limits_{{b} \rightarrow {10\ km}}\frac{C(10\ km)\ -\ C(b)}{A(10\ km)\ -\ A(b)}\ =\ \frac{C'(10\ km)}{A'(10\ km)}$. That’s awesome\! How I got the derivatives is kind of fascinating, too. I double checked it on Wolfram|Alpha, but I actually did think of it on my own beforehand: What I did was this: $\lim\limits_{{b} \rightarrow {a}}\frac{C(a)\ -\ C(b)}{A(a)\ -\ A(b)}=y(a)$, (the unknown). Then, $\frac{d}{da}C(a)=\lim\limits_{{b} \rightarrow {a}}\frac{C(b)-C(a)}{b-a}$ and $\frac{d}{da}A(a)=\lim\limits_{{b} \rightarrow {a}}\frac{A(b)-A(a)}{b-a}$, so therefore $\frac{\frac{d}{da}C(a)}{\frac{d}{da}A(a)}=\ \frac{\lim\limits_{{b} \rightarrow {a}}\frac{C(b)-C(a)}{b-a}}{\lim\limits_{{b} \rightarrow {a}}\frac{A(b)-A(a)}{b-a}}=\lim\limits_{{b} \rightarrow {a}}\frac{\frac{C(b)-C(a)}{b-a}}{\frac{A(b)-A(a)}{b-a}}=\lim\limits_{{b} \rightarrow {a}}\frac{C(a)\ -\ C(b)}{A(a)\ -\ A(b)}=y(a)$, and thus $\frac{\frac{d}{da}C(a)}{\frac{d}{da}A(a)}=y(a)\ \Rightarrow \ \frac{C'(a)}{A'(a)}=y(a)$. Now that’s fun\! Listen, I’m not a genius or anything – I only thought of this because I was on the hunt for derivatives anyways, (because that only seemed fitting for all this instantaneous stuff), and I just reverse engineered the problems from there. That’s a very beautiful result, actually: $\frac{C(x)}{A(x)}$ tells you the percent of C-type asteroids over some diameter $x$, and $\frac{C'(x)}{A'(x)}$ tells you the percent of C-type asteroids *at* some diameter $x$. Now all I need to do is find these two functions somewhere online, and do the equation.   
Actually, I can’t/don’t know how to find these data results, so for now let’s just assume the number comes out to be small like the video said. Now we just need to figure out if this datapoint follows a kind of normal, or should I say “even” distribution. So, remember, the attribute is: *Hooma is a carbonaceous chondrite*, and we have answered *is a 10 km Hooma being a carbonaceous chondrite likely* as NO, so now we need to answer *does Hooma being a carbonaceous chondrite follow a balanced distribution?* I mean, it could be the case, and we’re just happening to be looking at one of those rare and Rebetary data points, but the odds tell us a different story – the most likely scenario here is that the answer to this question is a flat NO. Why? Because, if it followed a balanced distribution, (so basically a fair randomness from 0 to 100% – like Math.random() I assume in Java), then it would be closer to its expectancy of $50%$, and not down by wherever the heck $\frac{C'(x)}{A'(x)}$ comes out to, at some low number. So while we can’t prove it, we can suggest with a pretty solid degree of certainty that this question comes out to FALSE. If that’s the case, then the rest of that contrapositive idea holds, and we get this: *Hooma being a carbonaceous chondrite is NOT Rebetary to the optimality of the Eta Miracle*. That is, there’s some kind of connection there between Hooma being a carbonaceous chondrite and the actual occurrence of the Miracle.  
But, as I imagine I’m going to see as I watch more of the video, the way around this is probably to make Hooma actually be *more* likely to be a Carbonaceous Chondrite, which we would do by simply differing its likelihood at being one from $\frac{C'(x)}{A'(x)}$. How is that possible, you might ask. Well, $\frac{C'(x)}{A'(x)}$ simply tells us the *percentage* of Carbonaceous Chondrite asteroids at Hooma’s size – but it tells us nothing about the odds, at least technically speaking. If every asteroid has the same chance of hitting Earth, without any discrimination, then $\frac{C'(x)}{A'(x)}$ is the odds of a Hooma sized Carbonaceous Chondrite hitting Earth – but the second we give certain asteroids, be it due to region, composition, or whatever, a higher shot at hitting the Earth, then our true value differs from $\frac{C'(x)}{A'(x)}$, and just might tend closer to that expectancy of 50%. It doesn’t *have* to, actually, but the closer it gets, the less and less our assumption that we’re not looking at a balanced distribution gets, and the closer we get to having no way to prove that Hooma being a carbonaceous chondrite is not Rebetary to the Miracle’s events. In other words, if Hooma being a carbonaceous chondrite truly is Rebetary to the Miracle, and we learned that composition didn’t make a difference, then the natural conclusion would be that $\frac{C'(x)}{A'(x)}$ doesn’t tell us the odds of a Carbonaceous Chondrite sized Hooma hitting Earth as opposed to other asteroids, and instead that Carbonaceous Chondrites get the whole system rigged in their favor for some reason. And, then again, there’s always that lingering conclusion too that it was just dumb luck for the Carbonacous Chondrites, and $\frac{C'(x)}{A'(x)}$ still holds valid. But that’s not what the odds are, assuming that $\frac{C'(x)}{A'(x)}$ is small like the video says.   
Here’s also an updated version of the statement: “***IF a Miracle attribute has biased probability, THEN that attribute is related to the optimality of the Miracle.***”

## **Telltale Imperfection Magnitude Drop**

How do you know you’re dealing with an imperfection magnitude drop?  
I think we need two terms to describe what to expect.   
Maybe “inside-out” deals with when we know the attributes well from the timeline, and we tweak things to align with that known.   
The opposite of this is “outside-in”, which means we forcefully push an attribute into the system, which runs the risk of totally butchering the Optimality-related clockwork of it.   
I think of this as like the [Library of Babel](https://libraryofbabel.info/search.html), where inside-out is like the search feature, whereas “outside-in” is like the pick a random page feature. One is totally legible, and the other has an infinitesimally small chance of being legible. 

## **Fundamental Postulate of the Optimal**

### *Thursday, December 2, 2021*

The fundamental postulate of the Optimal Earth concepts is that our Earth that we live on has not sustained any Imperfection Magnitude Drops away from the perfectly Optimal Earth which is constant as a concept in our universe. 

## **Dual Optimal Rebitality Principles**

Yohkay – so we already have the principle that: “***IF an Earth Attribute is Rebetary to the existence of the observer, THEN that Attribute holds an unbiased probability of occurrence.***”  
But now, to add to that, how about we look at the situation where the attribute is *not* Rebetary, and see what happens then\! “***IF an Earth Attribute is near-Linked to the existence of the observer, THEN the Route in which Earth attained that Attribute should hold a pseudo-random percentile among all possible Routes.***”   
The effect of this is an interesting razor we can observe, based upon the fact that *there are more low-probability routes that can be imagined than high probability routes*: “***IF an Earth Attribute is near-Linked to the existence of the observer, THEN the infinitely-vast majority of Routes you conceptualize that lead to said Attribute are below the Optimality of the Route Earth took for that Attribute.***”  
Also, if you name an Attribute, then the quantity that assigns to the frequency of instances of that Attribute in a set is most definitely *probability*, however as we stack more and more Attributes together, this probability goes down accordingly – and if we do this infinitely, to the point where we declare a *route*, then now we have but a single point in the Optimality spectrum, which is like an infinitesimal of probability and in fact does not hold a nonzero probability of its own, due to the nature of the route consisting of infinite attributes. (So like a string of attributes).   
Here’s three new words to define for this: *Attribute*, which we already know to mean an element of a Golden Trek. Now, there’s also *Attribute Set*, which consists of a set of Attributes which must all be satisfied in order to be valid – and then there’s a *Route*, which is just an Attribute Set consisting of no less than infinite Attributes which altogether come together to form a kind of instantiation so to speak of a Golden Trek, which follows exact measures in its path. Earth, for instance, would consist a Route. And then I guess there’s also the *Finite Attribute Set*, to consider, which just means those Attribute Sets which hold finite elements rather than infinite elements like a Route. And that’s some good info right there\!   
So maybe that allows us to rephrase that last philosophical razor there to the following: “***IF an Earth Attribute is near-Linked to the existence of the observer, THEN the infinitely-vast majority of non-conceptually-dependent Attribute Sets you may conceptualize that lead to said Attribute are in full below the Optimality of the Route Earth took to that Attribute.***” In short: “Earth did it better than you could.”  
And ANOTHER way of putting this razor, albeit pessimistic in nature, is: “***IF an Earth Attribute is near-Linked to the existence of the observer, THEN you will not be able to imagine a separate (and  non-conceptually-dependent) Route/Attribute Set that would, in practice, lead to the same Attribute but with higher Optimality.***”  
Also, about all this conceptually dependent madness, I’m basically saying you can’t just define your Attribute Set as something like *That which follows any Route holding higher Optimality than Earth’s corresponding Route*, at least in the scope of the razor that is.

Now, right off the bat, we know that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1$, since it’s a unit vector and all, so we can use this to reshape the vector into $⟨x,\ y,\ \pm \sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}⟩$. It’s strikingly simple what we need to do – we pick the up-and-down $z$ coordinate as a random number from \-1 to 1, (potential z-bounds of a unit sphere), and then we pick a random angle $\theta$ to use as longitude at the circle which holds that random $z$ value. And that’s all there is to it\! Beautiful\! So, let’s write the unit vector in terms of these two variables. We’ll define the random variables, by the way, as ${\sigma }_{1}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}$, such that $z={\sigma }_{1}{\ }$ and $\theta ={\sigma }_{2}\times 2\pi$, (so that all $\sigma$s can be over the range $[0,\ 1]$). The radius of the circle at $z$ should be $r=\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}$, so therefore the vector itself would be given by $⟨\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\times cos(\theta ),\ \sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\times sin(\theta ),\ z⟩$. Then, last but not least, if we put everything in terms of the two random variables, we get $⟨\sqrt{1-{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}\times cos(2\pi {\sigma }_{2}),\ \sqrt{1-{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}\times sin(2\pi {\sigma }_{2}),\ {\sigma }_{1}⟩$. And there, friends, is a random unit direction vector\! From here, the next part is simple: just apply the magnitude\!  
And this gives us a final answer for star velocity vectors of $⟨42\ \sqrt{1-{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}\times cos(2\pi {\sigma }_{2})\times er{f}^{-1}\left({2\ {\sigma }_{3}-1}\right),\ 42\ \sqrt{1-{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}\times sin(2\pi {\sigma }_{2})\times er{f}^{-1}\left({2\ {\sigma }_{3}-1}\right),\ {42\ \sigma }_{1}\times er{f}^{-1}\left({2\ {\sigma }_{3}-1}\right)⟩$.

* ${z}_{n}(t)\ =\ {\ \sigma }_{4}\times \sqrt[3]{\frac{3\ n}{4\ \pi \ w}}\ +\ {42\ \sigma }_{1}\times er{f}^{-1}\left({2\ {\sigma }_{3}-1}\right)\ \times \ t$

And so, here’s the Maclaurin Series for this data: $\mu =\frac{{L}^{2}}{110}\ morts\ per\ \left({millennium\ square\ parsec}\right)$, which in pares comes out to $\mu (L)\ =\ {L}^{2}\ \times 1.8\ micropares\ per\ square\ parsec$.   
Well then, without further ado, let’s substitute\!  
If we want to take $\mu (1\ light\ year)$, then we should get $\mu (1\ light\ year)\ =\ 0.17\ micropares$, which gives a Life Expectancy of $800,000\ years$. Very cool\! Also, if we look at a plain parsec, we get a danger of $\mu (1\ parsec)\ =1.8\ micropares$, however this value is probably too big, actually, because of the error of the Maclaurin Series – or in other words, pretty much don’t trust this approximation for anything over a lightyear\!  
As for the lower values, we can see the danger of the star coming within the hypothetical *Planet Nine’s* distance at [$\mu (56\ billion\ miles)$](https://www.inverse.com/science/planet-9-location-orbit-distance-name-black-hole-news#:~:text=Planet%20Nine's%20average%20distance%20from,about%2056%20billion%20miles%20away.), which is $\mu (56\ billion\ miles)\ =\ 15.4\ picopares$. For reference, that’s a Life Expectancy of $8.8\ billion\ years$, or in other words, NOT GONNA HAPPEN\!   
Working things in the reverse direction, if we want to find the distance which corresponds to a Life Expectancy of $4\ billion\ years$, say, then we get $1200\ au$, which is well into the Oort Cloud. For reference, the most recent visitor to our Solar System, called Scholz’s Star, was $52,000\ au$ away, a value which holds a Life Expectancy of $1.2\ million\ years$. By the way, the Life Expectancy formula is [$T\ =\ \frac{800\ millennium\ square\ light\ years}{{L}^{2}}{\ }$](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=%28800+millennia+lightyear%5E2%29+%2F+%28%5Bx%5D%5E2%29). And that enables us to get our star distance in terms of the Life Expectancy, now, with [$L\ =\ 1200\ light\ years\ \sqrt{\frac{year}{T}}$](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=1200+lightyears+*+sqrt%28year+%2F+%5Bx%5D%29). (Which, bonus, I guess is also technically equal to $L\ =\ 1200\ c\ \times \ \sqrt{\frac{yea{r}^{3}}{T}}$, where $c$ is the speed of light\!)  
And what’s more – we can even calculate the gravitational force felt on us by those stars, using Newton’s Equations\! That gets us $g\ =\ \frac{G\ M\ T}{1400\ {c}^{2}\ {decade}^{3}}$. That’s a very neat result\! Remember, this tells us the max gravitational field strength we’re going to feel of a star of mass $M$ after some time $T$. Okay, I’m back from doing that, and sadly I didn’t find any way to do this, so I guess I’m just going to do the lazy thing here and throw the weighted average star mass in for that field because, well, because I can I guess. That result would be [$g\ =\ 0.61\ \frac{mm}{{year}^{3}}\ T$](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=%28gravitational+constant+*+solar+masses+%2F+%282.4+speed+of+light%5E2+*+century%5E3%29%29+*+%5Bx%5D). Judging from this, if we take the entirety of Earth’s history as $T$, we get the maximum gravitational field Earth had ever been in from a star besides the sun at expectancy ${g}_{max}=2800\ km\ per\ square\ year$. For reference, the sun pulls on your body with $0.593\ cm/{s}^{2}$, which is a good two million times that\!   
And, that closest star ever probably put an irradiance on Earth of about $77\ microwatts\ per\ square\ meter$, which compared to the modern moon is about $2%$ of the full moon. So… interesting – bright, just not *crazy* bright. For MORE reference, this is about $700$ times brighter than the brightest star in the night sky, Sirius.   
The last thing to discuss about all this – what role does it play in Earth’s Optimal history? I mean, I’ve noticed quite a trend of things normally meaning disaster being used aptly by the Optimality to actually dodge an Imperfection Magnitude Drop, a noteworthy example being Hooma of course. Normally an asteroid would be devastating, but in the case of Hooma, it was intertwined right into the Optimal in a way you would never expect it to be beforehand. Is this passing star concept anything similar?   
Something particular this has got me thinking about is maybe Panspermia stems from this concept. If we wanted to analyze what conditions would have led to this Panspermia, we of course would want a passing star to near very close to the Earth – a figure that would make that $1200\ au$ very sought after by the Optimality. However, on the other hand, we have to remember that the closer the approach, the less likely it is to happen in the first place, by that squares principle and everything, so it’s almost like we have these competing probabilities that we need to find a balance of. Here’s the mathematical path my brain just gave me: *why not find the probability of life surviving a trip at length $L$, and the danger of that minimal star $L$ being reached, and then at that point build a percentile scale, and pick a random value on it?*  
First of all, the danger of reaching a distance of $L$ is $\mu (L)\ =\ {L}^{2}\ \times 1.8\ micropares\ per\ square\ parsec$. As for the probability of surviving from there, we need to look at the temporally based info of Archaea and Bacteria survival, since those are the closest living relatives to the panspermia organism, which must have been ancestral to LUCA. I read [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panspermia#Radiopanspermia) that bacteria could survive “up to six years” in the vacuum of space, but specifically if they were kept inside of clay or meteorite powder to simulate the voyage on a space rock – which is pretty contrasting to the fact that if they were naked in space, they would only survive a few seconds. So, great. For now, we’ll keep this $6\ years$ number in the back of our mind, and call it $T$, the Life Expectancy of organisms during their space rock trip. That would make the danger $\mu \ =\ \frac{ln(2)\ morts}{T}$, and the risk of surviving $t$ time as $R(t)=1-{2}^{-t/T}$. Great\! Now, if we have a distance to cover of $L$, at an average velocity of $v$, then since $t=\frac{L}{v}$, then we can rephrase this concept at $R(L)=1-{2}^{-\frac{L}{T\ v}}$. (Fun fact, that denominator value $T\ v$ is technically a constant, so I guess it can be viewed as a kind of “distance expectancy” for the prokaryotic life aboard the asteroid\!)  
Anyways, now we need to figure out how to put these two values together\! Also, slight tweak – I’m going to convert that “Risk of death” value to “Chance of Life”, by a simple flip from one, like so: $C\ ={2}^{-\frac{L}{T\ v}}{\ }$. Together with our danger of star closeness value, this makes a product of $\mu \times C={L}^{2}{\times 2}^{-\frac{L}{T\ v}}\times \frac{{morts}^{2}}{110,000\ years\ square\ parsecs}$. Beautiful\! If we write this in the form $y={x}^{2}\times {2}^{-\frac{x}{a}}\times b$, where $a=Tv$ and $b=\frac{{morts}^{2}}{110,000\ years\ square\ parsecs}$, then we can integrate this as $A=\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }y\ dx=\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\times {2}^{-\frac{x}{a}}\times b\ dx=\frac{2\ {a}^{3}\ b}{{ln}^{3}(2)}$. Now that’s fantastic. Also, as for why I chose to integrate it – well, I just got a look at the graph, and that seemed like the best thing to do honestly. ANYWAYS, if we want to make the integral under our entire graph equal to one, then we just do $\frac{y}{\frac{2\ {a}^{3}\ b}{{ln}^{3}(2)}}=\frac{{x}^{2}\times {2}^{-\frac{x}{a}}\times b}{\frac{2\ {a}^{3}\ b}{{ln}^{3}(2)}}=\frac{{x}^{2}\ {2}^{-\frac{x\ +\ a}{a}}\ {ln}^{3}(2)}{{a}^{3}}$, which interestingly cancels out our $b=\frac{{morts}^{2}}{110,000\ years\ square\ parsecs}$ in its entirety. What does this mean? Well, if you remember back, this represented the units on the passing-star danger stuff, which pretty much means the actual scale factor / coefficient on the star danger is actually arbitrary\! I mean, wow\! All that matters is the relative comparisons between distances in that scope. Very interesting. Now, last but not least, let’s define our percentile scale $P$ as $P(x)=\int\limits_{0}^{x}\frac{{x}^{2}\ {2}^{-\frac{x\ +\ a}{a}}\ {ln}^{3}(2)}{{a}^{3}}\ dx$, which comes out to $P(x)=1-\frac{{2}^{\frac{a\ +\ x}{-a}}\left({2\ {a}^{2}\ +\ {x}^{2}\ {ln}^{2}(2)\ +\ a\ x\ ln(4)}\right)}{{a}^{2}}$. Now, the problem with this being our cumulative distribution function, is that it makes it kind of hard for us to get at an $x$. So, here’s an idea – we’ll define a new $x$, which is $u=\frac{x}{a}$, such that $x=ua$, and see if this helps things a little bit – so literally $u$ is $x$ measured with units $a$. With this, the equation turns into $P(u)=1-{2}^{-u\ -\ 1}\ \left({2+u\ \left({u\ {ln}^{2}(2)+ln(4)}\right)}\right)$.   
As for the few interesting things we can try with this – if we look at where the 50th percentile falls, then we get something like $u=3.8578535536469661698…$, which is pretty interesting. So, in other words, when taking a unit of *distance expectancy*, then the expected star distance, as according to this math, is about 4 of those *survival distance expectancies* away from the Earth. (Which doesn’t factor in any Solar System disruptions by the way that might also change things, but hey, whatever for now). Also, if we’re looking at the 75th percentile, that gets us $5.656\ SDEs$, (survival distance expectancy). And… the 25th percentile falls at $2.492\ SDEs$. Keep in mind that, like, by definition, everything above $1\ SDE$ is more likely to die than survive the trip, so we are quite literally betting everything on this kind of thing going right. And of course, (assuming panspermia is the source of life), it did\! Just look around you\! Another thing to note here: in order for there to actually be a 50-50 chance of the life surviving the trip, at $1\ SDE$, we would have to find ourselves somewhere around the $3.331%$ percentile, which is pretty dang close to one in thirty for reference.  
[Here’s the Wolfram|Alpha input](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=1+-+2%5E%28-1+-+u%29+%282+%2B+u+%28u+log%5E2%282%29+%2B+log%284%29%29%29) so you can try all this yourself, by the way\!  
So, I guess that’s basically everything\! And here’s another note I’m thinking about, too – what if there are multiple life asteroids carrying the panspermia life from the adjacent star to Earth? Well, I’m pretty sure just by the looks of it, that we can treat ALL that life as a set, and consider $SDE$ as the distance over which you expect the last one to survive. Like and-danger, if you will – the unit set only dies once EVERYBODY is dead, and we give a survival distance expectancy value to that entire set’s longevity at $SDE$.   
Also, if we do in fact have a parent star system which passed LUCA ancestors to us via panspermia, then we can conclude from some of my expectancy measurements that that planet had never hit a Delta Miracle, since such a thing is a very unlikely occurrence. For all we know, that original planet could have had life for billions of years, and yet all of it was prokaryotic, and hence nobody there had ever opened eyes to see. If you want to think like a sci-fi writer, you might say something like, “well, what if there was intelligence on that planet, and they chose to send the life our way rather than an asteroid???”, and to that I would say, *okay, cool, but to do that, you have to weigh the probability of Golden Life appearing on that planet and doing such a thing, as compared to all the math I’ve shown here regarding this double-chance occurrence. I don’t think it’s that hard to show that as against-the-odds this panspermia by asteroid hypothesis is, we’ve shown here that it’s at least plausible, at least by several orders of magnitude more than the intelligence scenario. So literally, if you shuffle through some of my mindset/property things alone, you’re going to see very quickly that they all scream the same statistical result at you – the Delta Miracle never happened on the original planet.*   
Also, if this panspermia thing truly is what happened 3.8 billion years ago, then we can literally extend the Bubble of Perfection further back in time to encompass that original planet. And this gets us fascinating results – for one, we have to ask ourselves the question, *why was the spawning of life in a separate Solar System Optimally superior to just spawning life in our system and never having to take the risks of system transfer in the first place?* In other words, by some of these Optimal guidelines, we can conclude that whatever risks were taken during the panspermia exchange were statistically outweighed by the risks that would have happened instead had life appeared originally on Earth and not gone through whatever processes it went through on the other planet. I mean, for all we know, when it comes to actually *generating* life out of organic matter, our Solar System represents an Imperfection Magnitude Drop – and if panspermia were legit, for that matter it probably would be. We know our Solar System is near-Optimal for every Miracle spanning from LUCA to the Golden Point, but what if a white star with four terrestrial planets and four gas giants just *ISN’T* Optimal for life generation? What if a red dwarf is best for life generation, or an orange star, or a white star with three types of planets all forming a factory of sorts with a binary red star surrounding them – or frankly something totally different altogether? If that were the case, and the particular setup of our Solar System was an Imperfection Magnitude drop for life generation, well then OF COURSE panspermia would be a key part of our past. And these minute risks of going over a few $SDEs$? Sign us up\!   
[Here’s a link to a music artist](https://open.spotify.com/artist/5R8khW93Qg4eeaIxw4mA2H?si=7CXdVUcKSfuH2D6zMyaRTg) that I really like the sounds of for video.   
I’ve done some pretty cool results so far, but I think it’s come time for me to try and approximate the $SDE$ unit. This isn’t set in stone or anything, but it’ll still be cool to try\! So, here goes: judging by ʻOumuamua’s orbital velocity of $5.55\ au\ per\ year$, and a guess of the Life Expectancy at $14\ years$, (taking the geometric mean of 6 years and 32 years), we can roughly calculate that maybe $SDE\approx 77\ au$? Therefore, if that were the case, then the expectancy of the closest approach to that other star system would be around $300\ au$.   
But I honestly don’t like that number very much – so how about I jack up the life expectancy a little bit and see where that takes us\! According to [this link here](https://www.cnn.com/2020/08/26/world/earth-mars-bacteria-space-scn/index.html#:~:text=Based%20on%20the%20scientists'%20estimates,eight%20years%20in%20outer%20space.), the prokaryotes may have a shot at surviving 45 years in the cold dark vacuum of space, so if we take, say, *42 years* as the Life Expectancy, then the new SDE becomes $SDE\approx 233\ au$, and the stellar distance becomes $900\ au$ pretty much on the dot. So thank goodness – the 300 au figure felt wrong, and this one looks and feels much more probable.   
Ok, so I’m doing research about Panspermia, and I have a few pet peeves I want to lay out. First of all, there seems to be a general consensus that Panspermia is a sign that life is very common in the universe, HOWEVER I would argue that one is not a function of the other. If Panspermia happened in the way I’m laying out here, (which apparently doesn’t seem to be common knowledge lol), then I guess we’ll call that *Jump Panspermia*, which specifically involves rare life on the universe, which “jumps” from one star system to another as they pass by their closest approach. This bypasses the risk of having to cross massive interstellar distances, not to mention seems to be what the Optimization math I did tells us. Also, it isn’t a sign that life is common at all, because whether life is common or life is rare, (which translates to whether Jump Panspermia is a common, low risk phenomenon, or a rare, high risk phenomenon), is technically Rebetary to our existence, since either way we will continue to exist. That is, whether this Jump Panspermia happens a million times or one time, we would still find ourselves in one of those situations where it *did*, which, what do you know, we do, (obviously, since we exist – it’s like saying we exist so therefore we exist – easy\!)  
But I want to define another kind of “Panspermia”, too, which is the process of life traveling between different planets in the same Solar System, which, as I have already calculated at some point, should actually be pretty dang common\! And so there we have it – these are two fundamentally different concepts, *Jump Panspermia* and *Interplanetary Panspermia*, to the point where I think they are both vital to our existence in their own way, but at the same time separate. 

## **Attributes of the Pre-Panspermia Star System**

### *Saturday, December 12, 2021*

So, if we again assume that life on Earth was transmitted here by some form of stellar-Panspermia, in which case, (as I literally calculated [here](#doomsday-by-passing-star-concept)), there should be an expectancy of about a 3:1 or 4:1 ratio between the distance life had to travel versus the distance after which they should be expected to die. The evidence for new things by Optimal methods is extraordinary given the assumption that life on Earth did indeed originate outside the Solar System, but perhaps a more general piece of evidence is regarding how bacterial life is unusually good at surviving in space. Environments that would render us dead in no time seem to be strikingly within their realm of survivability, to the point where I would go as far as to define some kind of attribute term of a lifeform for survivability in space, like *durabilis* or something along those lines. But just as placental Mammals should be expected to be good at Hooma-surviving, since we were the ones who predominantly came out the other side, if this panspermia hypothesis were indeed true, well then you would expect these microbes to most certainly have this *durabilis* attribute just because our retrospective existence depends on it. If there was no need for panspermia, then we would expect these microbes to not evolve so fluently in that direction, so the fact that they have this in their toolkit alone is perhaps evidence that there is some Optimality involved in the mix.   
But anyways, what I’m coming here today to do is try and paint a picture of the pre-panspermia solar system using what information is available by the Optimal. Not everything is accessible, however one of my favorite abilities of these “laws” of Optimality I’ve made is how they can expand on known information, turning a gigabyte into two gigabytes so to speak. I’ve already done some of this expanding in the last entry, but my hopes now are to see how far I can take this.   
I feel like it would be an assumption in and of itself to call the habitat of life in this old system, *a planet*, because it could be *many planets*, or *a brown dwarf*, or *something unlike anything we can imagine* territory. So to avoid oversimplification, I’m going to call the set of environments that this life could sustainably live in, *the habitable zone*. This could be a planet surface, somewhere on an asteroid, a conveyor belt between planets or atmospheres, and frankly anything else too that fits the build. Just in calling it *the habitable zone*, we’re acknowledging the unknown factor of specifically what was going on.   
So right off the bat, what attributes can we identify about this ancestral habitable zone? Well, for one, it had to have an abundance of water. Also, it had to be Optimally efficient in the process of abiogenesis. Earth’s efficiency in this would represent an Imperfection Magnitude Drop by compassion, the reason being that the AHZ, (ancestral habitable zone), would have had a life generation probability, which we’ll call ${a}_{0}$, as well as a doomsday-avoidance probability, which decreases exponentially by time existed, which we’ll call, say, ${b}_{0}$, and then the probability of the transfer to Earth going right, ${c}_{0}$, and lastly everything else not considered in those first three values, which we’ll refer to as ${d}_{0}$. And then to look at the alternative situation, life on Earth simply pulling off abiogenesis on its own within the time frame would have the simple probability of ${a}_{1}$. Now, thanks to our Optimal laws regarding alternate scenarios, we can expect that ${a}_{0}\times {b}_{0}\times {c}_{0}\times {d}_{0}>{a}_{1}$, so therefore by algebra, we get $\frac{{a}_{1}}{{a}_{0}}<{b}_{0}\times {c}_{0}\times {d}_{0}$. And it doesn’t take rocket science to realize that ${b}_{0}\times {c}_{0}\times {d}_{0}$ is a pretty dang small number – remember this is the odds of life surviving the deadliness of the universe trying to kill it for billions of years, (${b}_{0}$), then leap frogging across Solar Systems with the perfect lifeforms going to the perfect target like trying to hit a fly with a shotgun, (${c}_{0}$), and then change (${d}_{0}$) – so as tiny as this value would be, it would be BIGGER than the degree of Imperfection Magnitude Drop of doing abiogenesis on Earth instead, taken as $\frac{{a}_{1}}{{a}_{0}}$\! In other words, we’re pretty much looking at an Imperfection Magnitude Drop here.   
(Also, using that product of probabilities method is kind of a great visualization of one of my concepts – so let me write that down as a rule of sorts here: *for some arbitrary set containing $n$ attributes, where ${a}_{k}$ is the $k$th attribute in the Optimal version of the set, ${b}_{k}$ is the $k$the corresponding attribute in the Earth version of the set, and ${c}_{k}$ is the $k$th corresponding attribute in an Imaginative version of the set, then it holds true that $\prod\limits_{k=1}^{n}{a}_{k}>\prod\limits_{k=1}^{n}{b}_{k}>\prod\limits_{k=1}^{n}{c}_{k}$*. Beautiful\! And [here’s a link to my Glossary Page](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1FRS7lLs4sQz0D6rjLLp_uglclCjHo4pQUdDDrLz6j04/edit?usp=sharing), where I go more in depth about this.)  
Other things I have already determined about the AHZ is that it had no signs of Eukaryotic life, for a whole multitude of reasons – which I guess I’ll explain actually. I mean, think about it. Eukaryotic life can only evolve if there is oxygen as a resource, and even then we need to pass over a Miracle to actually make Eukaryotic life itself. Moreover, we have some kind of decimal randomness in the mix, because after all, AHZ predated the bacteria-archaea evolutionary divergence, so we would have to bridge that complexity gap completely separately in evolution. And even if we did manage to pull off the Flukes of evolution, we still wouldn’t have any oxygen – evolving oxygen production in the first place is a fluke of its own, and then filling an entire air supply with it is like the next level past that – which only happened on Earth remember once the cyanobacteria producers were able to stay in the sun long enough to get cooking, [which required the days to be long](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.1bgx2mw42p0o) – a feat that only occurred billions of years into the game on planet Earth. This would just seem like a very random direction for the AHZ life to go in, mostly because, well, it is. And there wouldn’t be any Optimality driving it like there was on the later Earth, which obviously also makes quite a difference. To sum it up directly with an instantiation of my Rebetary Attribute Principle, *a parallel to Eukaryotic life developing in the AHZ would be near-Rebetary to our existence right now, and so therefore we can expect for a usual statistic to occur, which, judging by the Flukiness of things, would mean that there were no parallels to Eukaryotic life whatsoever in the AHZ*. You might say, though, “but Ajax, what if Eukaryotic intelligent life on the AHZ sent those microbes here instead of Panspermia\! Then it *COULDN’T* be Rebetary\!” But my response to that would be this: sure, that’s possible, but amongst the infinite abyss of all possibilities, unless it magically were to have a high relative probability, it’s probably not what happened. If we were to conceptually imagine a scenario where Earth was seeded with microbes by an intelligent lifeform, which we can prove by geologic analysis would have happened *prior* to the endosymbiotic event by the way, well then we would have to conclude that that intelligent life form itself came from someplace, which instantly throws some more probability into the mix. By the Optimal, the full breadth of the probability of that intelligence coming into existence due to purely natural phenomena would have to weigh more the probability of everything involving this AHZ stuff coming to pass. Now, judging by what it takes to build intelligence on *Earth*, that would mean extending a should-be vastly unlikely phenomenon to a higher probability then everything that went down in the AHZ. In other words, if we assume that this ancient sci-fi style intelligence occurred roughly the same way we *would have* given purely natural circumstances, then taking the info from this *would have*, which I’ve already laid out quite nicely here – so that’s everything in the AHZ as WELL AS everything on Earth, and roughly assigning that to the Alien intelligence’s history – and it would still have to be *less* than the probability of our AHZ compiled probabilities. To write this algebraically, if we call ${x}_{0}$  the intelligent aliens’ abiogenesis probability, and ${y}_{0}$ as their probability of making it to the Golden Point from there, then if we call ${x}_{1}$ *our* abiogenesis probability, and ${y}_{1}$, *our* probability of everything beyond that point until now, then it should be the case by the Optimal that ${x}_{0}\times {y}_{0}>{x}_{1}$. And if we write the ratio $r$ between the aliens’ post-abiogenesis probability to ours, such that $r=\frac{{y}_{0}}{{y}_{1}}$, then it will be the case that ${x}_{0}\times {y}_{1}\times r>{x}_{1}$, and rearranging makes $r>\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{0}\times {y}_{1}}$. Now, if we call $a$ the ratio of $r$ to $\frac{{x}_{0}}{{x}_{1}}$, such that $r=\frac{a\ {x}_{0}}{{x}_{1}}$, then $\frac{a\ {x}_{0}}{{x}_{1}}>\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{0}\times {y}_{1}}$, which rearranges to $a\ {x}_{0}^{2}\ {y}_{1}>{x}_{1}^{2}$, and thus $a>\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{x}_{0}^{2}\ {y}_{1}}$. $a$, by the way, should be expected to be around $a\approx 1$, because that would mean that our ratios of abiogenesis probability is about the same as our ratios of post-abiogenesis, “Earth”, probability, and so therefore it is approximately so that $\sqrt{{y}_{1}}>\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{0}}$. Now, ${y}_{1}$ is an insanely small number by the Rare Earth hypothesis, and $\sqrt{{y}_{1}}$ represents the geometric mean of that with an 100% chance, which, for the record, is probably still insanely small. Like, if we were a one in a trillion chance of existence, then this figure would be one in a million chance. Another way of writing this is $1\gg \sqrt{{y}_{1}}>\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{0}}$, and so by the transitive property, $1\gg \frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{0}}$, and therefore ${x}_{0}\gg {x}_{1}$. It’s funny, looking back at the original inequality, you could have pulled this from it just intuitively, so I guess this is one way of doing it, lol\! And we can convert this idea to a statement like this: *Unless our supposed Abiogenesis process would have been an Imperfection Magnitude Drop relative to the Optimal Abiogenesis Mission, then we were likely NOT seeded onto Earth by an intelligent alien sometime before the Endosymbiotic Miracle*.   
Here’s another idea, too – why not come up with a name for this hypothetical original organism on Earth. Whatever organism/organisms actually crash landed on our planet however many billions of years ago – whatever *their* last common ancestor is, we should name *Prodavus*. So, if there was a single cell that survived the whole journey, then that cell itself would be Prodavus, and if it was multiple, then whatever their LCA is would be Prodavus. Simple enough. Now, relating Prodavus to the tree of life, it would technically be ancestral to LUCA, (the last universal common ancestor).   
Also, while I’m on the topic, I think I should come up with the word for *life which can survive a trip in outer space*, once and for all. Here’s the word I think I’m going to go with: *Tenaxament*. This has to do with all things panspermia – life which can travel aboard an asteroid from here to Mars or Jupiter or anyplace else and survive the trip would be Tenaxament. Examples are bacteria, archaea, fungi, algae, and even tardigrades. Examples of life forms that are decidedly *not* Tenaxament are Ghasts, Fish, and Humans. Regardless of whether Jump Panspermia is historical, there are definitely Aurumans who are old enough to have qualified as Tenaxament, so that’s something interesting in and of itself – however since modern Aurumans are no longer Tenaxament, we can tell that there was some point when this Tenaxament ability was lost. But when was that? Maybe we could give a name to that species on that basis of undergoing the loss of such an Adamantine and Tenacious characteristic. It was a Prerequisite, and yet I can imagine it was hard to lose when it comes to evolution’s goals. But it was anyways, and that in and of itself was quite interesting.

## **Organization of Progress**

### *Saturday, December 25, 2021, 2:31 PM EST*

Here’s an interesting idea I just thought of – why not devise a way to organize the increase/decrease factor of Goodness over time? One of my earliest postulates of Goodness is that it tends to increase over time in Retrospect, almost “avoiding” downhill travel across the timeline. But can we actually map this travel?  
So, here’s the idea: if we define a function, $f\left({t,\ g}\right)$, which calculates the “proportion” of all points whose progress falls below $g$ by the time of $t$. Therefore, it’s pretty straightforward to generate $f\left({t,\ {g}_{b}}\right)-f\left({t,\ {g}_{a}}\right)$, which tells us the proportion of points before time $t$ whose progress falls between ${g}_{a}$ and ${g}_{b}$. Pretty awesome\! Now, to generate the proportion of points between a range of two values of $t$, well… I guess a range function between two time points looking like $f\left({{t}_{a},\ {t}_{b},\ g}\right)$ would mean by simple averages, (in that the proportion of all before time ${t}_{b}$ is the weighted average of that before time ${t}_{a}$ and between the two times ${t}_{a}$ and ${t}_{b}$), that $f\left({0,\ {t}_{b},\ g}\right)=\frac{{t}_{a}\ f\left({0,\ {t}_{a},\ g}\right)\ +\ \left({{t}_{b}\ -{\ t}_{a}}\right)\ f\left({{t}_{a},\ {t}_{b},\ g}\right)}{{t}_{b}}$, so if we solve for $f\left({{t}_{a},\ {t}_{b},\ g}\right)$, we get $f\left({{t}_{a},\ {t}_{b},\ g}\right)=\frac{{t}_{b\ }f\left({0,\ {t}_{b},\ g}\right)\ -\ {t}_{a}\ f\left({0,\ {t}_{a},\ g}\right)}{{t}_{b}\ -\ {t}_{a}}=\frac{{t}_{b\ }f\left({{t}_{b},\ g}\right)\ -\ {t}_{a}\ f\left({{t}_{a},\ g}\right)}{{t}_{b}\ -\ {t}_{a}}$, which looks quite nice indeed\!  
Now, to just turn this into a nice, usable function to find the proportion of points under $g$ progress directly at time $t$. To do this, we simply need the limit, which is $\lim\limits_{{{t}_{a}} \rightarrow {{t}_{b}}}f\left({{t}_{a},\ {t}_{b},\ g}\right)=\lim\limits_{{{t}_{a}} \rightarrow {{t}_{b}}}\frac{{t}_{b\ }f\left({{t}_{b},\ g}\right)\ -\ {t}_{a}\ f\left({{t}_{a},\ g}\right)}{{t}_{b}\ -\ {t}_{a}}$. Using some of the logic I came up with [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.q7u0at59wg1j), (which I’m only realizing now is glorified L’Hospital’s rule, but eh, we’ll go with it), we can try to solve this expression as $\lim\limits_{{{t}_{a}} \rightarrow {{t}_{b}}}\frac{\frac{d}{d{t}_{a}}\ \left({{t}_{a}\ f\left({{t}_{a},\ g}\right)}\right)}{\frac{d}{d{t}_{a}}\ {t}_{a}}=\lim\limits_{{{t}_{a}} \rightarrow {{t}_{b}}}\frac{f\left({{t}_{a},\ g}\right)\ +\ {t}_{a}\ \frac{d}{d{t}_{a}}\ f\left({{t}_{a},\ g}\right)}{1}$. Also, to put it all back in terms of just the $t$, let’s write this final result as $f\left({t,\ g}\right)+t\ \frac{d}{dt}f\left({t,\ g}\right)$. Cool stuff\!  
If we define $h\left({t,\ g}\right)=f\left({t,\ g}\right)+t\ \frac{d}{dt}f\left({t,\ g}\right)$, (so $h$ is the instantaneous proportion of “points” below progress $g$ at the moment of $t$), then where to next? Well, I want to set a goal to try and write the average progress of $-\frac{ln\left({{p}_{0}}\right)}{T}$, where $T$ is the total amount of time in the timeline, and ${p}_{0}$ is the Original Goodness Constant, all in terms of this new $f$ algorithm.

Just [Googling this now](https://math.stackexchange.com/a/2516459) confirms this, so I’m free to move on to the next part. Now, just as we can find more negatives in lower Optimality, we can quite easily find *less* negatives in lower Optimality, too. Look – I’ll show you – let’s imagine the Route where the Goodness follows a perfect line on the way to the Golden Point, starting at the Original Goodness constant and working perfectly linearly up to Gold. However long this takes is besides the point – I don’t know, we’ll call it $T$, so that $p={p}_{0}+\left({\frac{1\ -\ {p}_{0}}{T}}\right)\ t$, and the Progress $g=\frac{\dot{p}}{p}=\frac{\frac{1\ -\ {p}_{0}}{T}}{{p}_{0}+\left({\frac{1\ -\ {p}_{0}}{T}}\right)\ t}=\frac{1}{\frac{{p}_{0}\ T}{1\ -\ {p}_{0}}\ +\ t}$. Now, it isn’t hard to tell that this Goodness function is perpetually increasing, and thus it is literally so that $y(0)=0$. The other thing about this Imagined Golden Trek – is that it has EXTREMELY low Optimality. Like, crazily so. This is an Imperfection Magnitude Drop on like, a thousand fronts. What would it even look like, anyways? I mean, in order to get such a clean uptick of Goodness, things would have to be happening in an almost impossibly unnatural way, like on the level of Quantum Fluctuations before anything we could imagine. If we take my approximation for the Original Goodness Constant at $~1\ :\ 10\ trillion$ as reference, then this here Imaginative Golden Trek begins with a Progress of pretty much $\frac{10\ trillion}{T}$, (so like if $T$ were the same as Earth, we get a 25% increase in Goodness per hour), and then by the time of the Golden Point, it would only be increasing at 22% per billion years if assuming Earth timescales again for $T$. And again, this is all just too neat, too continuous, too clear – anything with Optimal points is not only going to be looking more exponential, but is going to have that messy Abstract Art feel rather than anything perfectly linear. The point of this is that you can’t just say that going down in Optimality will change $y(0)$ in any set way, because the reality is this kind of crazy-Rebetary relation of anything goes – you decrease your Optimality, and $y(0)$ could get bigger, or it could get smaller, all depending on which story you’re selecting to analyze.
