## **More on Progress Accumulations** {#more-on-progress-accumulations}

### *Monday, December 27, 2021, 10:43 AM EST*

I was thinking back on [my entry from yesterday](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.v6zktaldoz5j), where I mentioned something about a situation where the Delta Miracle has to happen twice over, thus installing quite a bit of Negative Progress into the Golden Trek. What I thought of first of all, is about how in this situation for each Negative Progress instance, there must be a Positive Progress to cancel it out somewhere, whether or not they spend the same amount of time on it is another story, but we can justifiably say that any downhill Progress will be counteracted with an equal span of uphill Progress, which together have equal and opposite Aurutance. So, for instance, maybe they have the same time, like a decade of $-12\ Gress$ Progress, and then another decade at some point of $12\ Gress$ Progress. But this same time is not a given, and thus isn’t the heart of the property, because you could very well have $-12\ Gress$ for a decade, and then three scores at just $2\ Gress$, which will again cancel out. Just, so long as the Golden Point is reached, all downhill Progress has to map to some uphill progress. In property form, this looks like: $-{g}_{a}{\ \Delta t}_{a}={g}_{b}\ \Delta {t}_{b}$. Consider this a property of Aurutance if anything, just it has some application to Progress as its, ya’know, derivative. In the case of the three scores example, we can fill in the variables in the algorithm with $-\left({-12\ Gress}\right)\times \left({10\ years}\right)=\left({2\ Gress}\right)\times \left({60\ years}\right)$.   
If we call $g(t)$ the Progress at time $t$, then I guess it is also the case that $-\int\limits_{{a}_{1}}^{{a}_{2}}g(t)\ dt=\int\limits_{{b}_{1}}^{{b}_{2}}g(t)\ dt$, which is equivalent to $\Delta A\left({{a}_{1}}\right)-\Delta A\left({{a}_{2}}\right)=\Delta A\left({{b}_{2}}\right)-\Delta A\left({{b}_{1}}\right)$.  
Oh – and something I just want to briefly mention while it’s on my ADHD brain – when I talk about “*the probability of a Miracle*” when calculating the [ratio of Goodness](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.43df9rm6y1jd) before to after a Miracle, I’m not really talking about the “probability” of the event that had just transpired happening. That event would, as a matter of fact, be a [Route](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1FRS7lLs4sQz0D6rjLLp_uglclCjHo4pQUdDDrLz6j04/edit#gid=0&range=B37), which, like, by definition basically, has an infinitesimal probability of occurrence. So, as regards another idea I’ve been having lately, specifically involving the [Eventive Hierarchy](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1FRS7lLs4sQz0D6rjLLp_uglclCjHo4pQUdDDrLz6j04/edit#gid=0&range=B12), one easy way to get the general idea of a Route is to chunk it into bite-sized Missions, which are *non-Infinitesimal* in probability, and thus more easy to handle. If we drop a point a little while before Hooma in the timeline and call its timecode ${t}_{a}$ and Goodness $a$, and then if we trace ourselves to the era after Hooma, when Progress has settled down to pretty much “normal” values relative to the height of the spike, and then drop a timecode ${t}_{b}$ there with Goodness $b$, then between these two points is a Route. Now, this Route is one among uncountably infinite of them, but it has achieved the Mission of wildly increasing the Goodness in a few short years. Time for the analysis – and this is where we have to be creative, because the chunking process needs it. First of all, during this little Route Segment, or whatever you want to call it – that is, this span of time with a Route glued onto it – let’s see if we can shuffle through it and find a Prerequisite. All we need to do is find some Prerequisites whose Missions fall into the Route Interval, and that’s that. The closer we were to omniscience, or at least cleverness, the more/better Prerequisites we’ll be able to pull, but for the sake of this Hooma-associating interval I have chosen, I think the best Prerequisite would be the Mission to: “*destroy Akeldama and not destroy Veleda*”. Now, by reading my stuff, you might recognize this Prerequisite – because it’s just the Eta Miracle\! By virtue of being a Prerequisite, the Eta Miracle must occur to feasibly reach the Golden Point, (that is, reach it without an Imperfection Magnitude Drop), so therefore we can deduce that if the Eta Miracle’s Mission *fails*, then the odds of the Golden Point go down by quite a bit, and essentially are relatively indistinguishable from zero. Therefore, we can pretty much say, (with the tiniest margin of error – so it’s good\!) that *The Golden Point may only happen in the set of outcomes for which the Eta Miracle succeeds, so therefore the probability of the Miracle working is contained within the ratio of the pre-Goodness value to the post-Goodness value on the Route, meaning that ratio is less than the probability of the Miracle working*. (And remember, the Eta Miracle is just a Prerequisite that sits nicely within the scope of the Route, so it definitely has a probability to it – however there are other things going on too, so it isn’t exactly synonymous with the Route itself, which is more encompassing). For one single Prerequisite, this trick works just fine, however keep in mind that if we start piling up Prerequisites and try to apply the trick, we get more and more of an accumulation for the slight Imperfection Magnitude Drop error, so don’t exactly try to tend this toward infinity Prerequisites because it will blow up in your face mathematically\!

## **More on Eta Probabilities**

### *Tuesday, December 28, 2021, 10:45 AM EST*

I think I’m going to slightly update the survival equation. I feel like the higher values just got too small too quickly, so I tried it with another approach, which is giving the 25 kg animals a one in seven thousand chance of survival, such that at least *one* of them will survive, and extrapolating the rest of the algorithm from there. The problem is, just as the first equation made things too small, this one made them too big, so I simply took the geometric mean of the two, and got a final answer of $S(m\ kg)={0.044}^{{m}^{0.75}}$. It’s practically identical to the first one, only this one has that $0.044$ constant which is ten times greater, (that is, only one zero after the decimal instead of two). This looks like it’s much more accurate\! It places a 25 kg animal at a 1 quadrillion chance of survival, which frankly is still pretty small, but much better nonetheless. A grey squirrel would have a 16% chance of survival, and a mouse would have an 85% chance of survival. A rat would have a 25% chance of survival.   
Eh… you know what – I think I’m going to stick with the original equation, actually, because this one just gives too much luckiness to the small animals without significantly affecting the big animals’ odds. So, let’s just go back to $S(m\ kg)={0.0044}^{{m}^{0.75}}$.  
Here’s another thought that’s going through my mind – maybe we can actually map the Goodness as the Miracle occurs, instead of just once at the beginning and once at the end. Such a thing will allow for us to follow the course of the Goodness and actually tend toward a continuous relation\! For instance, what is the bound for the Goodness directly after impact compared to sometime before the impact?   
If we call the Goodness *before* the impact, far enough away that the impact pretty much is random in all ways, (like speed, geography, energy, etc), something like ${a=p}_{1}$, and then the Goodness upon impact ${p}_{2}$, then what’s the lower bound for $\frac{{p}_{2}}{{p}_{1}}$? Well, if we call the Goodness after everything has officially settled down, $b$, then from the perspective of ${p}_{2}$, the Optimality of impact location has already been achieved, so all that’s left is to let things play out and see where it goes. From this perspective, the odds of Veleda being wiped out is something like, well… if we say there are ${n}_{1}$ species possessing Veleda pre-Hooma, and ${n}_{2}$ species post-Hooma, then assuming that ${n}_{1}=10\ {n}_{2}$ from that article from the last entry on this, we can say that the danger of proportion $x$ of ${n}_{1}$ being wiped out is what? Well, if we run a Risk function three times say, over time $T$, then the odds of no extinctions is ${\left({1-R}\right)}^{3}$, the odds of one extinction is $R\ {\left({1-R}\right)}^{2}$, the odds of two extinctions is ${R}^{2}\ \left({1-R}\right)$, and the odds of all three extinctions is ${R}^{3}$. So, if we have $n$ species, the odds of $m$ *or less* going extinct is $\sum\limits_{k=0}^{m}{R}^{k}\ {\left({1-R}\right)}^{n-k}$. If we write $x=\frac{m}{n}$, then the odds of $x$ proportion or less going extinct becomes $\sum\limits_{k=0}^{x\ n}{R}^{k}\ {\left({1-R}\right)}^{n-k}$, and this by the way simplifies to $\frac{{\left({1\ -\ R}\right)}^{n}\ \left({R\ -\ 1\ +\ {\left({1\ -\ R}\right)}^{-n\ x}\ {R}^{1\ +\ n\ x}}\right)}{2\ R\ -\ 1}$ according to Wolfram|Alpha. Then, all that’s left is to do $\lim\limits_{{n} \rightarrow {\infty }}\frac{{\left({1\ -\ R}\right)}^{n}\ \left({R\ -\ 1\ +\ {\left({1\ -\ R}\right)}^{-n\ x}\ {R}^{1\ +\ n\ x}}\right)}{2\ R\ -\ 1}$. HOWEVER – one slight problem – this is the binomial theorem, isn’t it? Huh. In that case, I forgot the coefficients of pascal’s triangle in here\! So, really, since these events can happen on multiple occasions, the expression looks like $\sum\limits_{k=0}^{x\ n}{\frac{\left({x\ n}\right)!}{k!\ \left({x\ n\ -\ k}\right)!}\ R}^{k}\ {\left({1-R}\right)}^{n-k}$, and then the simplified form looks like ${\left({1-R}\right)}^{n\ -\ x\ n}$. Beautiful\! If anything, that looks *nicer* than the other expression, and here I was worrying it would look messier\! Well, doing things all over again, if we tend $\lim\limits_{{n} \rightarrow {\infty }}{\left({1-R}\right)}^{n\ -\ x\ n}$, then that’s the same as $\lim\limits_{{c} \rightarrow {0}}{\left({1-R}\right)}^{\frac{1\ -\ x}{c}}=\lim\limits_{{c} \rightarrow {0}}\sqrt[c]{{\left({1-R}\right)}^{1-x}}$ – and now clearly this infinity attempt doesn’t work, which is a sign to me that we can’t do this kind of thing – so the key is to actually do this with a finite count. Anyways, putting this back through our logic from before, if we have an $R$ risk of death for a Mammal, then ${R}^{{n}_{1}\ -\ {n}_{2}}$ is the likelihood of no less than ${n}_{2}$ of those species dying out. Since ${n}_{2}=\frac{{n}_{1}}{10}$, then we can also rewrite this as ${R}^{\frac{9}{10}\ {n}_{1}}$, and we can write the odds of *all* of them going extinct as ${R}^{{n}_{1}}$. Another interesting thing to note – if we call the situation which *actually went down*, ${R}^{\frac{9}{10}\ {n}_{1}}$, as “expectancy”, (which I don’t know how that will clash with the Optimal, but whatever for now), then ${R}^{\frac{9}{10}\ {n}_{1}}=\frac{1}{2}$, and therefore $R={2}^{-\frac{10}{9\ {n}_{1}}}$, so $S=1-{2}^{-\frac{10}{9\ {n}_{1}}}$. Converting this back to the odds of “all death” gets us an odds of Veleda going extinct at roughly ${\left({{2}^{-\frac{10}{9\ {n}_{1}}}}\right)}^{{n}_{1}}={2}^{-\frac{10}{9}}\approx 46.3%$. Therefore, taking the complement of this gets us $53.7%$ chance of Veleda surviving at the instant that Hooma hit the Earth. This value, times the odds of Akeldama being wiped out as of that same instant, gets us the jump relative to $a$.  
If we reference $S(m\ kg)={0.0044}^{{m}^{0.75}}$, then the odds of the Ghasts surviving all this is very low – practically zero, relative to the Mammals, so we can say that ${S}_{Gh}$, for Ghast species Survival chance, is less than a one in thirty-three times that of the Mammals by ${m}^{0.75}$. (Also, another piece of insight I’m having is that maybe we should shorten the exponential by a little bit, instead of fifteen years, and bringing it to like six years, which will make it slightly more linear I think). But a $32:33$ chance of death is still quite close to one, so I think we’re safe to go with it\! ## **Latest Description of the Dark Era Theorem** {#latest-description-of-the-dark-era-theorem}

### *Saturday, January 1, 2022 (Rewording of Theorem originally proposed June 9, 2020, 11:41 AM EST)*

* Picture you could stand on the Earth two hundred and fifty million years ago, at the dawn of the Triassic period, at the event of a staggering timeline split which would determine if humans would ever come to exist or not.   
  * Imagine you had a time-telescope, allowing you to peer into the far future and see what the Earth looks like millions or billions of years into the future. Now, there isn’t just one future, but an infinite number of them, all depending on the tiniest little changes that are made like the butterfly effect. Depending on where you point your time-telescope, you will see a different potential future, and you can then see what the world looks like in your chosen future of direction.  
  * Just as a lookout aboard a sailing ship scans the horizon for land, you are scanning the potential futures for humans, all from the perspective of the Triassic period, 250 million years ago. You keep looking and looking, scanning over all the potential futures, until you see a human waving back at you.  
* At this point, you point your time-telescope to two potential futures \- one in which the dinosaurs evolve, and another in which the dinosaurs never come to be. If you were standing at the beginning of the Triassic 250 million years ago, this dinosaur divide would be the dominant effect you would notice, just because of the sheer difference it would make upon the future. If you looked down the future where dinosaurs evolve, and you are still looking for humans, then it would be absolutely critical for you to find a future among all the dinosaur futures where those dinosaurs are wiped out, so that humans will be able to evolve, (which is just restating the definition of the Great Filter). The problem with this, is that it is very flukey that the dinosaurs are to ever be wiped out, say no more than a 5% chance because 5% of Earth’s surface is shallow water for the asteroid to hit. Therefore, we can say that a very small sum of the dinosaur involving futures which you observe with your time-telescope contain humans, because in order for that to happen, they are relying in full on the fluke that is the asteroid which killed the dinosaurs. You’d be crazy not to conclude that there is an extreme scarcity of humans among the dinosaur-involving futures.  
* But now let’s say you point your telescope a different way altogether, and look to the futures where dinosaurs never evolve. Well great, you think \- now I can find a much higher percentage of humans amongst these futures, because that requirement of dinosaur extinction is no longer an issue\! (Like finding an abundance of humans because the asteroid no longer severely limits humans \- you don’t have to worry about finding futures where dinosaurs were wiped out, because they never evolved in the first place\!)  
  * But there’s a problem here\!  
  * We as a society know for a fact, (just by digging up fossils from the ground), that the future that ended up occurring is the very future which had dinosaurs in it \- because, well, *there were dinosaurs*\! But if the no-dinosaur future had been so much more likely to make humans, then it wouldn’t make statistical sense, (at least according to the simplest form of the mediocrity principle), that we would be born in this timeline of human scarcity rather than a timeline of human abundance. Therefore, my realization was that the no-dinosaur timeline, as observed from the beginning of the Triassic 250 million years ago with your time-telescope, must ALSO contain an extreme scarcity of humans, and in fact even MORE of a scarcity of humans, so that there is even a hint of a chance that humans be born in the dinosaur-timeline where the extinction of dinosaurs is such a pressing required fluke.   
* Conclusion? Dinosaurs never existing would make humans extremely scarce in all the futures observed from the beginning of the Triassic 250 million years ago. If dinosaurs never happened, then humans wouldn’t have a prayer, which is kind of a crazy result given how the dinosaur-timeline was already bad news enough for humans, (because of how unlikely it was for dinosaurs to get the boot).   
  * And this begs the question, why do we depend on dinosaurs so much, then? I mean, their never existing would doom us, eh? Then why\!? And *that’s* how I realized that the evolutionary pressure from hunting by Theropod, carnivorous dinosaurs, actually had a massive effect on the evolving proto-human brain during the Mesozoic \- an effect more extreme than we could have imagined at that.   
* That’s it.  
  * :-)

## **The Math of Exponentially Falling Danger**

### *Wednesday, January 12, 2022, 3:29 PM EST*

Okay\! So, [if we take danger to follow](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.k09b8wfewvac) $\mu =\frac{\dot{R}}{1-R}$, where $R$ is risk, well then what will happen if we turn our danger graph into an exponential decay graph starting at $t=0$???  
Well, an exponential decay might be described by the function $\mu (t)=a\ {b}^{-t}$, so there’s our first step figured out, *and*, if we solve for $R$ in our relation equation, we get something like $R(t)=1-{e}^{\int\limits_{t}^{0}\mu \left({T}\right)\ dT}$, so from there it’s easy\! Just substitute our danger formulation, and we get a Risk of $R(t)=1-{e}^{\frac{a\ \left({{b}^{-t}\ -\ 1}\right)}{ln\left({b}\right)}}$, (from Wolfram|Alpha – yeah, okay, I was too lazy to do the integral myself, get over it\!). Now, what I noticed [from graphing this](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/traociresm), is that there’s actually a non-one horizontal asymptote going on here, which is kind of fascinating\! That is, provided that the danger is decreasing exponentially, the Risk will never quite reach 100%, as observed from any old present. Frankly, there’s still a Risk of death because it’s still *something*, but the key thing to observe is that it doesn’t curve away to 100%, but instead some lesser value, which we’ll call $p$. What is the value of $p$, then? Well, it should be this: $p=\lim\limits_{{t} \rightarrow {\infty }}R(t)=\lim\limits_{{t} \rightarrow {\infty }}\left({1-{e}^{\frac{a\ \left({{b}^{-t}\ -\ 1}\right)}{ln\left({b}\right)}}}\right)=1-{e}^{-\frac{a}{ln\left({b}\right)}}$. (Provided that $b$ is greater than one of course\!)  
Written clearly, that’s $p=1-{e}^{-\frac{a}{ln\left({b}\right)}}$, which is quite nice indeed\! Relative to any starting danger $a$, and an exponential decrease factor of $b$, then your Risk will never, ever get above this magical value shown here\! I’m pretty sure that a natural conclusion you can take out of this, is that with this, you essentially have a $1-p$ shot at immortality by this. That is, if you imagine your final risk as a spectrum to either fall *in*, or *not in*, by a random dice roll, then so long as you fall *not in*, then you’re by definition, *immortal*. That is, since there’s a $1-p$ chance of survival at infinite time in the future, then if you actually *fall into* that category by the random chance, you would literally *be alive infinitely far in the future*, hence the whole “definition of immortal” stuff. Beautiful\! Just beautiful\!  
Also, to clean things up a bit, I’M ABOUT TO CHANGE THE ESSENCE OF THESE VARIABLES HERE, SO DON‘T CONFUSE THEM WITH THE PRIOR ONES\!\!\!\!\!  
Here’s what I’m going to do: a statement\!  
For any exponential decrease in danger, given by $\mu \left({t}\right)=a\ {e}^{-b\ t}$, the system in question has a likelihood of immortality at ${S}_{\infty }={e}^{-\frac{a}{b}}$. And [here’s](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/f1ygdefwcm) the cleanliest Desmos version of this.   
I’m also going to define a quick sub-property of this, which is: *No matter what the starting danger is, for any system of perpetually exponentially decreasing danger, there is a nonzero finite probability of immortality of that system*.   
It goes without saying that this idea has the potential to be huge for my Golden-Point ideas, because well, immortality\!? I’ve already described, like, a “Feedback Mechanism” for Golden Civilizations like over and over again, and now here we have a kind of “putting it all in perspective” means mathematically. And exponential is the baseline, too – I mean, if you think about it just with intuition, a danger staying *under* an exponential, (like a transformed error function would for example), will of course also have this property\! I can easily see the Golden Point internal-danger acting as an exponential decrease, and moreover, I can easily see it staying *under* that, too\! Therefore, the sky’s the limit for the implications of this math\!   
And, just for the fun of it, why not try this error function bit, too\! That would look like this: $R(t)=1-{e}^{a\ \left({\frac{\ {e}^{-{b}^{2}\ {t}^{2}}-\ 1}{\sqrt{\pi }\ b}\ +\ t\ erf\left({b\ t}\right)\ -\ t}\right)}$. And… if we take the limit $\lim\limits_{{t} \rightarrow {\infty }}1-R(t)$, we get a survival chance ${S}_{\infty }^{erf}={e}^{-\frac{a}{\sqrt{\pi }\ b}}$. WOW\! That’s an amazing result\! It’s pretty much the same thing as the other one, just off by a factor of the square root of pi in the exponential, or in other words, *This is the $\sqrt{\pi }$th ROOT of the other version\!* Very fascinating indeed. And, of course, this is going to be even more of an immortality chance than the other one, as roots make us close the gap to one. Also, for reference, [here’s](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/vpncnukhr8) the Desmos to that.   
This also just prompted me to [throw this concept together](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/bavmf0rxyx), which simply relates any Risk value to its corresponding square root pi-th root concept of inverse or whatever – or in other words, if the $x$\-axis takes the form of the Risk of not being immortal for *the exponential*, then the $y$\-axis gives the corresponding Risk of not being immortal for *the error function*, and yes, note that they are functions of one another\! They kind of have to be\! One cool example of this function in action is how “*if you have a 50-50 chance of dying indefinitely far in the future by the exponential, then for the corresponding error-function, you’ll only have a 1 in 3 chance of death*”. From here, I wanted to see what I could do to skew it. Now, you can’t just generate an ellipse, sadly, because one of the key parameters is that it fit into a square, so there’s that. This is what I did: We’ll call our desired result function, $g(x)$, and then, for one, define $g(x)=f\left({\sqrt{x}}\right)$. Very nice indeed\! If we simplify that particular option out, that makes $g(x)=\sqrt{2\sqrt{x}-x}$, which fits all three parameters\! [*Desmos*](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/ihbocmyfty).

Now, we already know from [a previous entry](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.k05dpo95mkrz) that $r=\frac{n}{10\ billion\ years}$, where $n$ is the number of potential planets in our range, so therefore we can rewrite the Golden Count as $\frac{n}{10\ billion\ years}\ \int\limits_{0}^{t}{p}_{0}(t)\ dt$. Now, for that pesky ${p}_{0}$. Here’s one idea: let’s make a bell curve for it – defined as ${p}_{0}(t)=erf'\left({at+b}\right)$. Okay, so then what? Well, if we integrate this, then we get $\int\limits_{0}^{t}{p}_{0}(t)\ dt=\int\limits_{0}^{t}erf'\left({at+b}\right)\ dt={\left[{\frac{erf\left({at+b}\right)}{a}}\right]}_{0}^{t}=\frac{erf\left({at+b}\right)\ -\ erf\left({b}\right)}{a}$. All that’s left is to multiply by the factor of $r=\frac{n}{10\ billion\ years}$, and we get our answer of $\frac{n\ erf\left({at+b}\right)\ -\ n\ erf\left({b}\right)}{10\ billion\ years\ \times \ a}$.  
Ok – so this is kind of good, but I want to make positive $b$s the default – counting as a rightward shift, so I’m just going to swap those $b$s out for their opposite, which gets us a new version of $\frac{n\ erf\left({at-b}\right)\ +\ n\ erf\left({b}\right)}{10\ billion\ years\ \times \ a}$. Also, now to just get it back to the right form, we can do $\frac{n\ erf\left({a\ \left({t-10}\right)}\right)\ +\ n\ erf\left({10\ a}\right)}{10\ \times \ a}$, where $t$ is in billions of years, or [gigayears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billion_years), if you will. As for how this has to do with the [*Golden Civs increase linearly*](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.f5bofzguglxk), which we can kind of see from this *is not the case* – not to worry – because the scale factor with non-Golden Civilizations is still constant, so you can picture that we’re skewing both representations proportionally. In other words, it still holds up logically, just there’s a little bit of a bend to it now.

## **Proof For Danger???**

### *Thursday, January 20, 2022, 8:46 PM EST*

I was just building some computer code to figure out varying danger, and did I just stumble upon a proof for danger???  
Here’s what we’re going to do – for some danger $\mu$, we’re going to list out a stream of infinitesimal Risks with infinitesimal times, and see where it gets us\!  
First of all, for an infinitesimal time $dt$, we have infinitesimal Risk $dR=\mu \ dt$, and so if that percentage of the whole population dies, we get $R(t+dt)=R(t)\times \left({1-dR}\right)$. Let’s start at $t=0$ and $R=1$, standing for the whole population alive at time $0$. Then… as we do more and more $dR$s, we lose parts multiplicatively\! This is equivalent to $R(t+dt)=R(t)\times \left({1-\mu \ dt}\right)$, by the way – and this looks to me like it’s integral worthy\! Let’s call $R(t)=a$ and $R(t+dt)=b$, so $1-\frac{b}{a}=\mu \ dt$, (just by algebra), and since $1-\frac{b}{a}$ would also technically be infinitesimal, how’s about we name it $dx$ or something. Oh, actually that’s just $dR$ I guess\!   
Actually – I think I’m going that wrong, because Risk starts at zero\! (Jeez I’m kind of tired I guess). So… how about we’ll use Chance instead\! $C$\! We start at $\left({t,\ C}\right)=\left({0,\ 1}\right)$. Okay\! So, ${C}_{2}={C}_{1}\times \left({1-\mu \ dt}\right)$. How about we make a differential equation? So, the rate of change of $C$, given as $\frac{{C}_{2}-{C}_{1}}{dt}=\frac{dC}{dt}$, will make er… how about we just do a logarithmic derivative? That makes $ln\left({\frac{{C}_{2}}{{C}_{1}}}\right)=ln\left({1-\mu \ dt}\right)$, and hence $ln\left({\frac{{C}_{2}}{{C}_{1}}}\right)$ is infinitesimal, so $\frac{ln\left({\frac{{C}_{2}}{{C}_{1}}}\right)}{dt}=\frac{dx}{dt}$ is a derivative of sorts. That would make $dx=ln\left({1-\mu \ dt}\right)$.   
OH MY GOD\! Mark this moment in the history books\! 9:46 PM\! I might just be slap happy, but this feels like potentially one of the most important moments in me life\! [Look for yourself](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/pzwuu87z6j). I made the program, and printed out a bunch of results. In this example, I made the danger increase linearly\! Then, from there, I calculated with [my varying danger equation](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.k09b8wfewvac) what that would come out to according to my logic, and I plotted that curve on top of my Desmos stuff – and sure enough, it came out perfectly\! This is awesome\! (Granted, I did a function regression there, and I’m still yet to see if my actual coefficients come out right – but that’s the next step\!)  
So, to actually plug in coefficients, here we can see that, (based on my code), the danger formula is $\mu =time\times 1{0}^{-11}$. Awesome\! This means my integral would come out to $\int\limits_{t}^{0}t\times 1{0}^{-11}dt=-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2\times 1{0}^{-11}}$. Therefore, the coefficient $m$ in $100,000\ {e}^{-m\ {t}^{2}}$ should be $0.000000000005$, and *what does the Desmos come out with…?* Why, $0.00000501451159274$. How close is this, then? This is pretty much exactly a million times more – and because it’s such a perfect power of ten difference, that basically tells us it’s right right there. (Also, I forgot I divided off a million in the program for the units, so… there\!)  
I like wanna cry right now this is so awesome\! My instinct, exactly 236 days of pure math ago, WAS FREAKING RIGHT\! This means it’s officially set in stone that $\mu =\frac{\dot{R}}{1-R}$, so I’ll write that equation just there in bold colored letters to get the point across\! Anyways, I’d better get to sleep right now if I want to wake up in the morning\! Peace\!

| One key question regarding our Golden Trek, and the potential of a Golden Point in our future, is how these things might apply to our actions in the future. Clearly, certain actions are superior to others, because they contribute further to the Golden Point.  The most basic type of ethical system to apply is some form of *Binary Golden Ethics*, which states that for every action of two potentials – that is, one action, or its inverse – the action with the higher Aurutance should be selected rather than the alternative. For example, if throwing a can in the recycling increases the Achievement of the Earth by a higher amount than throwing it in the trash, then by Binary Golden Ethics, given this decision of two possibilities, the recycling option is ethically superior. The amount of Achievement for which the Earth increases upon the action of the decision is called the action’s *Aurutance*, and altogether, the set of the two potential actions, the decision itself, holds a property called its *Golden Binary Weight*, which is the Aurutance of the high decision minus the Aurutance of the low decision. Most decisions of two outcomes hold a low Golden Binary Weight, but some hold a much higher value, such as the decision during the Cuban Missile Crisis to not unleash nuclear war.  |

## **Revisited T. rex Population Study / Danger**

### *Saturday, January 29, 2022, 8:05 AM EST*

I mean, lately I’ve been working on some pretty hard core stuff, like paper writing and Golden Point considering, so I thought I might give myself something of a “break” so to speak, to think of something simple and light just for the fun of it. And, as my eureka-mind tells me, that thing is going to be T. rex population studies.   
Now, I already did this once before, however I want to kind of just totally redo it from scratch now, so that I might have insights I glossed over the first time.  
Essentially my goal is this – rather than angrily scanning over useless graphs I find online, I’m going to try and do a much more *to-the-root* analysis, for which I almost, like, generate the wanted data from scratch and stuff. I have something of a skill with breaking a query down to its smallest parts, and then resembling them into some kind of algorithm or logical statement – or at least I’ve found that I can do this better than the people around me, for whatever reason. So, how’s about we put that to the test in this no-stakes, math for the fun of it session to start my morning.   
Now – the first thing to consider – is that a nest of ${n}_{0}$ T. rexes are born. If we can average-ly follow them all the way to adulthood, then we have something of a function of T. rex populations. So, right off the bat, we can define a little pocket-equality: a T. rex needs to eat a constant $\varepsilon$ food kilograms per time for every kilogram of its own weight. That is, a T. rex that’s twice as big needs twice as much food, and that’s all there is to it. That gets us $E=\varepsilon \ m$, where $m$ is the mass of the T. rex, and $E$ is the rate at which it eats food, (so, units mass per time). Now, if a constant amount of food is available at any given time, then we can create the rate of food availability variable as $F$. (The reason it’s rate, is because it’s all about the replenishing instead of the net availability, which is pretty much constant). Now, for food availability $F$, we are allowed a maximum of $n=\frac{F}{E}$  T. rexes in order to be fully sustained, because anything more than that, and the amount of food available will be less than the amount of food the T. rexes need to keep them all fed. Therefore, if we substitute around with this, we get $n=\frac{F}{\varepsilon \ m}$, and thus that gives us something of an equation for the number of T. rexes at any given mass – roughly.   
But there’s something of a problem to this – technically, this $n$ would be infinitesimal in real life, because for every exact mass value, there is an infinitesimal number of rexes which exist in some area of land. But still, if we can get relative values between different masses, then we’re in business nonetheless. For instance, if we look at a T. rex of one unit mass, and another T. rex that’s double the size, then what? Well, the double the mass one should have to eat double the food to sustain itself, assuming they have similar-ish metabolism, and so it all comes down to what is comparatively available. For this – let’s try and picture the Cretaceous ecosystem for a second.  
So, a small T. rex is going to be eating small things – small reptiles, mammals, and dinosaurs – whereas a big T. rex will eat big things, like Triceratops and others like that. If we imagine that the kill-rate in both is roughly optimized by evolution, such that they are pretty much the same overall, then we can imagine a cumulative distribution of prey masses just as we do for T. rex masses. We might define $b\left({{m}_{b}}\right)$, which is such a cumulative distribution. Now, obviously, the lower masses ${m}_{b}$ will mean higher numbers of individuals, $b$, but to what extent that is? Well, if we assume that these individuals all sit roughly at the second trophic level, then altogether they will be roughly eating the same “plane” of foliage. That is, if for mass ${m}_{b}$, a herbivore eats at a rate of ${\varepsilon }_{b}\ {m}_{b}$ plant mass per time, then if there are relatively $b'\left({{m}_{b}}\right)$ of animals at that mass, this means a relative rate of eating at ${\varepsilon }_{b}\ {m}_{b}\ b'\left({{m}_{b}}\right)$, and so if we integrate that, now we have a function of cumulative distribution of amount of food eaten for each mass, which is ${\varepsilon }_{b}\ \int\limits_{0}^{{m}_{b}}x\ b'\left({x}\right)\ dx$. Now, because $b\left({{m}_{b}}\right)$ is dimensionless, the units on ${\varepsilon }_{b}\ \int\limits_{0}^{{m}_{b}}x\ b'\left({x}\right)\ dx$ are going to have to be *mass per time*, which is just an eating rate in and of itself. Now, if we call the largest herbivore mass ${w}_{b}$, then ${\varepsilon }_{b}\ \int\limits_{0}^{{w}_{b}}x\ b'\left({x}\right)\ dx$ is the total amount of food eaten by all herbivores, and yeah.

### *Saturday, January 29, 2022, 12:02 PM*

You know what – actually – I think I’ve been overcomplicating this – so how’s about we look at it differently.  
We already can get the relative numbers of T. rexes with $n=\frac{F}{\varepsilon \ m}$, so we’re onto something just with that. This makes almost like a probability density function of T. rex count. And because of that fact, if we call the original number of T. rexes ${n}_{0}$, then the proportion which survive to each age is $\frac{n}{{n}_{0}}$\! Beautiful\! That’s amazing, because it’s actually pretty dang fundamental if you think about it\! Therefore, for an original mass of ${m}_{0}$, corresponding to an original number, (which is essentially population density in essence), of ${n}_{0}=\frac{F}{\varepsilon \ {m}_{0}}$, we get a total result of $\frac{n}{{n}_{0}}=S=\frac{{m}_{0}}{m}$. This, my friends, is the proportion of T. rexes which survive to each new age, simply put. Now, reusing [one of my old regression equations of the mass](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.a766fmvmbiis) of a T. rex by age at $m=\frac{5855}{1\ +\ 213\times {e}^{-0.319\ t}}$, (in kilograms and years), we get a value of $S$ which is $S\left({t}\right)=\frac{1\ +\ 213\ \times \ {e}^{-0.319\ t}}{1\ +\ 213\ \times {\ e}^{-0.319\ \times \ 0}}$, otherwise known as $S\left({t}\right)=\frac{1\ +\ 213\ \times \ {e}^{-0.319\ t}}{214}$. I think just from the *constant rate of food input per kilogram of mass* figure is just enough that is needed to at least show strong evidence for the fundamentality of this, so onward, I guess\!  
Now, since danger is the negative logarithmic derivative of survival chance with respect to time, we get a danger of $\mu \left({t}\right)=-\frac{\dot{S}}{S}$, and so in this case, $\mu \left({t}\right)=\frac{67.947}{213\ +\ {e}^{0.319\ t}}$. But, keep in mind that this is written in terms of years, (as was an original defining property), and so in order to convert to millipares, we must simply multiply by a factor of $195.7$, because that is the value of $\frac{1\ mort\ per\ year}{14\ micromorts\ per\ day}$, which is equivalent to $\frac{1\ mort\ per\ year}{1\ millipare}$. Thus, the final millipares danger is $\mu \left({t}\right)=\frac{13.3\ \times \ 1{0}^{3}\ millipares}{213\ +\ {e}^{0.319\ t}}$, which can also be cleaned up a little into the form of $\mu \left({t}\right)=\frac{13.3\ pares}{213\ +\ {e}^{0.319\ t}}$. Very beautiful indeed\! [Here’s the Desmos](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/tyiep9yfs7) to go with that, too, by the way\!   
Note that this equation represents merely the *lower bound* of T. rex danger – built off of what is possible at a minimum to sustain the population. There should be, however, other ecological forces which come into play as well, and those other forces will of course affect this, too. This also tells us that the danger that T. rexes face at birth is no less than $62\ millipares$, which is actually quite a bit – about the same as that which is faced by a 21st century *98 year old*. As for the steps to actually solve that, if we [*look back to one of my previous entires*](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.d2mr0jbv3l9o), pulling the danger equation, ($\mu \left({t}\right)=\frac{34443.5\ {e}^{0.091\ t}\ +\ \left({41.94\ -\ t}\right)\ \left({30.9571\ +\ t}\right)\ \left({591.421\ +\ \left({t\ -\ 44.9596}\right)\ t}\right)}{3.3\ \times \ 1{0}^{6}}\ millipares$), and setting it to our millipare danger value, we get the result of $t=98\ years$. So, literally, being a ninety-eight year old in modern society is no less dangerous than being a newborn Tyrannosaurus rex during the Dark Era. Also, just for the fun of it – which human and T. rex ages have equivalent danger? Why – that would be age 34, where the two equations are actually equal, (meaning their curves just so happen to cross, as one goes up, and the other goes down). This means that if you’re in your early thirties, a T. rex who is the same age as you would have just about the same danger, interestingly\!   
Now, I’m going to try to figure out the egg situation again, and see where it takes me. If there exists an egg-laying constant $\xi$, such that a T. rex with mass $m$ will lay eggs at a rate of $\xi \ m$, then how about we try and figure out some egg stats with that. I think the best statistical balance of things would be to set the math up such that exactly one egg for each T. rex will live to sexual maturity, (say at 14 years of ago), after which point it will start to lay its own eggs, thus propagating the recursion or whatever. The goal of this is for the population size to stay exactly constant throughout the generations, which means that for every couple of T. rexes, there are two eggs laid, or in other words, one new egg for every T. rex. So, if a T. rex lays eggs at a rate of $\xi \ m\left({t}\right)$, then at age $t$ beyond sexual maturity, it will have laid $\int\limits_{15.5}^{t}\xi \ m\left({t}\right)\ dt$ eggs. Now, if we come up with a constant of $q$, which tells us the proportion of T. rexes who live to sexual maturity, then T. rexes which live beyond sexual maturity should lay an average of exactly $\frac{1}{q}$ eggs, such that the two balance out – or in other words, so that one egg will last for every T. rex which is laying them. So, let’s math\!   
Since the mass equation is already known as $m\left({t}\right)=\frac{5855}{1\ +\ 213\times {e}^{-0.319\ t}}$, then we can automatically turn our integral into $\int\limits_{15.5}^{t}\frac{5855\ \xi }{1\ +\ 213\times {e}^{-0.319\ t}}\ dt$, which tells us the total number of eggs laid up until age $t$. Let’s define this as the function $E(t)$, such that $E\left({t}\right)=\int\limits_{15.5}^{t}\frac{5855\ \xi }{1\ +\ 213\times {e}^{-0.319\ t}}\ dt=18354.2\ \xi \ \left({-5.86759+ln\left({213+{e}^{0.319\ t}}\right)}\right)$. Now, with this determined, it must follow that *the average number of eggs laid in the life of a sexually mature T. rex is 1 egg*. Here’s what I’m going to do, actually, by looking through some of my old calculations in the form of [Desmos](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/urw79klby2): for a survival chance function $S\left({t}\right)=\frac{1\ +\ 213\ \times \ {e}^{-0.319\ t}}{214}$, and thus a risk of death function $R\left({t}\right)=1-\frac{1\ +\ 213\ \times \ {e}^{-0.319\ t}}{214}$, the number of eggs laid in the lifetimes of T. rexes who survive to percentile $x$ is $E\left({{R}^{-1}\left({x}\right)}\right)$, (such that ${R}^{-1}\left({x}\right)$ is measuring the age of death of said percentile). Then, because of how averages work in integration, the average number of eggs laid by all T. rexes between percentiles $0$ and $x$ is $\frac{\int\limits_{R\left({15.5}\right)}^{x}E\left({{R}^{-1}\left({x}\right)}\right)\ dx}{x\ -\ R\left({15.5}\right)}$, and so therefore the average number of eggs laid among all T. rexes is $\frac{\int\limits_{R\left({15.5}\right)}^{1}E\left({{R}^{-1}\left({x}\right)}\right)\ dx}{x\ -\ R\left({15.5}\right)}$. The final result we want is for $\frac{\int\limits_{R\left({15.5}\right)}^{1}E\left({{R}^{-1}\left({x}\right)}\right)\ dx}{x\ -\ R\left({15.5}\right)}=\frac{1}{q}$, so how about I start building this in a new Desmos to make that happen graphically and everything.  
Ok – I’m back\! And [*here’s that Desmos I was talking about*](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/7s0ouy6xgd). And I was able to take this amazing constant out of it: $\xi =0.00761464761965\ \frac{eggs}{year\ kilogram}$. If we try to pick the very best unit for this constant, we can also write this as $\xi =21\ \frac{eggs}{metric\ kiloton\ day}$. This tells us that a T. rex like Sue, [which weighed about $8,460\ kg$](https://www.history.com/news/worlds-biggest-t-rex-canada-scotty-dinosaur#:~:text=rex%20fossils%2C%20including%20the%20famous,Persons%20said%20in%20a%20statement.), would have been laying an average of about $5.4\ eggs\ per\ month$, or 65 eggs per year. That’s about an egg per week. On the other side of things, a T. rex which has just reached sexual maturity would only be laying 18 eggs per year. Remember, ecologically speaking, these are essentially two different species, they’re so different. One weighs a good two and a half times as much as the other, they’re hunting different animals, and their anatomies are very different in key ways. One is a runner while one is a tank, and so on. Some other interesting stats, too? [Here’s the Desmos graph](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/hq9q1odxbd) of the proportion of eggs laid by T. rexes under each age. Half of all eggs laid are laid by a T. rex younger than 21 years of age, and a third of all eggs are laid by a T. rex younger than nineteen years old. Also, another third of eggs are laid by T. rexes older than twenty-three. The top fourth of eggs come from a T. rex older than twenty-four, and the bottom fourth come from T. rexes younger than eighteen. As a matter of fact – I think I’m going to make a rough table right in this document to showcase what this function tells us\! Here goes:

The inflection point, you will notice, is during the 16th year – and that is when the most eggs out of any single age are expected to be laid. Here’s a fun exercise I want to try, actually – why not take this distribution here, and find its standard deviation?  
I tried to look for an algorithm to get this for over an hour now, (yep, this has been painstaking\!), but I still haven’t managed to make anything work\! So, what I ended up doing was just zooming into the graph of the probability density function, and then just dropping a bunch of points on it as closely accurate as I could, and then just stuck a regression on that. Here’s my result: *standard deviation of about $15.6\ years$*. Because the function I had going on already is more or less an approximation, in being a lower bound and everything, I guess the normal distribution of $\frac{{e}^{-\frac{{\left({t-15.5}\right)}^{2}}{107}}}{9.4}$ is accurate enough that all is well. And, obviously this integrates to an error function rather than a logistic function – but I kind of like that in a way, as it puts more of a limiting factor on older ages than the logistic can, which in a way is closer to the truth, once the effects of aging kick in and all. The cumulative distribution of this, by the way, would be $f(x)=erf\left({0.0966736\ t-1.49844}\right)$. I took the liberty of slightly altering it from just the pure integral of the other version over there, as this has to in fact roof off at one. Just a small, like 3% magnitude shift, but the $f(x)$ version I put there is definitely better. Now, this isn’t exactly purely fundamentality informed, and more represents something of a regression, but it is still close enough that it holds legitimate information to it like a sponge with water kind of.   
Here’s another good fun fact about this by the way: The T. rex age group which represents the fiftieth percentile in egg-laying output has members which are just about half the size of full grown rexes, and remember are 20 years old. They had a danger of 14.9 millipares, about the same as a modern 80 year old human, and their danger was in fact falling by 3.6 millipares per year, which is past the inflection point of 5 millipares loss per year, which had occurred three years earlier – and in fact this 20 year old rex danger value is about a fourth the original danger upon the event of hatching. ## **Quick Cool Immortality Calculation**

Hey there\! Here’s a quick calculation I just did for the chances of a system being immortal with the following danger equation: $\mu \left({t}\right)=a\ {e}^{b\ t}\ {cos}^{2}\left({t}\right)$. Wolfram|Alpha processed all the heavy calculations for me, and the only creative-ish thing I did was take out a huge term from one of the risk functions upon realizing that it would equal zero as $t$ tends to infinity – provided that $b$ is a negative number in fact, which of course is our default given when it comes to this stuff anyway\! So, the final answer, which is the probability of immortality of this system, is ${S}_{\infty }={e}^{\frac{a\ \left({2\ +\ {b}^{2}}\right)}{b\ \left({4\ +\ {b}^{2}}\right)}}$.  
Since the exponential version of this, holding danger function $\mu \left({t}\right)=a\ {e}^{b\ t}$, (which is essentially just the same thing – just not occupying that downward wave pattern), holds immortality chance ${S}_{\infty }={e}^{\frac{a}{b}}$, then literally the wave version can be thought of as the $\frac{4\ +\ {b}^{2}}{2\ +\ {b}^{2}}$th root of it\! *And*, if we want to be even more creative – if you think about it, this wave version in particular tends to sit fully under the exponential, however if we want to really picture the exponential which best fits to the wave function, then we might consider the one which fits perfectly through the middle. Because ${cos}^{2}\left({t}\right)$ alternates between zero and one, the middle is at a half, which is like its “equilibrium point” so to speak, so if we divide the exponential by half, essentially halving $a$, we get an immortality chance of ${S}_{\infty }={e}^{\frac{a}{2\ b}}$, meaning compared to *that* function, which neatly splits the wave in half at every point, the wave immortality chances represents the $\frac{4\ +\ {b}^{2}}{4\ +\ {2b}^{2}}$th root of it\! Actually, I’m noticing now that this number can never be greater than one for any negative, (and therefore real) $b$, *which means that* we shouldn’t write this as a root at all, but instead as a power\! So, for danger equation $\mu \left({t}\right)=\frac{a}{2}\ {e}^{b\ t}$, the wave version has a probability of immortality which is the clean version to the power of $\frac{4\ +\ 2{b}^{2}}{4\ +\ {b}^{2}}$. Neat\! So, if $b=-1$, for instance, this turns into $\frac{6}{5}=1.2$, which isn’t actually a super huge difference. In fact – I wonder how far this can go – (like, I just tried to set it to two, (so we get a square), but Wolfram|Alpha told me that that was in fact impossible). So, if we do $\lim\limits_{{b} \rightarrow {-\infty }}\frac{4\ +\ 2{b}^{2}}{4\ +\ {b}^{2}}$, we get $\lim\limits_{{b} \rightarrow {-\infty }}\frac{4\ +\ 2{b}^{2}}{4\ +\ {b}^{2}}=2$. So, heh\! There’s the two, I guess\! (As for why that’s the limit, it’s easy – just do lead polynomial term over lead polynomial term and stuff\!)  
This means that the clean function’s immortality chances can never be less than the square root of the wave function’s immortality chances\!

Anyways, so all we need to get ${S}_{\infty }$ is obviously just the ${S}_{\infty }=1-\lim\limits_{{t} \rightarrow {\infty }}R\left({t}\right)$, which is, well… $R\left({t}\right)=1-{\left({\frac{{e}^{k\ {t}_{0}}\ +\ 1}{{e}^{k\ t}\ +\ {e}^{k\ {t}_{0}}}}\right)}^{\frac{L}{k}}$, so when $t$ goes to infinity, $k$ MUST be a negative number to further any simplification, which yields $1-{\left({\frac{{e}^{k\ {t}_{0}}\ +\ 1}{{e}^{k\ {t}_{0}}}}\right)}^{\frac{L}{k}}$, and thus $1-{\left({1+{e}^{-k\ {t}_{0}}}\right)}^{\frac{L}{k}}$. ## **A Couple Ways to Write Round Toward Zero**

### *Friday, February 4, 2022, 5:39 PM EST*

Ya’ know how the floor function always rounds *down*, even for negatives? Well, I just thought of a couple of ways to make a function which *rounds to the nearest integer in the direction of zero*, so, like, $-3.5$ would go to $-3$ instead of $-4$. I guess I’ll put all the ways in a bullet list in the order I think of them\!

1. $\frac{x}{\left|{x}\right|}\ floor\left({\left|{x}\right|}\right)$

This one is the simplest way I could think of – essentially we want to replicate the floor function in negatives like the floor function on positives, at least when disregarding the negative sign. So, let’s *literally* disregard the negative sign, with an absolute value\! This way, we’re doing the positive version for any sign of $x$. But, once that’s done – so a floor of an absolute value – we need to flip the negatives back to their rightful place, so we just do that with a simple multiplication of a sign function\!

2. $floor\left({x}\right)+\frac{1\ -\ \frac{x}{\left|{x}\right|}}{2}$

This one just works as a clever translation. I noticed how for this new function, all of the values on the negative side are just one unit greater than the floor function there, so I just took advantage of that by shifting around the sign function to make the positives zero and the negatives one, and then add like so and you’re done\!

3. $floor\left({\frac{x\ +\ \left|{x}\right|}{2}}\right)+ceiling\left({\frac{x\ -\ \left|{x}\right|}{2}}\right)$

This version just takes advantage of how the negative side of this new function is pretty much just the ceiling function, whereas the positive side is the floor function. Therefore, if we set all the negatives to zero, but keep the positives constant, by taking the average of the absolute value and the linear, and then take the floor of all *that*, then we have the floor on the positives, and zero on the negatives. Next, if we do the opposite on the negative side, but with the ceiling function – which this time instead of being an average of the line and the absolute value, is an average of the line and the *negative* absolute value – then now we get the ceiling function for the negatives and zero for the positives. All you have to do with these is add them, and you have your answer\!  
(Plus, the added bonus of this version is that all points are in the domain, unlike the first two, which technically don’t contain $x=0$)\!

4. I didn’t think of a four\! I’m sorry, alright\!

Ok, that’s it. Peace\!

| THESE MUST BE SATISFIED TO HAVE IMMORTALITY |
| :---: |
| $\lim\limits_{{t} \rightarrow {\infty }}\mu \left({t}\right)=0$ |
| $\lim\limits_{{t} \rightarrow {\infty }}\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=1$ |

First of all, for the first one\! $\lim\limits_{{t} \rightarrow {\infty }}a\ {e}^{b\ t}\ {cos}^{2}\left({c\ t+d}\right)=0$. I think this one’s kind of obvious – $b$ needs to be negative, such that $b<0$. I mean, either that, or $a=0$. Either will do\! Anything differing from this automatically fails the property, so you can think of it as we’ve just condensed the set of what works to $b<0$ essentially.   
Now, for the second property\! The first derivative of this, $\frac{d}{dt}\left({a\ {e}^{b\ t}\ {cos}^{2}\left({c\ t+d}\right)}\right)$, is $\mu '\left({t}\right)=a\ b\ {e}^{b\ t}\ {cos}^{2}\left({c\ t+d}\right)-2\ a\ c\ {e}^{b\ t}\ sin\left({c\ t+d}\right)\ cos\left({c\ t+d}\right)$, which I guess is also equivalent to $\mu '\left({t}\right)=a\ {e}^{b\ t}\ cos\left({c\ t+d}\right)\ \left({b\ cos\left({c\ t+d}\right)-2\ c\ sin\left({c\ t+d}\right)}\right)$. That one I did mentally, but I’m going to take advantage of Wolfram Alpha for the second derivative, just so I’m not here all night\!   
My result, then, is $\mu ''\left({t}\right)=a\ {e}^{b\ t}\ \left({\left({{b}^{2}-2{\ c}^{2}}\right)\ {cos}^{2}\left({c\ t+d}\right)-4\ b\ c\ sin\left({c\ t+d}\right)\ cos\left({c\ t+d}\right)+2\ {c}^{2}\ {sin}^{2}\left({c\ t+d}\right)}\right)$.  
Now, all that’s left is to put them all into $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}$, and do out the limit. Again, I’m going to use Wolfram|Alpha just to lower the calculation time – and that gets us $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=1-\frac{2\ {c}^{2}}{{\left({b\ cos\left({c\ t\ +\ d}\right)\ -\ 2\ c\ sin\left({c\ t\ +\ d}\right)}\right)}^{2}}$, and then so if we take the limit – we’re going to need that second term $\frac{2\ {c}^{2}}{{\left({b\ cos\left({c\ t\ +\ d}\right)\ -\ 2\ c\ sin\left({c\ t\ +\ d}\right)}\right)}^{2}}$ to equal zero exactly, which means the denominator of it $\left({b\ cos\left({c\ t\ +\ d}\right)\ -\ 2\ c\ sin\left({c\ t\ +\ d}\right)}\right)$ needs to be an asymptote – which it is decidedly not\! Huh\!  
So, this gave me quite the surprise a few minutes ago when I first graphed it – but luckily all is not lost, because I have a perfectly good explanation for why this paradox of sorts occurred\!  
Essentially what’s happening with this, is that this graph keeps kissing zero danger, and then leaping back up to the tip of the exponential, before falling down and up again. Flatly speaking, zero danger is practically impossible. So just by defining it in this function – which *hypothetically* would indeed grant a possibility of immortality – still runs the problem of being physically impossible itself. You just can’t put this kind of danger function in the real world. But no problem – I thought – because we can instead stop the kissing zero danger phenomenon, with something like this: $\mu \left({t}\right)=a\ {e}^{b\ t}\times \left({1-\frac{{cos}^{2}\left({c\ t+d}\right)}{2}}\right)$. This, in the least, is physically possible, which is a start. Let’s try the same algorithms on this and see if it works.  
The first property, again, has the same result – and the second property? Jumping straight to $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}$ in [Wolfram|Alpha](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=%28%28%28a+exp%28bt%29+%281-%28cos%5E2%28c+t+%2B+d%29%29%2F2%29%29%29+%2F+%28%28d%2Fdt+%28a+exp%28bt%29+%281-%28cos%5E2%28c+t+%2B+d%29%29%2F2%29%29%29%5E2%29%29+*+%28%28d%2Fdt+d%2Fdt+%28a+exp%28bt%29+%281-%28cos%5E2%28c+t+%2B+d%29%29%2F2%29%29%29%29), we get [*this*](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=-%282+%281+-+1%2F2+cos%5E2%28c+t+%2B+d%29%29+%28%28b%5E2+-+2+c%5E2%29+cos%5E2%28c+t+%2B+d%29+-+2+b%5E2+-+4+b+c+sin%28c+t+%2B+d%29+cos%28c+t+%2B+d%29+%2B+2+c%5E2+sin%5E2%28c+t+%2B+d%29%29%29%2F%28b+cos%5E2%28c+t+%2B+d%29+-+2+b+-+2+c+sin%28c+t+%2B+d%29+cos%28c+t+%2B+d%29%29%5E2), (which I think’ll be too insane to actually write out, so i just linked to it there), and then if we take the limit of that as $t$ heads to infinity, it becomes… well… something or other. The problem here is that the infinite tendency of this is some sort of wave, so the answer alternates like the sequence $0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1…$. Now, the thing is, we can still find the value of $0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1…$, though, by setting $A=0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1…$, and thus $A=1-A$ just by looking at how the terms work, and thus algebra gets us $A=\frac{1}{2}$. I think we can apply the same trick to our particular $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}$ here. My hunch is is that if we take the average value of the function over one of its periods, then we’ll be in business. First of all, then – what’s the period? Well, because the inside of all of these waves have to look the same by the chain rule – $\left({c\ t+d}\right)$, (that is, none of them are able to be changed by the transformations we’ve taken – derivatives and division), we can say that when $\left({c\ t+d}\right)=2\pi$, we’re looking at at least one period since $\left({c\ t+d}\right)=0$, and in fact the number of full periods is an integer, either one or greater. This is really useful, because now all we have to do is take the average of this function over any single multiple of $2\pi$ for the integral range, and then we’re good. Let’s do this, then\! If we pick $\left({c\ t+d}\right)=2\pi$ as our high bound, then that’s $t=\frac{2\pi \ -\ d}{c}$ for the high bound, and $t=-\frac{d}{c}$ for the low bound. Awesome\! If we integrate our particular version of $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}$, which again I didn’t write down because it’s too long – but you can just imagine it I guess – we get an indefinite integral which I don’t mind writing down because it’s so conveniently short, of $\frac{d}{c}+t-\frac{2\ c\ sin\left({2\ \left({c\ t\ +\ d}\right)}\right)}{b\ \left({-3\ b\ +\ b\ cos\left({2\ \left({c\ t\ +\ d}\right)}\right)\ -\ 2\ c\ sin\left({2\ \left({c\ t\ +\ d}\right)}\right)}\right)}$, and then simply applying the bounds gets us $\frac{2\pi }{c}$. Awesome\! Or… is it? I mean, this only works with the principle for $c=2\pi$, and frankly that’s a little upsetting. Maybe this only works for product integrals or something? Maybe the very fact that this magical function $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}$ runs *through* one now and again, and decidedly doesn’t ever shoot off to infinity in an asymptote is sufficient? I mean, I looked at one example of this function, where I substituted $c=1.\ d=0.\ b=-1$, and it did indeed run through one twice per period.   
Actually – here’s an idea – let’s see if I can physically find a function for which $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=2$. Do any even exist? The answer was pretty much easier than I expected – I just write down that differential equation into Wolfram|Alpha, and it gave me $\mu \left({t}\right)=\frac{{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}\ +\ t}$. Well, that was easy\! What about for $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=\frac{1}{2}$? Well, that would be $\mu \left({t}\right)=\frac{{c}_{1}^{2}\ {t}^{2}}{4\ {c}_{2}}+{c}_{1}t+{c}_{2}$. Interesting\! The first one is definitely some form of shifted rational-hyperbola, whereas this one is decidedly a quadratic. Who knew quadratics behaved this way\!? To take this further, if we set $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=3$, then we get $\mu \left({t}\right)=\frac{{c}_{2}}{\sqrt{{c}_{1}\ +\ 2t}}$. Wow, this is magnificent\! This feels like when in [*Defending Your Life*](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0101698/?ref_=ext_shr_lnk), they get to see their past lives – totally different stories which are popping up out of the aether\! Also, I guess, if $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=\pi$, we get $\mu \left({t}\right)={c}_{2}\ \sqrt[1-\pi ]{{c}_{1}-\pi t+t}$. Interesting… and if $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=-1$, we get $\mu \left({t}\right)={c}_{2}\ \sqrt{{c}_{1}+2t}$. And – this is really going to be the crazy one – if $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=i$, then Wolfram|Alpha returns $\mu \left({t}\right)={c}_{2}\ {\left({{c}_{1}+\left({1-i}\right)\ t}\right)}^{\frac{1+i}{2}}$. I think I’m noticing something of a pattern, now – depending on what we set $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}$ to, on the last three of those, if we substitute it around, we get the desired result – like, if we swap the $\pi$ out for an $i$ or a $-1$ or whatever, it perfectly maps to the new version. Even the $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=2$ making $\mu \left({t}\right)=\frac{{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}\ +\ t}$ version follows this trend, if you’re willing to make ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ their opposites comparatively. Ok – last crazy one – if we set $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=t$, then we get $\mu \left({t}\right)={c}_{2}\ {e}^{\frac{2\ {tan}^{-1}\left({\frac{1\ -\ t}{\sqrt{2{c}_{1}\ -\ 1}}}\right)}{\sqrt{2{c}_{1}\ -\ 1}}}$, which is pretty dang interesting. If I plot this in Desmos, then I get [*this craziness*](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/g3qgo8a2ix). Ok – one last crazy one for real this time – let’s make something that decidedly *isn’t* $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=1$, but *tends that way* nonetheless\! How’s about we try $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=1+{e}^{-t}$. Technically, because this limit tends to one, this danger function would have a shot at immortality\! Anyways, Wolfram’s differential equation solver gives me $\mu \left({t}\right)={c}_{2}\ {\left({1-{c}_{1}\ {e}^{t}}\right)}^{-\frac{1}{{c}_{1}}}$. And, [in Desmos…](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/ilxqywl95t) I guess we could also write this as $\mu \left({t}\right)=\frac{{c}_{2}}{\sqrt[{c}_{1}]{1\ -\ {c}_{1}\ {e}^{t}}}$, by the way. Also, technically at $t=0$, this function has a $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}$ value of $\frac{\mu ''\left({t}\right)\ \mu \left({t}\right)}{\mu '\left({t}\right)\ \mu '\left({t}\right)}=2$, so there it behaves something like a $\frac{1}{x}$ function, which is kind of cool to think about.   
Just one last thing I wanted to try during this entry – how about we look at the function $\mu \left({t}\right)=a\ sin\left({{e}^{-t}}\right)$, which according to my table WORKS for potential immortality, (and it isn’t a wave, so we don’t have to worry about any of those crazy repercussions there) – so why don’t we calculate the physical chance of immortality for this kind of function? First up, we need to get the survival chance function, $S\left({t}\right)$, so if we punch the relation into Wolfram|Alpha: $a\ sin\left({{e}^{-t}}\right)=-\frac{S'\left({t}\right)}{S\left({t}\right)}$, we get $S\left({t}\right)={c}_{1}\ {e}^{a\ Si\left({{e}^{-t}}\right)}$, where $Si$ represents the *Sine Integral*, defined as $Si\left({z}\right)=\int\limits_{0}^{z}\frac{sin\left({t}\right)}{t}\ dt$. Pretty fun integral there\! Now, looking at our resulting survival chance function, there, I think we can generalize better than that, actually\! How about we swap out the danger function for the more general $a\ sin\left({{b\ e}^{-c\ t}+d}\right)=-\frac{S'\left({t}\right)}{S\left({t}\right)}$, and see where that takes us? Well, according to Wolfram|Alpha’s built in differential equation solver, this means equates to $S\left({t}\right)={k}_{1}\ {e}^{\frac{a}{c}\ \left({sin\left({d}\right)\ Ci\left({b\ {e}^{-c\ t}}\right)\ +\ cos\left({d}\right)\ Si\left({b\ {e}^{-c\ t}}\right)}\right)}$, where now we also have the *Cosine Integral*, defined as $Ci\left({z}\right)=\int\limits_{\infty }^{z}\frac{cos\left({t}\right)}{t}\ dt$. Cool\! Oh, and also we have to solve for ${k}_{1}$, such that substituting $S\left({0}\right)=1$, and that gets us $S\left({t}\right)={e}^{\frac{a}{c}\ \left({sin\left({d}\right)\ \left({Ci\left({b\ {e}^{-c\ t}}\right)\ -\ Ci\left({b}\right)}\right)\ +\ cos\left({d}\right)\ \left({Si\left({b\ {e}^{-c\ t}}\right)\ -\ Si\left({b}\right)}\right)}\right)}$. Now, the last step – run ${S}_{\infty }=\lim\limits_{{t} \rightarrow {\infty }}S\left({t}\right)$. First of all, if we make $c$ positive, then this would have to be ${S}_{\infty }={e}^{\frac{a}{c}\ \left({sin\left({d}\right)\ \left({Ci\left({0}\right)\ -\ Ci\left({b}\right)}\right)\ +\ cos\left({d}\right)\ \left({Si\left({0}\right)\ -\ Si\left({b}\right)}\right)}\right)}=DNE$, so that much is weeded out. Therefore, if $c$ is negative, then we get ${S}_{\infty }={e}^{\frac{a}{c}\ \left({sin\left({d}\right)\ \left({Ci\left({\infty }\right)\ -\ Ci\left({b}\right)}\right)\ +\ cos\left({d}\right)\ \left({Si\left({\infty }\right)\ -\ Si\left({b}\right)}\right)}\right)}={e}^{\frac{a}{c}\ \left({sin\left({d}\right)\ \left({\ -\ Ci\left({b}\right)}\right)\ +\ cos\left({d}\right)\ \left({\frac{\pi }{2}\ -\ Si\left({b}\right)}\right)}\right)}$, (provided that $b$ is positive). And that gets us a final, simplified answer, of ${S}_{\infty }={e}^{\frac{a}{c}\ \left({\left({\frac{\pi }{2}\ -\ Si\left({b}\right)}\right)\ cos\left({d}\right)\ -\ Ci\left({b}\right)\ sin\left({d}\right)}\right)}$. If we’re writing this purely in standard form, too, (so it can be Desmos compatible), then we might write ${S}_{\infty }={e}^{\frac{a}{c}\ \left({\left({\int\limits_{b}^{\infty }\frac{sin\left({z}\right)}{z}\ dz}\right)\ cos\left({d}\right)\ +\ \left({\int\limits_{b}^{\infty }\frac{cos\left({z}\right)}{z}\ dz}\right)\ sin\left({d}\right)}\right)}$. I love the symmetry in that\! Actually – though – for physical Desmos, I’m going to do a slight alteration, into ${S}_{\infty }={e}^{\frac{a}{c}\ \left({\left({\frac{\pi }{2}\ -\ \int\limits_{0}^{b}\frac{sin\left({z}\right)}{z}\ dz}\right)\ cos\left({d}\right)\ +\ \left({\int\limits_{b}^{\infty }\frac{cos\left({z}\right)}{z}\ dz}\right)\ sin\left({d}\right)}\right)}$, that way we don’t have to deal with infinities as much\! Here’s [Desmos](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/vbv38rrfcs), and here’s [Wolfram](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=exp%28%28a+%28-Ci%28b%29+sin%28d%29+%2B+cos%28d%29+%28%CF%80%2F2+-+Si%28b%29%29%29%29%2Fc%29). If we try substituting with the example of $\mu \left({t}\right)=a\ sin\left({{e}^{-t}}\right)$ in mind, then $a=a,\ b=1,\ c=1,\ d=0$, so therefore ${S}_{\infty }={e}^{a\ \left({Si\left({1}\right)\ -\ \frac{\pi }{2}}\right)}$. (Also, just for the record – something happened along the way I think where $c$ got negated – so now it’s supposed to be negative instead of positive to make everything work. I mean, don’t ask me\!) Anyways, this is a pretty cool result it is\! So, like, for instance, if we start with the danger of a pare, so $a=1\ pare=5.11\ \frac{morts}{year}$, and from there we drop by this function, then we get a likelihood of immortality of ${S}_{\infty }=4.1%$. I mean, not a lot – but something nonetheless\! (Especially for a pare to start\! Jeez\!)  
Yeah, I mean – I drank coffee for the first time this morning, so I don’t know if you can tell the difference in my workflow or not – if there even is one. Just jotting this note down so we have the data and stuff. Anyways, peace out home slices\!

## **Shorter and Longer Golden Treks than Us**

### *Sunday, February 6, 2022, 6:12 PM EST*

I’ve been theorizing for a while now about how a notably shorter Golden Trek than us would likely be an Imperfection Magnitude Drop, but I want to take this time, now, to explain exactly why, and maybe even throw in a few extra mathematical goodies in the process.  
I want to start by considering what I talked about [in this entry](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.1bgx2mw42p0o). Why did the Delta Miracle take so long? This time, what I’m thinking about just now, is that not only is it crazy that the Delta Miracle took so long on the one hand, but the fact that the pressure from Doomsday Departure is involved makes things even crazier. I mean, you always have this background danger of Doomsday Departure, and while, sure, it varies here and there, it’s pretty much constant overall. Why? Because, er, it wouldn’t have any reason *not* to be\!  
So, let’s imagine, for a minute, that we could shave $t$ hundred million years off of the time between the dawn of life, and the Delta Miracle, or in other words, if, say the real-life Delta Miracle happened $2\ billion\ years\ ago$, then we would imagine that it happened $\left({2\ billion+t\times 100\ million}\right)\ years\ ago$. Got it? If we apply my fourth postulate of the Optimal Earth Conjecture, (and yes, I’ve named the postulates now\! See my scientific paper for more details\!), then in doing this transformation, we’re making the Optimality go down, (other than that tiny unknown value of $t$ which would technically *make it go up*, but obviously this is against the norm, so is kind of insignificant overall), or in other words we’re making the odds of the Golden Point go down. Now, if the Doomsday Departure danger has a value of ${\mu }_{𓇽}$, then having shaved off $t$ hundred million years, we’re sparing ourselves a factor of ${e}^{{\mu }_{𓇽}\ t}$ in Doomsday Departure, which as a sparing force heightens the probability of the Golden Point. But, because the probability has to go down overall, every other factor together, which we’ll call $r\left({t}\right)$, must follow $r\left({t}\right)<{e}^{{-\mu }_{𓇽}\ t}$. And of course, $r\left({t}\right)$ is a downhill factor, representing all of the worse off things that would result from making the Delta Miracle happen earlier\! Altogether, then, when we multiply the downhill $r\left({t}\right)$ by the uphill ${e}^{{\mu }_{𓇽}\ t}$, we get ${r\left({t}\right)\ e}^{{\mu }_{𓇽}\ t}<1$, which of course is equivalent to $r\left({t}\right)<{e}^{{-\mu }_{𓇽}\ t}$ conceptually\! Beautifully, too, this holds for any $t$ value, with the exception of a tiny wiggle room in either the positive or negative direction, where $t$ is between $0$ and some constant $k$, as described in the logic [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.mxu114ghls3q). Essentially, if you picture a bell curve of where you drop the Miracle, (described by $x$\-axis $t$), and the $y$\-axis of likelihood of the Golden Point, then Earth represents a random place in the area of this bell curve by the First Postulate, which by the Second Postulate has to be very quite close to the crest of the bell curve. Thus, if you move in the direction of the crest, (which could either be positive or negative – who knows), by that tiny little increment – then the probability will go up a little, and then settle back down as you traverse down the other side of the crest, until we reach the same level of probability as the Earth – and the difference in the $x$\-axis measure associated with this is just that $k$ value I wrote about above. Now, the thing is, $k$ has got to be quite small by the Second Postulate, so it’s hardly worth considering – I just wanted to write about it because *technically* it’s a thing, however miniscule. But, whichever direction it goes in, if you look at the opposite direction of $t$, it just goes straight down, and doesn’t sustain any of this up-the-hill hocus pocus, so there’s that, too. But all things considered, any significant $t$ you put through that relation $r\left({t}\right)<{e}^{{-\mu }_{𓇽}\ t}$, and you’re dealing with truth. Even something like ten million years, and you’re going to see the effects very clearly of this inequality. Also, now we also know that $r\left({t}\right)$ drops *at least* exponentially as you increase $t$, because it has to stay under the graph of an exponential, which by large values of $t$ is quite a bit smaller than for lesser $t$ values. If we’re dealing with some kind of Gaussian distribution in my bell curve idea, then we know that the probability ${r\left({t}\right)\ e}^{{\mu }_{𓇽}\ t}$ follows some ${r\left({t}\right)\ e}^{{\mu }_{𓇽}\ t}=a\ {e}^{-{\left({b\ t}\right)}^{2}}$, and hence $r\left({t}\right)$ would equal $r\left({t}\right)=a\ {e}^{-{\mu }_{𓇽}\ t\ -\ {\left({b\ t}\right)}^{2}}$. But this much, of course, is probably overly speculative. What we do know for a fact, though, is that $r\left({t}\right)<{e}^{{-\mu }_{𓇽}\ t}$, and hence $ln\left({r\left({t}\right)}\right)<{-\mu }_{𓇽}\ t$, which is another way of writing how if we imagined moving the Delta Miracle backwards in time further than it already is, the further we move it, the worse off the Golden Trek would be, and *in the least EXPONENTIALLY so\!*  
And, the last part of this entry: *why would significantly shortening the entire Golden Trek represent an Imperfection Magnitude Drop???* Well, the reason is because, if we shorten the entire Golden Trek by, say, a factor of $\frac{3}{4}$, then now every single process in the entire Golden Trek must occur in only 75% the time. Obviously, the most Optimal scenario there wouldn’t just be what happened here, but perfectly scaled down in time – rather, events which can afford to be shorter would take on some of the shortness, and allow events which need to take their time to be longer. But all in all – even this level of contraction would definitely be an Imperfection Magnitude Drop from what I can see, because too much is just lost. Even the most Optimal rearrangement of spans we can handle, and we’re causing just too many events to suffer. We already know by the Fourth Postulate that this is lower Optimality than Earth, just now I’m saying it’s *really* low Optimality\! 

## **Blunder Regarding Immortality Math**

### *Monday, February 7, 2022, 4:51 AM EST*

What a glorious day\! It looks like I just rooted out my first legit blunder\! Here’s what happened: I jumped the gun when I saw decreasing exponential danger leading to possible immortality, and went – *oh, this must be a property of exponentials\!* Thing is, I was wrong. It’s NOT just a property of exponentials – it’s a property of any danger curve whose area from one point through infinity is FINITE. That is, take the integral from the present through infinity, raise Euler’s number to the negative of that, and you’re set\!   
How I stumbled upon this, is I was dealing with the danger function of *1/(1+t^2)*, and I realized that if you run the right differential equation steps on that, it turns out you’ll get an answer of immortality probability at *e^(-π/2)*. So… yeah I guess. But, perhaps this is good news for the future, actually\! Now that *any area curve will do*, essentially if we can beat 1/x in curve decrease ability, we’ve got our awesomeness right there. This also means, as a future Golden Civilization, we may not have to worry about keeping our danger exponential, so long as we can keep a steady decrease quadratic on it\!   
I mean, it’s kind of embarrassing I didn’t see this before, especially considering my other form of the varying danger equation, which has the integral in the exponent like, right there on display, which should have told me this story immediately. Moreover, with the results I got from the wave danger functions, the result should have been even more set in stone, but funnily enough, it hasn’t been until now\!   
But anyways, this is a good result\! Negative area under danger function translates to longevity of civilization, such that once the decrease stops, and we get a danger which is nonzero but constant, only then does immortality become impossible. This is a great visualization of the phenomenon I touched on in the paper – where in the distant future, when starlight is no longer sufficient to fuel us, or whatever else ends up changing about the universe which counteracts the decrease in danger phenomenon – so long as we get a danger function which tends toward infinite area, even if that means just a sliver of danger away from nothing, or even a *1/x* kind of function – then only upon this do we put a timer on the longevity of the civilization, however staggeringly long that timer may be. But by then, I’m sure we’ll have other ways of looking / interacting with the cosmos and the fabrics of reality, so hardly something to worry about now, when our danger is perhaps trillions of times greater than it will be someday if things go right\! 

## **Continuous Standard Deviation**

Alright – I’ve officially had enough of not knowing what a continuous standard deviation formula looks like\!
