First of all, I’m going to derive a formula for that $\mu$ over there, which I assume is the mean of the function I guess. Well, if we have a function $f\left({x}\right)$, then the mean of that function between $x=a$ and $x=b$ is just going to be $\mu =\frac{\int\limits_{a}^{b}f\left({x}\right)\ dx}{b\ -\ a}$, so there’s our first equation figured out already\! Now for the rest of it – the standard deviation itself\! So, what we’re essentially doing, is taking every single item in our set, squaring its difference from the mean, and then summing all those squares together and dividing off the size of the population. I mean, because the size of the population is just the number of individuals in the set, I guess we can just think of this as the average of the squares of all the elements of the population’s difference from the mean, which itself we’ve already calculated above\! So, if we write the discrete version of that, $\frac{\Sigma {\ \left({{x}_{i}-\mu }\right)}^{2}}{N}$, then how now might we convert that to a continuous version? Well, if we call the function $g\left({x}\right)$ as the square of the difference from the corresponding $f\left({x}\right)$ to the mean, well then the average of $g\left({x}\right)$ is our desired equivalence\! Thus, that average comes out to $\frac{\int\limits_{a}^{b}g\left({x}\right)\ dx}{b\ -\ a}$. And of course, relating this to the discrete version, the standard deviation itself is just the square root of this, and thus we get a standard deviation written out as $\sigma =\sqrt{\frac{\int\limits_{a}^{b}g\left({x}\right)\ dx}{b\ -\ a}}$. But we’re not done yet\! The last step is to substitute for $g$ based on its definition, which is pretty easy – it’s just $g\left({x}\right)={\left({f\left({x}\right)-\mu }\right)}^{2}$, thus, the final answer for standard deviation of a continuous function is nothing but $\sigma =\sqrt{\frac{\int\limits_{a}^{b}{\left({f\left({x}\right)\ -\ \mu }\right)}^{2}\ dx}{b\ -\ a}}$. And that’s our desired answer\!   
Okay – with this in mind, I want to do a little test to make sure everything’s working properly – the normal distribution itself\! ## **Divergent Area Under Survival Graph**

### *Wednesday, February 9, 2022, 11:50 AM*

Here’s a quick idea: why not generate a “Survival” likelihood, (anti-Risk) function for which the area under it is not convergent, like a constant danger would make it be. I mean, how about $S\left({t}\right)=\frac{1}{t\ +\ 1}$, for instance? (Just so we can have the $1/x$ function, but where it starts at one like it should for a Survival function). What danger function would correspond to this?   
Well, since $\mu =-\frac{\dot{S}}{S}$, taking the first derivative of the Survival graph grants $\dot{S}=-\frac{1}{{\left({t\ +\ 1}\right)}^{2}}$, then, completing the rest of the expression, we get $\mu \left({t}\right)=\frac{1}{t\ +\ 1}$. Well that was a surprise\! They’re the same funcion\! Ha\!   
This actually makes sense conceptually – if the danger was increasing up toward infinity, then the survival graph would have to be *at least exponential*, because, well, that’s *more* extreme than anything constant. So, in order for the Survival graph to head toward zero, but be divergent when it comes to integrals and series, why, this fits the description perfectly\! 

## **Bounding the Background Doomsday Danger** {#bounding-the-background-doomsday-danger}

### *Wednesday, February 9, 2022, 6:00 PM*

We already know that there is the relation $r\left({t}\right)<{e}^{{-\mu }_{𓇽}\ t}$ from [a few entries ago](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.e6mhu4f51izn), so here’s a quick idea I thought of – why not actually run this in reverse, and figure out the bound on the doomsday danger part? First of all, we’ll do it with the simple $r\left({t}\right)$. If we were to somehow know $r\left({t}\right)$ well, then we could take that value, and use it to show that $ln\left({r\left({t}\right)}\right)<{-\mu }_{𓇽}\ t$, and thus ${\mu }_{𓇽}<\frac{ln\left({\frac{1}{r\left({t}\right)}}\right)}{t}$. So I guess that would put an upper bound on the Doomsday-Departure Background Danger\!   
Also, if we’ve only calculated *a portion* of $r\left({t}\right)$, such that there is a known amount $\alpha \left({t}\right)$, and an unknown amount $\beta \left({t}\right)$, where $\alpha \left({t}\right)\times \beta \left({t}\right)=r\left({t}\right)$, then well since all of these values are less than zero, it can be stated that $r\left({t}\right)<\alpha \left({t}\right)$. I was hoping to be able to compare $\alpha \left({t}\right)$ to ${e}^{{-\mu }_{𓇽}\ t}$, but sadly that looks to be impossible – since these are just any two old numbers which are greater than $r\left({t}\right)$, which don’t necessarily have to have any relation to one another besides that.   
Maybe the best way to find that upper bound on ${\mu }_{𓇽}$, then, is to just run approximation concepts on all kinds of different Miracles in the timeline, try to get $r\left({t}\right)$ for multiple different times, (and vitally, from multiple different approaches and methods), and then just average together like hell. If we have a large enough dataset, we might just be able to stick that upper bound on ${\mu }_{𓇽}$ – and upper bound it would indeed be, because the Survival Chance it generates has to remain above the internal-Earthen Optimality magnitude shift. 

## **Functions Which Dwell Above Exponentials**

### *Sunday, February 13, 2022, 1:30 PM*

I mean, jeez. I don’t exactly know what’s up, lately, but I’ve been in something of an intermission right now with my Math Doc, which is pretty ironic considering I’m just hovering below the 400 page mark. As of right now, Google Docs tells me I have a hardy 397 pages cooking, so three more to go for 400, baby\!   
Because of this intermission, I haven’t exactly been coming out with the most stupendous shit, but I do have a little fragment to tack onto my previous entry of [*Bounding the Background Danger*](#bounding-the-background-doomsday-danger), which is a concept I figured I might try and think about mathematically. What can you figure out using this principle?  
Well, here’s what I want to do – in order to figure out a function which always signifies a drop which is *more extreme than an exponential*, then I want to come up with the set of all functions, which we’ll call $f\left({x}\right)$, which satisfies one little property – $f\left({x}\right)>a\ {e}^{b\ x}$, like, for but one single function where $x>0$, $a>0$, and $b>0$. In other words, what kind of functions will always perfectly stay *above* but a single exponential whose $a,\ b>0$. If we could take our function, $f\left({x}\right)$, then it only gets to get the green check mark if we can find any single exponential where $a,\ b>0$ IN EXISTENCE, such that will stay *under* $f\left({x}\right)$ for every single comparison we can make on the positive side of the $x$\-axis. If every single exponential function where $a,\ b>0$ manages to get above $f\left({x}\right)$ at but a single point in all the positive $x$\-domain of possibility, then $f\left({x}\right)$ doesn’t get to be in this set, and it gets the red X instead of the green check mark. So, if we define $f\left({x}\right)$ as the set of all functions which get the green check mark, well then what can we know about that function, like, in terms of an equation???  
Hmmm. I think, to start, we should list some functions which work. For one, there’s ${f\left({x}\right)=e}^{x}+1$. We can name plenty of exponential functions which stay under it all all points, for instance, ${e}^{x}$ itself, or any $a\ {e}^{b\ x}$ for which $b$ is between one and zero, provided that $a$ isn’t too high. But, obviously, a single example is enough to give this $f\left({x}\right)$ to green check mark, and we’ll call that example just the ${e}^{x}$. Great\! What else? Well, there’s $f\left({x}\right)={x}^{x}$, which also gets the green check mark, because we can name, say, $\frac{1}{3}{e}^{x}$, which sure enough always stays below it. But, now let’s start naming some of the functions which *can’t* be $f\left({x}\right)$s, which I guess we’ll call $g\left({x}\right)$s. One $g\left({x}\right)$ is, like, any polynomial\! No matter how slow the exponential, as long as it’s positive and increasing, it will have to overtake your polynomial of choice. Consequently, there exists *no exponentials* at all which get to fall in the desired category, and some polynomial $p\left({x}\right)$ turns out to be one of the $g\left({x}\right)$s.   
Here’s an idea for cracking this code equationally – let’s find the largest value of $a$ for which some of these functions hold as $f\left({x}\right)$s\! For starters, with the ${f\left({x}\right)=x}^{x}$ example, depending on the $b$ value, the largest $a$ value which still works is, well, what? OH\! Oh, I got something\! I’m going to use logarithms to my advantage here. So, if $Q\left({x}\right)$ is our function in question, (in this case $Q\left({x}\right)={x}^{x}$), then if we take the logarithm of everything, then now we’re asking the same questions, except with lines instead of exponentials. That is, for a function $ln\left({Q\left({x}\right)}\right)$, what *line* stays forever below it. Okay? So, to get the actual boundary of things, let’s just find the equation of the tangent line\! That would be, well, a derivative to get the line slope of $\frac{Q'\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}$, and for the rest of the equation, we get $ln\left({Q\left({p}\right)}\right)+\frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}\left({x-p}\right)$. Now, in order to put our $a$ and $b$ in terms of this, let’s raise $e$ to the power of our line equation of $ln\left({Q\left({p}\right)}\right)+\frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}\left({x-p}\right)$, to turn things back exponential-ward. That gets us $a\ {e}^{b\ x}={e}^{ln\left({Q\left({p}\right)}\right)+\frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}\left({x-p}\right)}={e}^{\frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}x}\times {e}^{ln\left({Q\left({p}\right)}\right)\ -\ \frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}p}$, and thus it must follow that $a={e}^{ln\left({Q\left({p}\right)}\right)\ -\ \frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}p}$, and $b=\frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}$. Hence, we can figure out the whole spectrum of possibilities of highest-exponential equation just using this magical $p$ variable. And yes, this is just the “exponential of best fit”, here, which pretty much is documented territory for me already, (ironically enough, considering it took so much brainpower to get at this\!)  
Now, it must be the case for $a>0$ and $b>0$ as our previous given, which now translates to ${e}^{ln\left({Q\left({p}\right)}\right)\ -\ \frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}p}>0$ and $\frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}>0$, so let that work as your condition if you will\! So, essentially, just with this, if there exists a value of $p$, *greater than zero*, (because $p$ signifies the $x$ value for which the intercept happens), for which this holds, well then you win\! Green checkmark\! (I guess a way of weeding out situations which *don’t* work, by the way, is to just take the square root of these two suckers, and add those together to see if you get something real or imaginary\! The value of $a$ will wind up being non-real anyways for negative functions, so we can keep that as it is, and add it the the $b$’s square root, giving us a result of ${e}^{ln\left({Q\left({p}\right)}\right)\ -\ \frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}p}+\sqrt{\frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}}\in ℝ$. If we can find a single $p$ for which this works, well then great – you’ve got a $Q\left({x}\right)$ function which gets the green check mark\!)  
WAIT\! THE LAST PARAGRAPH IS WRONG\! It’s part of it, but I overlooked the fact that there’s more\! Truly, what needs to happen, is that once we get our tangent exponential given by $a={e}^{ln\left({Q\left({p}\right)}\right)\ -\ \frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}p}$ and $b=\frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}$, we need to find some value of $p$ for which ${e}^{ln\left({Q\left({p}\right)}\right)\ -\ \frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}p}+\sqrt{\frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}}\in ℝ$, but ALSO we need to make sure that said value of $p$ generates a tangent exponential function which always stays BELOW $Q\left({x}\right)$, except for the one point of course where they meet. The alternative is that it will always stay *above*, or maybe even spend some of the time above, and other time below.   
I mean, here’s an idea – if we want to see if a tangent line is above, or below a function, then we look at the second derivative, to get the concavity. Maybe we can do this with exponentials, here, by taking, say, the second derivative of the logarithm of $Q\left({x}\right)$, and hope that it’s positive, (signifying that the linear version of the exponential stays *above* a line at that point). The best idea I can think of to tell if this stays positive over the whole function, is to take the average-integral of the sign function of this value, and see if it equals one or not. That is, $\lim\limits_{{t} \rightarrow {\infty }}\int\limits_{0}^{t}\frac{1}{t}\ sgn\left({\frac{Q''\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}-{\left({\frac{Q'\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}}\right)}^{2}}\right)\ dx=1$. If it is even the slightest bit off, well then we’re dealing with a function which finds itself under its tangent exponential in a place. Here’s an even better idea, actually – we can build the integral away from zero depending on the severity of negative sign. That looks like this: $\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({1-sgn\left({\frac{Q''\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}-{\left({\frac{Q'\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}}\right)}^{2}}\right)}\right)\ dx$. If this value is not EXACTLY zero, well then we have a function which falls below the tangent exponential in a place, (provided the other conditions are met). Also, that works with positives, so I guess we could also flip it to get negatives, like so: $\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({sgn\left({\frac{Q''\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}-{\left({\frac{Q'\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}}\right)}^{2}}\right)-1}\right)\ dx$. This way, now if we take the square root, with $\sqrt{\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({sgn\left({\frac{Q''\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}-{\left({\frac{Q'\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}}\right)}^{2}}\right)-1}\right)\ dx}$, only when the tangent exponential falls below the function $Q\left({x}\right)$ does this not immediately fall to the imaginaries. Thus, if we add this to the scope of the other conditionals, with ${e}^{ln\left({Q\left({p}\right)}\right)\ -\ \frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}p}+\sqrt{\frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}}+\sqrt{\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({sgn\left({\frac{Q''\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}-{\left({\frac{Q'\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}}\right)}^{2}}\right)-1}\right)\ dx}\in ℝ$, do we get a conditional which holds all three statements\! Also, that first term, ${e}^{ln\left({Q\left({p}\right)}\right)\ -\ \frac{Q'\left({p}\right)}{Q\left({p}\right)}p}$, seems to only be real when $Q\left({p}\right)>0$, AND the second term seems to only apply, according with the situation of the first term, when the derivative of the function is positive, so we can kind of simplify the whole thing to $\sqrt{Q\left({p}\right)}+\sqrt{Q'\left({p}\right)}+\sqrt{\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({sgn\left({\frac{Q''\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}-{\left({\frac{Q'\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}}\right)}^{2}}\right)-1}\right)\ dx}\in ℝ$. Beautiful\! Actually – maybe I can make this even better, by broadening the first two terms more. We want for every $Q\left({p}\right)$ where $p>0$ to be positive, as well as for every $Q'\left({p}\right)$ to be positive, so I guess we can just do the same sign trick as the other one. That’s $\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({sgn\left({Q\left({p}\right)}\right)-1}\right)\ dx$ and $\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({sgn\left({Q'\left({p}\right)}\right)-1}\right)\ dx$ both equalling zero. That turns the whole thing into $\sqrt{\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({sgn\left({Q\left({x}\right)}\right)-1}\right)\ dx}+\sqrt{\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({sgn\left({Q'\left({x}\right)}\right)-1}\right)\ dx}+\sqrt{\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({sgn\left({\frac{Q''\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}-{\left({\frac{Q'\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}}\right)}^{2}}\right)-1}\right)\ dx}=0$. But, as we did with the other ones, can we find some kind of simplification gimme with the final one, there, based on what the other ones already add to the table? I mean, maybe, but I can’t see it at this moment, so I guess we’ll just stick with this formulation\!   
Sadly, this doesn’t code perfectly into Desmos, because quite a lot of the functions which satisfy this make overflow errors lol\! But, nonetheless, I feel like this is definitely a big thing to consider\! If $\sqrt{\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({sgn\left({Q\left({x}\right)}\right)-1}\right)\ dx}+\sqrt{\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({sgn\left({Q'\left({x}\right)}\right)-1}\right)\ dx}+\sqrt{\int\limits_{0}^{\infty }\left({sgn\left({\frac{Q''\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}-{\left({\frac{Q'\left({x}\right)}{Q\left({x}\right)}}\right)}^{2}}\right)-1}\right)\ dx}=0$ is satisfied for a function $Q\left({x}\right)$, well then that is a potential $f\left({x}\right)$ where $f\left({x}\right)$ is the set of functions which always remain above at least one positive, increasing exponential function\! ## **What Happens if I Die?**

### *Tuesday, February 15, 2022, 6:39 AM EST*

I was getting out of the shower this morning, and I was thinking: *how does the Golden Trek get affected if I just accidentally drop dead???*  
I mean, yeah, a pretty macabre thought experiment, but hey, welcome to the party I guess. Well, first of all, let’s say that the set of whatever I’m “supposed” to do, (assuming again that I have even a lick of importance in things), has probability of occurring ${p}_{M}$, (this set might range from my Miracles idea publication to something else in the future – just we’ll stick it all together in that probability). Also, there’s a ${p}_{A}$ probability that *I’m* the one who instantiates this set, rather than somebody else. This is where it gets a little tricky – because my intuition is telling me right now that this is something of an oversimplification, but whatever for now – I have something of a way of starting my math out really stupidly simple, and then gradually growing it into something that’s more fundamental. Lastly, if the Goodness directly following this set of important events is ${p}_{+}$, then if we, (again, oversimplification), assume that this set is pretty much a Prerequisite, then the probability of the Golden Point with me alive is ${p}_{M}\ {p}_{A}\ {p}_{+}$, and with me dead is ${p}_{M}\ \left({{1-p}_{A}}\right)\ {p}_{+}$. Got it? All I did there was just flip the little me factor to give it another version. What next, then?

Then, simply add them together, and after time $t$ for me to be alive or dead, the probability of the Golden Point is $\left({{p}_{M}\ \left({{1-p}_{A}}\right)\ {p}_{+}}\right)\left({1-{e}^{{-\mu }_{A}t}}\right)+\left({{p}_{M}\ {p}_{A}\ {p}_{+}}\right)\left({{e}^{{-\mu }_{A}t}}\right)$. ## **Evo-Density Take 2**

I want to give a quick second go to Evo-Density while I’m in the mid-night mood\!   
So, here’s the series that’s currently in my mind: $E\left({0\ \Delta t}\right)\ {e}^{m\ \left({2\ \Delta t\ -\ 0\ \Delta t}\right)}\ \Delta s+E\left({1\ \Delta t}\right)\ {e}^{m\ \left({2\ \Delta t\ -\ 1\ \Delta t}\right)}\ \Delta s+E\left({2\ \Delta t}\right)\ {e}^{m\ \left({2\ \Delta t\ -\ 2\ \Delta t}\right)}\ \Delta s$. This attempts to keep the derivatives to a minimum, other than [the previous version](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.316t646y8f6v), which kind of overdid it with them.   
So, let’s break down as simply as possible – what is this series telling us? Well, first of all, if we picture a continuous divergence down the line of the primate family tree, diverging in twos each time, then the new part that traces away holds a constant Evo-Density of $E\left({t}\right)$, and given $x$ more time, say, it will hold a population size of ${a\ e}^{m\ x}$, where $a$ is the original population size, so together that will give it a product Bio-Golden Capacity of the whole diverged clade at $E\left({t}\right)\ {e}^{m\ x}\ a$. Now then, we just need to figure out what that $a$ value is, the original Bio-Golden Capacity at the time of divergence. Now, using the more official variables of the series, after a unit time of $\Delta t$, how big of a chunk of divergence occurs exactly then? Let’s call this coefficient, $c$, say, such that this starting value can become $c\ \Delta t$. From here, if we imagine the function of the amount of direct divergence coming off that is allowed to happen after time $t$ as $s\left({t}\right)$, then taking the derivative at $t=0$ with $\frac{ds}{dt}$ gets us $\frac{ds}{dt}=c$ so that $ds=c\ dt$ and stuff. So, how much direct “species” number is pulled off of divergence directly after some time, as if we could trace a bounding line down the divergence? You know what – let’s keep it at $c$ for now, and we can always substitute something else later, since we know it should be constant regardless of the time, (because the Aurumans have roughly constant “species” count, at one)\!  
At this point, we can write $E\left({0\ \Delta t}\right)\ {e}^{m\ \left({2\ \Delta t\ -\ 0\ \Delta t}\right)}\ c\ \Delta t+E\left({1\ \Delta t}\right)\ {e}^{m\ \left({2\ \Delta t\ -\ 1\ \Delta t}\right)}\ c\ \Delta t+E\left({2\ \Delta t}\right)\ {e}^{m\ \left({2\ \Delta t\ -\ 2\ \Delta t}\right)}\ c\ \Delta t$, which then transfers over to sigma notation at $\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n}E\left({k\ \Delta t}\right)\ {e}^{m\ \left({n\ \Delta t\ -\ k\ \Delta t}\right)}\ c\ \Delta t$. From here, if we substitute for $n$, we get $\sum\limits_{k=0}^{\frac{t}{\Delta t}}E\left({k\ \Delta t}\right)\ {e}^{m\ \left({t\ -\ k\ \Delta t}\right)}\ c\ \Delta t$, and then if we factor out the $t$ in the exponent, we get ${e}^{m\ t}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{\frac{t}{\Delta t}}E\left({k\ \Delta t}\right)\ {e}^{-m\ k\ \Delta t}\ c\ \Delta t$. Now, last but not least, converting to an integral yields ${e}^{m\ t}\ c\ \int\limits_{0}^{t}E\left({a}\right)\ {e}^{-m\ a}\ da$. (Or so I hope\!)  
Now then, if we substitute $c=m$, also, just because that seems like a roughly fundamental value in the scope of all this, then this also turns into ${e}^{m\ t}\ m\ \int\limits_{0}^{t}E\left({a}\right)\ {e}^{-m\ a}\ da$, and I’m honestly pretty happy with that\!  
From there, if we reimplement the *Goodness from time after Huma expression*, ${\left({\frac{{G}_{M}}{{G}_{\eta }}}\right)}^{\frac{t}{66\ myr}}\times {G}_{\eta }$, then what can we find out? ## **Evo-Density Take 4**

Yep, I’m doing an Evo-Density reform again\!  
This time, I kind of want to be as narrowed down and intuitive as can be, so let’s give it a shot, I guess\! Two new variables for y’all: $t$, which represents the time of divergence, (in millions of years after Huma), and $T$, which represents what I call, “the catching time”, meaning it’s the point in the timeline, (again measured in millions of years after Huma) for which we see if a Golden Point happens before. That is, for an animal which diverged at time $t$, we try to see the likelihood of it evolving to the Golden Point before a time of $T$, which is like the cutoff point I guess\!   
So, if we look at an individual divergence, which has an original clade-size of $m\ \Delta t$, (measured in units species), then we have the amount of species in that clade after we count out $n$ levels of $\Delta t$ (from Huma) of $m\ \Delta t\ {e}^{m\ \left({n\ \Delta t\ -\ t}\right)}$. Remember, that $t$ there is the time at which the divergence happened\! Now, the other thing to consider, is that there is a certain likelihood of the world ending during this time by the Doomsday Departure Point danger, so if we want to make a true [Miro-Sim Environment](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.34u6eig3iyh9), we need to include this in our calculations\! Because we know that the divergence occurred at time $t$, I think this means that we know the Departure Point has not occurred up until that point, so the only feasible Risk window for it to happen is from $t$, up through our catching time of $T$. So, the number of species in the divergent clade at time $T$ would have to be $m\ \Delta t\ {e}^{m\ \left({T\ -\ t}\right)}$, and if we take the weighted average of the number of species in all scenarios, because there is this number of species only in the non-Departure Point outcomes, this means that that total weighted average comes out to $m\ \Delta t\ {e}^{m\ \left({T\ -\ t}\right)}\ {e}^{-{\mu }_{D}\ \left({T\ -\ t}\right)}$, where ${\mu }_{D}$ is the background Departure Point danger of the External type. Therefore, if each species has an Evo-Density of $E\left({t}\right)$ in this range, we get a Golden Point probability of $E\left({t}\right)\ m\ \Delta t\ {e}^{m\ \left({T\ -\ t}\right)}\ {e}^{-{\mu }_{D}\ \left({T\ -\ t}\right)}$ by the time of $T$.  
All this means that, at a time, (man, we need another letter), of ${t}_{a}$, the total likelihood of the Golden Point occurring by time $T$ is if we look at the Goodness value, ($E\left({t}\right)\ m\ \Delta t\ {e}^{m\ \left({T\ -\ t}\right)}\ {e}^{-{\mu }_{D}\ \left({T\ -\ t}\right)}$), of every single little divergence, *up until ${t}_{a}$ remember*, and add them all up. Oh, also – I just realized – I think with this, we’re only counting the species at the very end for consideration with $m\ \Delta t\ {e}^{m\ \left({T\ -\ t}\right)}$, but technically the better idea would be to count up *every* species which comes to exist over that span, living or extinct\! It’s got to be a fair game, after all\! Here’s the idea, then – elephants have a danger graph, according to Damuth’s Law, of about ${\mu }_{E}=\frac{27.5\ mpr}{{e}^{0.078\ t}\ -\ 0.6}$, whereas a Dark Era sauropod’s danger is more like ${\mu }_{B}=\frac{0.8598\ {e}^{0.86\ t}}{0.189945\ +\ {e}^{0.86\ t}\ +\ 0.000608377\ {e}^{1.72\ t}}$. Now, I was thinking about this for quite a while in the shower just now, and what I thought for the next step was this – we need to write a function to get the danger of the sauropod as a function of its weight, instead of its age\! If we do this, it’ll be very helpful, because it will allow us to find a lower bound for the danger of elephants at the same weight in the Bio-Paste scenario\! So, I ran some math in Wolfram|Alpha to get the [weight of sauropods as a function of age](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MgKYm2uNGVG0p16SHesfTPAvrlZkwDuVxdx4gR04_mA/edit#heading=h.jm5fyuhhnv73), at which point I took the inverse of that function to get age as a function of weight, and then simply substituted that into the danger function. What it gave me is kind of amazing – it’s this weird looking graph that is all vertical-asymptote-y near the origin, but then proceeds to turn into pretty much just a line as it heads away. I think I’ll paste an image of the graph of this function in here, just for your reference\!   
So, what I think the problem here is, is that any weights below three are actually not part of the domain, just by the way the sauropod graph functions with that serving as a rightward horizontal asymptote\! Therefore, all that we should care about in this function is that which happens beyond a weight of three, and you’ll notice pretty quickly that such things are pretty much linear. Thus, I think it’s safe to just make a line out of this, and call that our function, for that will save our life later on when we need to do crazy integration\! So, the function itself, without the line-transformation, is $\frac{2.56927\times 1{0}^{7}\ \left({w\ -\ 25955}\right)\ \left({w\ -\ 3}\right)}{\left({w\ -\ 7.75328×1{0}^{11}}\right)\ w\ -\ 1.08998×1{0}^{6}}$, ([Wolfram](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=%282.56927%C3%9710%5E7+%28w+-+25955%29+%28w+-+3%29%29%2F%28%28w+-+7.75328%C3%9710%5E11%29+w+-+1.08998%C3%9710%5E6%29)), and I think I’m going to take the line from where the danger hits zero, (which I’m assuming is the maximum possible weight a sauropod can reach according to the age-to-weight function originally: $25,955\ kg$), which passes from there, through the opposite side of the curve in quadrant 2, which you’ll notice is symmetrical about that line\! The danger on that function there is about $336.679\ millipares$, and this is spaced at double the distance away from the max weight as is the y-axis, and hence that’s a distance of $51910\ kg$. Hence, we have our rise over run just in this\! Our rise is $-336.679\ millipares$, and our run is $51910\ kg$, and so, hence, the slope of the line is $-0.00648582\ millipares\ per\ kilogram$. This can approximately be written as $-\frac{1}{154}\ mpr\ per\ kg$. Therefore, if we convert it back to *morts per year* as $-\frac{1}{30174}\ morts\ per\ \left({kg\ year}\right)$, and then draw the line out through point-slope form, we get a line of $\mu =\frac{25955\ -\ w}{30174}$, and that should do it\!   
Now, since the elephant weight-by-age equation is ${w}_{t}=2660\ kg\times {\left({1-{e}^{-0.078\ \left({t\ +\ 6.53}\right)}}\right)}^{3}$, it means that if the Dark Era came back in full through a Bio-Paste mechanism, then by substituting, the elephants’ new danger by age would become ${\mu }_{E2}>\frac{25955\ -\ 2660\ {\left({1-{e}^{-0.078\ \left({t\ +\ 6.53}\right)}}\right)}^{3}}{30174}$. ([Wolfram](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=%2825955+-+2660+%281+-+e%5E%28-0.078+%286.53+%2B+t%29%29%29%5E3%29%2F30174)). In millipares, by the way, this would be closer to ${\mu }_{E2}>\frac{25955\ -\ 2660\ {\left({1-{e}^{-0.078\ \left({t\ +\ 6.53}\right)}}\right)}^{3}}{154}\ mpr$. Also note that I wrote these as inequalities, because an Elephant is very likely *less fit for dealing with giant Theropods than a juvenile sauropod would have been\!* This is crazy, because as I can see in Desmos – the *safest* part of the Dark Era elephant’s life is still more than twice as dangerous as the *most dangerous* part of the New Era elephant’s life: at birth. Also, just so I can include the aging danger parts, based on what I could find from Google, the oldest elephant ever lived to age 89, so I think we can roughly give Elephants the same aging-decay negative Remedy as humans – which is a danger graph of $\mu =4.12×1{0}^{-5}\ {e}^{0.091\ t}$ in morts per year. ## **Departure Optimality Binary**

### *4/23/2022, 3:44 PM*

Look, I get that this is a bit of an oversimplification and or covered territory, but I want to ask a simple question here to apply the Fourth Postulate of the Optimal Earth Conjecture. I just flipped a coin to see if I would stay at the beach house where I currently am, or go on an errand with Viva, my Dad, and Juliana. The coin came out as a tails, which means I stay. I jokingly even flipped it a couple more times to confirm with Bear, and it got tails both of those times, too. And this gave me an interesting idea – obviously, in the situation here, it’s probably just an Empty Fluke, (oh – that’s a cool word – how about an *Empty Fluke* is a Fluke which is Rebetary to the Golden Point), but if I saw this kind of thing unfold on a major scale in Earth’s historical Golden Trek, and I would cry *Miracle*\! So, just to start out with the basics, let’s do a thought experiment here – if getting three tails in a row was of vital importance to the Golden Trek – so that’s a one in eight chance of success – then what would some of the other stats of things look like in order to satisfy the Fourth Postulate??? Specifically, if I *didn’t* get three tails in a row, and ended up making the inverse decision accordingly, then what would be the minimum odds of the Departure Point in that scenario to make the probabilistic risk of three tails in a row worthwhile for the Golden Trek’s Optimality?  
Well, here’s the big picture – if we call the odds of the Departure Point $x$ in the scenario where I go, which is directly linked to *not* getting the three tails, then this scenario, which altogether has a $\frac{7}{8}$ chance of happening, altogether has a probability of the Departure Point at $\frac{7}{8}\ x$. In fact, if we assume that the scenario where I *stay*, (meaning I got the three tails) has no Departure Point chance, then that $\frac{7}{8}\ x$ is the full likelihood of the Departure Point in the whole grand scheme of things. Now, what we want, by the Fourth Postulate, is for the Golden Trek to naturally select the greater probability of the Golden Point out of these two scenarios, so that obviously means the *lesser* Departure Probability. Hang on – though – I’m realizing now that if we look at it that way, things won’t work out in this case, because, well, it’s more a random distribution than a Fourth Postulate Application here. Don’t get me wrong, the 4th Postulate is a great tool when we’re dealing with heavy-fluke scenarios, but this clearly isn’t one of them\! So… the First Postulate will do here\!   
Let’s add up the total Golden Point situations first, for our denominator of things. In the situation where I get the three tails, the Golden Point makes up $\frac{1}{8}$ of all timelines. On the other hand, if I miss one of the tails, then the Golden Point makes up $\frac{7}{8}\ \left({1-x}\right)$ of all timelines. This means, of course, that the total Golden Point timelines are $\frac{1}{8}+\frac{7}{8}\ \left({1-x}\right)$, which we can also write by doing one minus our Departure Point figure from before I guess, too: $1-\frac{7}{8}\ x$. Yeah, that looks much better, (and yes, I realize that it’s just the distributive property version or whatever of the other one\!) So, that’s our Golden Point probability – but what proportion of it do the two scenarios make up? Well, the “three tails” scenario makes up $\frac{\frac{1}{8}}{1\ -\ \frac{7}{8}\ x}$ of it, simplifying to $\frac{1}{8\ -\ 7\ x}$ by the way, so if we look at the supplementary case, that gives us $1-\frac{1}{8\ -\ 7\ x}$, has to be *less* than it. Therefore, it follows that $\frac{1}{8\ -\ 7\ x}>1-\frac{1}{8\ -\ 7\ x}$. If we do some algebra, we get $\frac{2}{8\ -\ 7\ x}>1$, and then $2>8-7x$, which finally simplifies into $x>\frac{6}{7}$. And that is the number I was looking for\! It’s approximately $86%$, by the way, so our identity would be that, so long as the Departure Point has more than an 86% chance of occurring in the scenario where I miss the coin flips, and it would be actually *more* Optimal for me to hit all three coin flips as opposed to the contrary. How about we generalize this, now\!?  
Here’s the main idea: we have two scenarios, and in the first scenario, the Departure Point has a probability of ${D}_{1}$, whereas in the second scenario, it has a probability of ${D}_{2}$. If we have a $x$ probability of falling into the first scenario out of the two, then the odds of the Golden Point happening in the first scenario with respect to the total is $x\ \left({1-{D}_{1}}\right)$, whereas for the second scenario, this value comes out to $\left({1-x}\right)\ \left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)$. Therefore, the probability of the Golden Point at the moment of decision between these two scenarios is $x\ \left({1-{D}_{1}}\right)+\left({1-x}\right)\ \left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)$, and so therefore the proportion of all Golden Points which involve the first scenario is $\frac{x\ \left({1-{D}_{1}}\right)}{x\ \left({1-{D}_{1}}\right)+\left({1-x}\right)\ \left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)}$, and for the second, $\frac{\left({1-x}\right)\ \left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)}{x\ \left({1-{D}_{1}}\right)+\left({1-x}\right)\ \left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)}$. In order to be more Optimal, now we want the first to have greater probability than the second, so we want for $\frac{x\ \left({1-{D}_{1}}\right)}{x\ \left({1-{D}_{1}}\right)+\left({1-x}\right)\ \left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)}>\frac{\left({1-x}\right)\ \left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)}{x\ \left({1-{D}_{1}}\right)+\left({1-x}\right)\ \left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)}$, which (I guess those denominators were unnecessary in the first place, but whatever), means it must hold that $x\ \left({1-{D}_{1}}\right)>\left({1-x}\right)\ \left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)$. If we multiply everything out on the right side of the inequality, we get $x\ \left({1-{D}_{1}}\right)>\left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)-x\ \left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)$, and then if we swap a term, we get $x\ \left({1-{D}_{1}}\right)+x\ \left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)>\left({1-{D}_{2}}\right)$. ## **Revisiting the Original Dark Era Theorem**

### *5/3/2022, 5:00 PM*

I want to take this time to revisit my original Dark Era Theorem from 2020, where I identified the Dark Era using math, (while I was bored and sitting on the couch during the pandemic – you know how it was\!)  
Now, here’s the thing: this proof has always been purely intuitive, and I’ve never made use of notation beyond that until I made a little walkthrough video last weekend. However, even that didn’t dive into *everything* the intuition covered, plus I think it missed some fundamentals that weren’t property transferred over to the notational version. What does that mean\!? I’m gonna do it here\!  
First of all – real simple – we’re going to imagine a timeline split during the Triassic\! One one timeline, dinosaurs evolve, and on the other, they don’t. We know that we have to be at the end of the dinosaur timeline, because there were in fact dinosaurs in our past, and hence they didn’t just not happen and stuff, as the alternate timeline would suggest for itself. We’re also going to break up our timeline a little bit\! We’ll call the probability of the dinosaurs being wiped out $W$, which is a major Prerequisite to our existence and hence must happen in the timeline, and we’ll call the probability of the Golden Point at the dawn of the Cenozoic, (so directly post-Huma), something like $C$. The remaining probability in this timeline all falls in the Mesozoic, so we’ll identify it as $M$. Together, these three variables multiplied together gives the probability of us existing at the root of the dinosaur timeline. In order to push further back still, we also need to identify the probability of us landing on the dinosaur timeline at all at the event of the split, so let’s just call this $S$ for timeline split. Now, as of directly before the split, the probability of us existing, (assuming dinosaurs happen somewhere in between) is $S\ M\ W\ C$. All that’s left to identify is the alternate timeline. If we call the whole timeline as having a probability of generating the Golden Point at $B$, then since the probability of it occurring at the split is $1-S$, it follows that the odds of us existing as of directly before the timeline split, however with no dinosaurs in the middle this time, is $\left({1-S}\right)\ B$.  
Now, by the Mediocrity Principle, we would expect that our timeline odds of existence $S\ M\ W\ C$ is greater than our alternate timeline odds of existence $\left({1-S}\right)\ B$, and so $S\ M\ W\ C>\left({1-S}\right)\ B$. If we solve for $\frac{B}{M}$, to look closely at the Dark Era, then we get $\frac{B}{M}<\frac{S\ W\ C}{1\ -\ S}$. Because, due to the shallow water principle, (meaning the asteroid had to hit shallow water, so the odds of the dinosaurs dying had to be less than 5%, because 5% of Earth’s surface is shallow water), we can substitute $W<5%$ and so $\frac{B}{M}<5%\times \frac{S\ C}{1\ -\ S}$. Also, if we write this as $\frac{B}{M}<5%\ C\times \frac{S}{1\ -\ S}$, since $S<\frac{1}{3}$ is extremely likely, because there were three eras in the Phanerozoic, and during all three dinosaurs would have been extremely unlikely to occur – however they did occur during one of them, making one third of eras dinosaur producing – and so for $S<\frac{1}{3}$, it follows algebraically that $\frac{S}{1\ -\ S}<\frac{1}{2}$, and therefore $\frac{B}{M}<5%\ C\times \frac{1}{2}$. Also, if we rewrite the $5%$ as its equivalent form of $\frac{1}{20}$, and simplify, we get $\frac{B}{M}<\frac{1}{40}\ C$. Lastly, if we bring out the $M$ into $B<\frac{C\ M}{40}$ and then isolate it, we get $M>\frac{40\ B}{C}$. That is our final form\!  
$M>\frac{40\ B}{C}$  
Now for some of the little tweaks\! Because it MUST BE SO that $C<1$, we could equivalently write that $M>40\ B$, so that’s one little visualization. Also, though, because $M<1$, it follows that $B<\frac{1}{40}$, or in rounded percentages, $B<3%$. This literally means that if the dinosaurs never evolved, then we would have less than a 3% chance of existence – and probably a *lot* less than that too\!

## **Evolutionary Divergence of the Dark Miracle**

### *5/11/2022, 8:44 AM*

Just a quick one today: I was playing around with evolutionary divergence dates, and I stumbled on something kind of fascinating.  
If we think of a clade’s “size” as directly proportional to the time since it split, then we can call the “size” of the placental mammal clade right now as a roughly \~90 mya sized clade. Now, that being said, what if we looked at the Amniote clade from the event of the Dark Miracle? Amniotes *right now* feel extremely separated based on whether or not you’re looking at a synapsid or a sauropsid, but it couldn’t have always been this way\! What if you could go back in time to the late Permian, and view the clade size from there? Well, the Permian ended about 252 million years ago, and amniotes were about \~60 million years old then, so, wow\! If you could observe the Earth in the late Permian, during the glory days of the gorgonopsids and Therisophalians before all hell broke loose, then you would note that reptiles and synapsids then were just about as divergent as a human is from a lemur today\! Crazy\! Shocking, really. That is to say, observationally speaking, you would notice just about the same “group size and variety” then as primates now. Does that make sense? The span of a group, so to speak\! Here I was thinking Gorgonopsids, Therisophalians, and Cynodonts would have felt like alien races next to one another – but that’s only relative to *now*. Relative to *then*, it would be like saying a cat, a dog, and a bear\! Tiny little changes to their anatomy and genetics then are nowadays charted as revolutionary adaptations, which is funny because it demonstrates well the differences in scale just based on your viewing perspective.   
Anyways, from there, I wanted to ask how far we can stretch this concept. Why not all the way to the Dark Miracle??? Literally the beginning of Akeldama and bloodslavery, so surely the evolutionary divergence had to be really far by that point… right???  
But no – here’s the big reveal you can get through simple subtraction: at the time of the Dark Miracle, Ghasts were just about as evolutionary distant from Aurumans as we are from the other end of the mammal family tree. (Placental mammals, that is). THAT’S INSANE\! I mean, think about that\! By the end of the Dark Era, obviously that gap is going to grow wildly, and start to look like the unimaginable differences between us and the Ghasts in the modern day, but at the *beginning* of the Dark Era, we were still just about basal enough to be separated from Ghasts just as little as we are from sloths and elephants today. If you were alive and categorizing at that time, you might as well call Ghasts and Aurumans as part of the same intuitive clade. (I mean, yeah, sure we do that today already, with the word “amniote”, but nobody knows that word like the word “mammal” – literally when I accidentally misspelled amniote with my sausage fingers a second ago, and autocorrect had no clue what the hell I was trying to spell\! *Case in point\!*) So, yeah\! Just crazy\!  
This is also kind of giving me an idea – I think based on this subtraction logic I’m defining here, we can make a very simple little trick to gauge the divergence between two species. Not only is it intuitive, useful, and easy, but now that I think about it, it kind of links up with the DNA changes really well, based on when I measured how fast DNA changes with danger analysis a little while back. Ok, so here it is:  
You’re going to need just three variables\! The time at which species A lived, ${T}_{A}$, the time at which species B lived, ${T}_{B}$, and then the divergence time, ${T}_{0}$. The clade size, then, based on this, would be ${T}_{0}-t$, where $t$ is your reference time, or I guess ${T}_{0}-min\left({{T}_{A},\ {T}_{B}}\right)$ if you want to select the most recent of your clades in question – but I want to expand on that with this newer argument – all you’ve got to do, is take your first clade, loop up to the divergence point, with ${T}_{0}-{T}_{A}$, and then loop back down to the other clade, with ${T}_{0}-{T}_{B}$. It’s literally tracing the tree of life chronologically from one node to the other, reversing your direction of travel at the last common ancestor. If we sum the whole thing together, we get $\left({{T}_{0}-{T}_{A}}\right)+\left({{T}_{0}-{T}_{B}}\right)$, or I guess by some simplification, $2{T}_{0}-\left({{T}_{A}+{T}_{B}}\right)$. Very nice indeed\! We’ll call this value the “divergence”, with $div=2{T}_{0}-\left({{T}_{A}+{T}_{B}}\right)$. For me and an elephant, the divergence comes out to about \~190 million years would be my guess\!   
For me and the first Ghast, this number is, well… here, the ${T}_{0}$ is about $315\ mya$, ${T}_{A}$ is $0\ mya$, and ${T}_{B}$ is about, oh I don’t know, $235\ mya$. If we put these together, we get $div=315\times 2-\left({235}\right)\approx 400\ myr$. So, the divergence between me and a proto-Ghast is just about twice the divergence between me and an elephant\! My bet right now is that if you took the natural logarithm of the genetic similarity proportions, and you would get almost the same ratios between them, too\! Pretty cool\!  
And of course, if we run the numbers between the Aurumans and the Ghasts at the event of the Dark Miracle, and the divergence is only \~160 million years. Smaller than the divergence between me and an elephant, even\! However, at the event of Huma, and the divergence between the Aurumans and the Ghasts rose all the way to about 500 million years, which is actually larger than my divergence from the first Ghast\! That is, the Auruman divergence from the last Ghast is smaller than the Human divergence from the first Ghast\! Crazy\! In genetic terms, “the first Ghast likely shared more DNA with a human than the last Ghast did with the Aurumans at the close of the Dark Era”.

For a low variety, there would be more scenarios which approach the Optimal in Optimality, whereas with a high variety, less Golden Treks would approach the Optimal’s Suboptimality. As far as I can tell, this phenomenon would spread evenly through the whole percentile scale, as a kind of taper distance or something like that.

## **Third Law Through Probability**

### *5/27/2022, 11:51 AM*

Let’s use the probability proportion value of $\frac{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}}{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ +\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}$ – this tells you the proportion of Golden Points which involve some mission having happened, as of the timeline split of the mission.   
Let’s also make use of one of my old Rebetary formulas, from my Rebetary Spectrum, setup with ${Reb}_{N}\ =\ {Reb}_{\frac{m}{1-2m}}={Reb}_{\frac{1-M}{2M-1}}$. In this case, our maximum probability $M$ in the binary is $M=max\left({\frac{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}}{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ +\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}},\ \frac{\left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ +\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}}\right)$, which by taking advantage of the positivity of things can be factored as $M=\frac{max\left({{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A},\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}\right)}{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ +\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}$. Now – I want to see where this goes – the maximum can be rewritten with absolute values as I proved in a previous entry, so let’s give that a try\! So, it holds that $max\left({a,\ b}\right)=\frac{a\ +\ b\ +\ \left|{a\ -\ b}\right|}{2}$, so therefore $\frac{1-M}{2M-1}$ can be rewritten as $\frac{1-\frac{a\ +\ b\ +\ \left|{a\ -\ b}\right|}{2}}{2\times \frac{a\ +\ b\ +\ \left|{a\ -\ b}\right|}{2}-1}$, which simplifies to $\frac{1-\frac{a\ +\ b\ +\ \left|{a\ -\ b}\right|}{2}}{a\ +\ b\ +\ \left|{a\ -\ b}\right|\ -\ 1}$ and then $\frac{2\ -\ a\ -\ b\ -\ \left|{a\ -\ b}\right|}{2\ \left({a\ +\ b}\right)\ +\ 2\ \left|{a\ -\ b}\right|\ -\ 2}=-\frac{a\ +\ b\ +\ \left|{a\ -\ b}\right|\ -\ 2}{2\ \left({a\ +\ b}\right)\ +\ 2\ \left|{a\ -\ b}\right|\ -\ 2}=\frac{a\ +\ b\ +\ \left|{a\ -\ b}\right|\ -\ 2}{-2\ \left({a\ +\ b\ +\ \left|{a\ -\ b}\right|\ -\ 1}\right)}$. But that’s the general case – with the specific case, $M=\frac{max\left({{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A},\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}\right)}{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ +\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}$, that turns into $M=\frac{\frac{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ +\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}\ +\ \left|{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ -\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}\right|}{2}}{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ +\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}$, and then $M=\frac{1}{2}\ \left({1+\frac{\left|{1\ -\ \frac{\left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}}}\right|}{1\ +\ \frac{\left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}}}}\right)$. I’m also noticing we can do a lot of notational simplifying here by writing some ratio in either order $r$, which tells you the direct ratio of Golden Point space between the two missions. So $r=\frac{\left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}}$ works just fine, but if you feel like it, you could also write $r=\frac{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}}{\left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}$. That way, we get $M=\frac{1}{2}\ \left({1+\frac{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}{1\ +\ r}}\right)$. Very nice looking indeed\! Now for just $\frac{1-M}{2M-1}$. Let’s start with the denominator, because that looks easy – $2M=1+\frac{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}{1\ +\ r}$, and then $2M-1=\frac{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}{1\ +\ r}$. Great\! Then the numerator, with $1-M$, which just turns into $1-\frac{1\ +\ \frac{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}{1\ +\ r}}{2}$, or just $\frac{1\ -\ \frac{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}{1\ +\ r}}{2}$. In total, that gets us $\frac{1\ -\ \frac{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}{1\ +\ r}}{2}\times \frac{1\ +\ r}{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}$, which turns into $\frac{\frac{1\ +\ r}{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}\ -\ 1}{2}$. And that’s it\! Low and behold, using any Golden Point binary ratio you want for $r$, we get the Rebetality factor $\frac{\frac{1\ +\ r}{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}\ -\ 1}{2}$, which compiles itself into ${Reb}_{\frac{\frac{1\ +\ r}{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}\ -\ 1}{2}}$. Awesome\!   
Now for the application to the Third Law – remember, this can only truly be applied when the case is fully Rebetary, which I represent here with ${Reb}_{\infty }$. This happens when $\frac{\frac{1\ +\ r}{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}\ -\ 1}{2}\rightarrow \infty$, or in a more real-world practical sense, when $\frac{\frac{1\ +\ r}{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}\ -\ 1}{2}$ is a very large number. Another way of thinking of this is where $r\approx 1$, or thus ${p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\approx \left({1-{p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}$. All of this, of course, is hopefully intuitive anyways. There’s also the *Linked* case to consider, when ${Reb}_{0}$ is your answer, or in other words, $\frac{\frac{1\ +\ r}{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}\ -\ 1}{2}\approx 0$, being a very very small number. This happens only when, algebraically, $1+r\approx \left|{1-r}\right|$, which can apply for a very small $r$ or a very large $r$, which is to say that either ${p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}$ or $\left({1-{p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}$ is near to zero. This is equivalent to saying that either failing or succeeding this mission – one of them, depending on the circumstances – and you wind up with a near certain Departure Point. In other words, an Imperfection Magnitude Drop\! So, any Mission which has the chance of becoming an Imperfection Magnitude Drop if failed or succeeded will be marked with $\approx {Reb}_{0}$. In fact, one class of such Missions, a *Prerequisite*, which specifically would be an Imperfection Magnitude Drop if failed, thus follows this, meaning for any Prerequisite, you should expect a ${Reb}_{\approx 0}$. In fact, Miracles are a further subclass of this, so yet again, for any Miracle, you’re going to expect a ${Reb}_{\approx 0}$ score. This is about as far away as you can get from Third Law applicable Missions with their ${Reb}_{\approx \infty }$ scores.   
We can also do this with linkage, (which honestly might be a little more intuitive for Miracles and Rebetary Missions). This looks like this: ${Link}_{\frac{2\ \left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}{1\ +\ r\ -\ \left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}}$. This time, for a very large Link Value number, we’ve got a Prerequisite or Anti-Prerequisite on our hands, and for a very small number, you have something that’s pretty much Third Law worthy, in that it doesn’t affect the Golden Point one way or another. For all Miracles, the Mission’s Linkage Value is a very high number. And it looks like every Mission in the whole Golden Trek can be assigned a Linkage Value by this logic, which is kind of interesting\! Keep in mind that epic failures actually have high Linkage Values, just like their Miraculous antitheses. Maybe that means we should create another stat to measure “fails” as negative. That is, take the entire Linkage Value spectrum, and just negate it if it’s a non-Optimal mission\! For it to be a non-Optimal Mission, $r$ would have to be below 100% *IF* its numerator is the Optimal Mission of the binary, or *above it* if the negative is the Nonoptimal Mission of the binary. So, for this case, let’s just write it out the usual way again, with $r=\frac{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}}{\left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}$, assuming $A$ is the Optimal Mission. (This applies just to the next formulation, so everything before this, dealing with the more general $r$ is still valid).   
Now we can get $\frac{2\ \left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}{1\ +\ r\ -\ \left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}$ for the base Linkage Value, and then with the multiplied coefficient, that turns into $\frac{2\ \left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}{1\ +\ r\ -\ \left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}\times sgn\left({r-1}\right)$. This then becomes $\frac{2\ \left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}{1\ +\ r\ -\ \left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}\times \frac{r\ -\ 1}{\left|{r\ -\ 1}\right|}$, and then $\frac{2}{1\ +\ r\ -\ \left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}\times \frac{r\ -\ 1}{1}$. I guess the next step from there is $\frac{-2}{\frac{1\ +\ r}{1\ -\ r}\ -\ \frac{\left|{1\ -\ r}\right|}{1\ -\ r}}$, and then $\frac{2}{sgn\left({1\ -\ r}\right)\ -\ \frac{1\ +\ r}{1\ -\ r}}$. I guess we’re also going to want to reverse this again, since $r>1$ is often present here, into $\frac{2}{\frac{r\ +\ 1}{r\ -\ 1}\ -\ sgn\left({r\ -\ 1}\right)}$. And there you have it\! The way of measuring the “Score” of a Mission\! A very large value is a Prerequisite, a very negative value is an Imperfection Magnitude Drop, and a value quite close to zero is a Rebetary Mission, which can have the Third Law applied to it\!  
Also, just so I can put things back in terms of the probabilities of Missions rather than $r$, we know that $r=\frac{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}}{\left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}$, so therefore $r+1=\frac{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ +\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}{\left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}$, and also $r-1=\frac{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ -\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}{\left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}$. Therefore, $\frac{r\ +\ 1}{r\ -\ 1}=\frac{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ +\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ -\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}$. As for the $sgn\left({r-1}\right)$, or $sgn\left({\frac{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ -\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}{\left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}}\right)$, which I’m realizing due to the positivity of the scale factor $\frac{1}{\left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}$ thankfully equates to $sgn\left({{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}-\left({1-{p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}\right)$, and so $\frac{r\ +\ 1}{r\ -\ 1}-sgn\left({r-1}\right)=\frac{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ +\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}{{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}\ -\ \left({1\ -\ {p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}-sgn\left({{p}_{A}\ {G}_{A}-\left({1-{p}_{A}}\right)\ {G}_{a}}\right)$.

## **The High Contrast Earth Hypothesis**

### *6/8/2022, 9:33 PM*

This is the driving force behind the Second Law of the Optimal Earth Conjecture for a little under a year now, but I thought at this point I would give it a name, and perhaps try to isolate it and write it in relation to the Rare Earth Hypothesis itself. So, here goes\!  
Essentially what this tells us, is that the – stay with me here – “the logarithmic derivative of the Suboptimality of a Golden Trek with respect to its Optimality percentile is extremely high”. Note that this is kind of vague in a way – as extremely high, even though it does tell you a lot – isn’t technically perfectly explanatory. But, the Rare Earth Hypothesis is kind of quite similar and stuff, as it can be defined as: “the hyper-universal average volume of a region of space defined as being closer to one Golden Trek’s biosphere than another is extremely high.”

### *6/11/2022, 12:38 PM*

A’ight\! At this point, I want to switch gears a little bit, and talk about “Miracle Danger”. All it is, is swapping out that concept of “Miracle Probability” with a little bit more of an instantaneous version\! This way, we can support an infinite stream of Miracle potential, and examine timeline splits that way – which feels a little bit more natural in a lot of ways.  
So, first of all, we’ve got that pre-standing bell curve of sorts of the probability of the Golden Point given a Miracle happening at different times. We’ll also center the timeline right at the crest of that bell curve, which represents the optimal time for the Miracle to occur\!   
Also, we’ve got a constant “Danger”, (positive connotation version), of the Miracle happening at any given time. Pretty good so far\!  
And so now the question becomes, firstly, what is the probability of the Golden Point throughout a range of times? (That is, between times $a$ and $b$?) I mean, I’m thinking, in a discrete setting, it has to do with the probability of landing on some portion of the histogram, and then that times the probability it grants. Then, add all those individual values together, and presto\! If we upscale this to continuous, then every little bit has a probability of you landing on it of $\mu \ dt$, and also every little bit grants a Golden Point probability individually of some $f\left({t}\right)$, and so the combined probability of both happening is $f\left({t}\right)\ \mu \ dt$. I also want to just slightly adjust that danger value there for a moment – because once we start stacking a bunch together, I want it to tend to risk. The probability of falling between $a$ and $b$ is, by the relation of things, ${1-e}^{\mu \ \left({a\ -\ b}\right)}$, and so the derivative of this tends to what? Well, I guess we can write it as $\frac{d}{dt}\left({1-{e}^{-\mu \ t}}\right)$, which comes out to ${\mu \ e}^{-\mu \ t}$. Hence, this is a slightly more accurate way of writing that danger, so instead of having $\mu \ dt$, which stays constant over a range, we can get the better ${\mu \ e}^{-\mu \ t}\ dt$. Neat\! Also, with the other function, of course, we get ${f\left({t}\right)\ \mu \ e}^{-\mu \ t}\ dt$. This should tell us the probability of 1\) Landing on that infinitesimal time value, and 2\) Reaching the Golden Point from it. Awesome\! Thus, if we add the values together for every little one of them, and we get the total probability of the Golden Point\! That, of course, is just an integral. $\int\limits_{-\infty }^{\infty }f\left({t}\right)\ {\mu \ e}^{-\mu \ t}\ dt$ should come out to the probability of the Golden Point. So, what to do now… I mean, if we call $f\left({t}\right)=\frac{1}{\sigma \ \sqrt{2\pi }}\ {e}^{-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2\ {\sigma }^{2}}}$, (the normal distribution centered at zero), then now the integral becomes $\int\limits_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sigma \ \sqrt{2\pi }}\ {e}^{-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2\ {\sigma }^{2}}}\ {\mu \ e}^{-\mu \ t}\ dt$, or in other words, $G=\frac{\mu }{\sigma \ \sqrt{2\pi }}\int\limits_{-\infty }^{\infty }{e}^{-\mu \ t\ -\ \frac{{t}^{2}}{2\ {\sigma }^{2}}}\ dt$. According to Wolfram|Alpha, this comes out to $G=\mu \ {e}^{\frac{{\sigma }^{2}\ {\mu }^{2}}{2}}$. Very nice\!   
Also, just in case you need it, here’s a way to derive the standard deviation of the Miracle’s bell curve as a function of the probability of the Golden Point: $\sigma =\frac{\sqrt{2\ ln\left({\frac{G}{\mu }}\right)}}{\mu }$. Also… I wonder if we can define another quantity, given by $\varpi$ or something, which is equal to $\varpi =\sigma \ \mu$. Therefore, using that, we can get $G=\mu \ {e}^{\frac{{\varpi }^{2}}{2}}=\frac{\varpi }{\sigma }\ {e}^{\frac{{\varpi }^{2}}{2}}$. ## **Outlook Probability vs. Golden Probability**

### *6/23/2022, 7:48 AM*

This is a concept that has been hugely important to the scope of Golden Science since at least the earlier stretches of 2021, so I figured now was as good a time as ever to actually give it a name\!   
First of all, is *Outlook Probability*. This is the probability we all know and love, which calculates the odds of an occurrence with respect to the modern moment, in the scope of the sky of futures so to speak. That is, what “percentage” of all futures hold the occurrence, and that’s your Outlook Probability, (in other words, the same Probability they teach you in sixth grade math class).  
But then there’s Golden Probability. It functions in much the same way, except instead of looking at the entire stretch of futures to see where your probability of occurrence lands, Golden Probability only looks at the Golden Point futures\! That is, what “real estate” so to speak does your occurrence hold in the Golden Point? And *that* is your Golden Probability\!  
As a matter of fact, you can write these probabilities in terms of one another\! If you’ve got your Outlook Probability, $p$, then the Golden Probability is written as $g={p\ G}_{1}+\left({1-p}\right)\ {G}_{0}$, where ${G}_{1}$ is the probability of the Golden Point in the event that the occurrence happens, and ${G}_{0}$ is the probability of the Golden Point in the event that the occurrence *doesn’t* happen\! From this, we can also trace the equation backward by algebra and reach the reverse conclusion that $p=\frac{g\ -\ {G}_{0}}{{G}_{1}\ -\ {G}_{0}}$.

([Wolfram](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=%282+erf%28a%2Fsqrt%282%29%29%29%2F%281+%2B+erf%28a%2Fsqrt%282%29%29%5E2%29)). Wolfram|Alpha now gave me that this satisfies 50% at $a\ ≈\ 0.342398778571294...$, which in fraction form is just about one third of a standard deviation of the Miracle. *So*, half of all Golden Points have said Miracle trigger within a third of a standard deviation away from the Optimal Temporal Placement of the Miracle.

If we imagine that the Golden Trek is near-to infinitely long, then how many Nescecions would we expect it to have picked up by the time it reaches its Golden Point? Well, interestingly, the trend for this follows a perfect geometric series of ½. Here’s the pattern: for some number of Nescecoins, $n$, the proportion of successful Golden Treks which contain that exact number of Nescecoins is ${2}^{-\left({n\ +\ 1}\right)}$. For instance, half of the Golden Points had zero Nescecoins, a quarter had one single Nescecion, an eighth had two of them, a sixteenth had three of them, and so on\! Kind of fascinating to wrap your head around, eh\!?  
Here’s the actual algebraic expression that led to this conclusion:  
Where $p\left({t,\ n}\right)={\left({1-{e}^{-\mu \ t}}\right)}^{n}-{\left({1-{e}^{-\mu \ t}}\right)}^{n\ +\ 1}$ is the Outlook Probability of obtaining exactly $n$ Nescecoins before time $t$, the Golden Probability of attaining that number of Nescecions $n$ is $g\left({n}\right)=\lim\limits_{{t} \rightarrow {\infty }}\frac{p\left({t,\ n}\right)\ {2}^{-n}}{\sum\limits_{k\ =\ 0}^{\infty }p\left({t,\ k}\right)\ {2}^{-k}}$.   
$g\left({n}\right)=\lim\limits_{{t} \rightarrow {\infty }}\frac{p\left({t,\ n}\right)\ {2}^{-n}}{\sum\limits_{k\ =\ 0}^{\infty }p\left({t,\ k}\right)\ {2}^{-k}}:\ p\left({t,\ n}\right)={\left({1-{e}^{-\mu \ t}}\right)}^{n}-{\left({1-{e}^{-\mu \ t}}\right)}^{n\ +\ 1}{\ }$  
This, as I said before, comes out to $g\left({n}\right)={2}^{-\left({n\ +\ 1}\right)}$. (Which I showed graphically).   
One of the points of doing this for me was to get a glimpse at the Background External Departure Danger, which, like this analogy, has a roughly constant danger, and gives a Departure Point in its failure, (as Nescecions do if they get tails). Essentially what the Background External Departure Danger does is tend all this Nescecion stuff to continuous rather than discrete, so if we imagine doing the same to $g\left({n}\right)={2}^{-\left({n\ +\ 1}\right)}$, we might get a similar result. If we call the percentile $x=g\left({n}\right)$, then $n={-log}_{2}\left({x}\right)-1$. Also I think the fully continuous formula would do away with that extra subtracted unit one, because of the whole limit toward zero thing, thus making $n={-log}_{2}\left({x}\right)$. If we call $a\ x$ a percentile with double the number of Nescecoins, such that ${-log}_{2}\left({a\ x}\right)=2\ n$, it follows that $\frac{{log}_{2}\left({a}\right)\ +\ {log}_{2}\left({x}\right)}{{log}_{2}\left({x}\right)}=2$, so therefore ${log}_{2}\left({a}\right)={log}_{2}\left({x}\right)$, and thus $a=x$. Therefore, if this generalization to continuous data is indeed valid, then squaring your percentile in the Optimality of the Golden Point will double the amount of accumulated Departure Probability from the Background External Departure Danger over the course of the Golden Trek. However, I still doubt this would be fully accurate in the complexity of real life, because after all there are tons of factors which can heighten and lower Optimality, besides just the BEDD. If BEDD alone were the arbiter of Departure Points, then technically the highest possible Optimality would coincide with the shortest Golden Trek. In that case, if you were in, say, the 20th percentile, then in order to double the amount of accumulated Departure Probability, you would have to square that percentile, getting you the 4th percentile. Hence, a Golden Trek at the 4th percentile, in this BEDD alone model, has *half as much Golden Point probability* throughout the full Golden Trek. To be clear – we don’t double the Departure probability – instead we half the Golden Point probability. Now, if the danger is constant, the other thing this means is that the timespan of the Golden Trek must increase\! So, in order to half the Golden Point probability, with a time-jump of $\tau$, the following equation must be satisfied: $2={e}^{\mu \ \tau }$. Therefore, $\tau =\frac{ln\left({2}\right)}{\mu }$. Now, if this happens every time you *square* the percentile, then if you put the percentile to the power of $n$, you would get $n={e}^{\mu \ \tau }$, and so therefore $\tau =\frac{ln\left({n}\right)}{\mu }$. This means that every time you put your percentile to the power of some number $n$, you are essentially adding the natural logarithm of $n$, over the danger time to your BEDD Golden Trek. This means that if our original percentile is $a$, and our secondary one is $b$, such that $n=\frac{ln\left({b}\right)}{ln\left({a}\right)}$, it follows that the additional time on a BEDD Golden Trek is $\frac{ln\left({\frac{ln\left({b}\right)}{ln\left({a}\right)}}\right)}{\mu }$, or in other words $\frac{ln\left({ln\left({b}\right)}\right)\ -\ ln\left({ln\left({a}\right)}\right)}{\mu }$.

Since $v=\frac{dx}{dt}$, this means that $\frac{dx}{v}=dt$, so $\sqrt{\frac{{a}_{🜨}}{2\ G{\ M}_{☉}\ \left({1\ +\ \frac{x}{d}}\right)}}\ dx=dt$, and thus $\int\limits_{0}^{d}\sqrt{\frac{{a}_{🜨}}{2\ G{\ M}_{☉}\ \left({1\ +\ \frac{x}{d}}\right)}}\ dx=\int\limits_{{t}_{start}}^{{t}_{end}}dt$.

If you detect which slit it goes through, then now our ethus knew that piece of information about it then, so it can only go through one slit to satisfy the ethus, and thus that much of its superposition is taken out of the picture. I like the word “compress” better, because really the art of these things regards removing elements of the superposition in the future which are definitively explained by the ethus. This means that beyond the actual measurement of which slit it goes through, there is still a superposition, just this time it regards all possible locations that can be reached from that slit. The point is, superpositions are totally valid, and all that’s happening is you have to shave parts of that superposition off every time you add something to the ethus through observation \- but when you do this, you only shave those parts off at the moment of ethus addition, and actually not in the past \- which itself remains unchanged.   
The weird part of this is that, according to this logic, these effects of superposition don’t stop at the quantum realm, and in fact are not fundamentally based just on quantum particles.
